chapters.title: Mowgli's Brothers
paragraphs:
Now Rann the Kite brings home the night
That Mang the Bat lets free--
The herds are shut in shed and hut
While free till dawn are we.
This is the hour of pride and power,
Talon and fang and claw.
Oh, hear the call!--Good hunting all
Who keep the Jungle Law!
_Night-Song in the Jungle_

At seven o’clock on a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills, Father Wolf woke from sleeping through the day. He scratched himself, yawned, and stretched each paw in turn to shake the drowsiness out of its tips. Mother Wolf lay with her large gray nose resting across her four cubs as they squealed and tumbled about, and moonlight fell through the entrance of their cave. “Augrh!” Father Wolf said. “Time to go hunting again.” He was about to leap down the hillside when a small shadow with a bushy tail slipped across the entrance and whined: “May good luck follow you, O Chief of the Wolves. And may the noble children have good luck and strong white teeth, and never forget those who go hungry in this world.”

The visitor was the jackal--Tabaqui, the Dish-licker. The wolves of India despise him: he scurries about stirring up trouble and spreading tales, and feeds on rags and scraps of leather from the villages’ rubbish heaps. Yet they fear him as well. More than any other creature in the jungle, Tabaqui is likely to go mad; then he forgets that he ever feared anyone and races through the forest, biting whatever crosses his path. Even the tiger flees and hides when little Tabaqui goes mad, because nothing more shameful than madness can happen to a wild creature. Our name for it is hydrophobia; theirs is dewanee--the madness--and they run away.
“Come in, then, and have a look,” Father Wolf said coldly, “but you will find no food here.”

“None for a wolf,” Tabaqui replied, “but a dry bone makes a fine feast for someone as humble as I am. Who are we, the Gidur-log [the jackal people], to be choosy?” He hurried to the rear of the cave, found a buck’s bone with a little meat still clinging to it, and settled down happily to crunch its end.

“My warmest thanks for such a fine meal,” he said, licking his lips. “What beautiful noble children! What great big eyes they have! And still so young! Truly, truly, I should have remembered that kings’ children are men from the moment they are born.”
Tabaqui knew perfectly well, as everyone did, that praising children to their faces brings the worst of luck. The discomfort on Mother and Father Wolf’s faces delighted him.
He remained sitting there, enjoying the trouble he had stirred up, before adding spitefully:
“Shere Khan, the Big One, has moved to new hunting grounds. He tells me he means to hunt in these hills through the coming moon.”
This Shere Khan was the tiger living twenty miles off, beside the Waingunga River.

“He has no right!” Father Wolf burst out angrily--“The Law of the Jungle gives him no right to move his home without proper warning. He will scare away every animal worth hunting for ten miles around, and I--these days I have two to kill for.”

“There was a reason his mother named him Lungri [the Lame One],” Mother Wolf said quietly. “One of his feet has been lame since the day he was born. That is why he has killed nothing but cattle. The Waingunga villagers are angry with him now, so he has come to make our villagers angry instead. Long after he has gone, they will search the jungle for him, and when they set fire to the grass, we and our children will have to flee. We certainly have a great deal to thank Shere Khan for!”
“Would you like me to tell him how grateful you are?” Tabaqui asked.
“Out!” Father Wolf snapped. “Get out and go hunting with your master. You have caused quite enough trouble for a single night.”
“I’m going,” Tabaqui said softly. “You can hear Shere Khan down in the thickets. I could have spared myself the trouble of bringing the news.”

Father Wolf stopped to listen. From the valley below, which sloped toward a little river, came a tiger’s dry, angry, snarling, singsong whine: the sound of a hunter who has caught nothing and does not mind letting the whole jungle know it.
“What a fool!” Father Wolf said. “Starting his night’s work with a racket like that! Does he imagine our bucks are like those fat bullocks of his by the Waingunga?”
“Hush. He is after neither a bullock nor a buck tonight,” Mother Wolf said. “He is hunting Man.”

The whining turned into a humming kind of purr that seemed to come from every direction at once. That sound confuses woodcutters and gypsies who sleep outdoors, sometimes sending them running straight into the tiger’s jaws.
“Man!” Father Wolf said, baring every one of his white teeth. “Faugh! Aren’t there beetles and frogs enough in the water tanks, that he has to eat Man--and here on our own ground!”

The Law of the Jungle never gives a command without good reason. It forbids any beast to eat Man unless he is killing to teach his young how it is done; even then, he must hunt beyond his pack’s or tribe’s hunting grounds. The true reason is that killing a man will bring, sooner or later, white men riding elephants and carrying guns, with hundreds of brown men bringing gongs, rockets, and torches. Every creature in the jungle suffers after that. Among themselves, the beasts explain that Man is the weakest, least protected of all living creatures, so attacking him is against the rules of fair sport. They also say--quite rightly--that man-eaters get mange and lose their teeth.
The purring swelled until it broke into the tiger’s full-voiced “Aaarh!” as he charged.
Then Shere Khan let out a howl--a howl quite unlike a tiger’s. “He missed,” Mother Wolf said. “What has happened?”
Father Wolf ran a few steps outside. He could hear Shere Khan stumbling about in the undergrowth, muttering and mumbling furiously.
“The fool had so little sense that he leaped at a woodcutter’s campfire and burned his paws,” Father Wolf grunted. “Tabaqui is there with him.”
“There’s something coming up the hill,” Mother Wolf said, one ear twitching. “Be ready.”

A faint rustle came from the bushes in the thicket. Father Wolf crouched, gathering his hind legs beneath him to spring. And then, had you been there to watch, you would have seen something truly wonderful--a wolf stopping himself halfway through a leap. He had sprung before he could see what he was springing at; once he saw, he tried to halt. That sent him shooting straight upward, four or five feet into the air, before he came down almost on the very spot he had leaped from.
“Man!” he barked. “It’s a man’s cub. Look!”

Right before him stood a naked brown baby, just old enough to walk, holding a low branch for support--as soft and dimpled a tiny thing as had ever arrived at a wolf’s cave in the night. He lifted his eyes to Father Wolf’s face and laughed.
“Is that what a man’s cub looks like?” Mother Wolf asked. “I’ve never seen one before. Bring it over here.”

A wolf used to carrying his own cubs can hold an egg in his mouth without cracking it, if he needs to. Father Wolf closed his jaws over the child’s back and set him among the cubs without so much as scratching his skin with a tooth.

“So small! So bare, and--so brave!” Mother Wolf murmured. The baby was squeezing between the cubs to reach the warmth of her skin. “Ahai! He’s feeding along with all the others. So this is a man’s cub. Tell me, has any wolf ever been able to boast that she had a man’s cub among her own children?”

“I’ve heard of it happening from time to time, but never in our Pack, or within my lifetime,” Father Wolf said. “There isn’t a hair on him, and one touch of my paw could kill him. Yet look at him gazing up, without the least fear.”
The light of the moon vanished from the cave’s entrance as Shere Khan thrust his huge square head and shoulders inside. Behind him Tabaqui squeaked, “My lord, my lord, this is where it went in!”
“What a great honor Shere Khan pays us,” Father Wolf said, though anger burned in his eyes. “What is it that Shere Khan wants?”
“The prey I’m hunting. A man’s cub came this way,” Shere Khan said. “Its parents ran away. Hand it over.”

Father Wolf had been right: Shere Khan had leaped at a woodcutter’s campfire, and the pain in his burned paws had driven him into a fury. But Father Wolf also knew a tiger could not squeeze through the narrow cave entrance. Even in his present position, Shere Khan’s shoulders and front paws were jammed in the cramped space, much as a man’s would be if he tried to fight inside a barrel.

“The Wolves are free people,” Father Wolf replied. “Their orders come from the Head of the Pack, never from some striped killer of cattle. The man’s cub belongs to us--to kill, if that is what we decide.”

“You choose, you don’t choose! What is all this talk about choosing? By the bull I killed, must I stand with my nose stuck into your dog’s den to claim what is rightfully mine? I am Shere Khan, and I am the one speaking!”
His roar thundered through the cave. Mother Wolf shook the cubs away from her and leaped forward. Her eyes shone like two green moons in the darkness as she faced Shere Khan’s blazing stare.

“And the one answering is I, Raksha [The Demon]. This man’s cub is mine, Lungri--mine and mine alone! No one will kill him. He will live to run beside the Pack and hunt beside the Pack; and in the end, mark my words, you hunter of tiny naked cubs--you frog-eater--you fish-killer--he will hunt you! Now get out, or by the Sambhur I killed (I do not feed on starving cattle), you burned beast of the jungle, I will send you back to your mother lamer than on the day you were born! Go!”

Father Wolf watched in astonishment. He had almost forgotten winning Mother Wolf in an open fight against five other wolves, back when she ran with the Pack and the name The Demon was no empty compliment. Shere Khan might have stood his ground against Father Wolf, but against Mother Wolf he could do nothing. He knew her position gave her every advantage, and that she would fight until she died. Growling, he backed out through the cave entrance. Once he was outside, he shouted:
“Every dog barks when he’s in his own yard! We’ll see what the Pack thinks of raising man-cubs. That cub belongs to me, and my teeth will get him in the end, you bush-tailed thieves!”
Mother Wolf dropped back among her cubs, gasping for breath, and Father Wolf spoke to her solemnly:
“Shere Khan is right about one thing. We have to show the cub to the Pack. Do you still mean to keep him, Mother?”

“Keep him!” she panted. “He came here in the dark, all alone, naked and terribly hungry, and still he showed no fear! Look--he’s already shoved one of my own babies aside. That lame butcher would have killed him, then run back to the Waingunga and left our villagers to hunt through every den we have for revenge! Keep him? Of course I will keep him. Lie quietly, little frog. Oh, you Mowgli--for I am going to name you Mowgli the Frog--one day you will hunt Shere Khan just as he has hunted you.”
“And what will the rest of our Pack have to say?” Father Wolf asked.

The Law of the Jungle states plainly that a wolf may leave his Pack when he takes a mate. But once his cubs can stand on their own feet, he must present them to the Pack Council--usually held every month under the full moon--so that the other wolves can learn to recognize them. Once inspected, the cubs may run wherever they wish. Until a cub has killed his first buck, there is no excuse whatever for an adult wolf of the Pack to kill him. If the killer can be found, the penalty is death; think about it for a moment and you will understand why it has to be this way.

When the cubs had learned to run a little, Father Wolf waited for the night of the Pack Meeting and led them, Mowgli, and Mother Wolf to the Council Rock. This was a hilltop strewn with enough stones and boulders to hide a hundred wolves. Akela, the great gray Lone Wolf, ruled the entire Pack through his strength and cleverness. He lay stretched out on his rock, with at least forty wolves seated below him, in every size and color: old fighters with badger-colored coats who could bring down a buck alone, and young black three-year-olds who imagined they could. The Lone Wolf had been their leader for a year. When young, he had twice been caught in wolf traps, and once beaten and abandoned as dead; he therefore understood the ways and habits of men. There was hardly any talk at the Rock. In the middle of the circle of parents, the cubs tumbled over one another. Every so often an older wolf would approach a cub quietly, examine him closely, and pad silently back to his seat. Sometimes a mother nudged her cub right out into the moonlight to make certain everyone had noticed him. From his rock Akela called, “You know the Law--you know the Law. Look closely, O Wolves!” The worried mothers echoed him: “Look--look closely, O Wolves!”

At last Father Wolf nudged “Mowgli the Frog,” as they called him, into the middle--and as that moment arrived, the hair on Mother Wolf’s neck stood up. Mowgli sat there laughing and playing with pebbles that sparkled in the moonlight.

Without lifting his head from his paws, Akela kept up the same steady call: “Look closely!” From beyond the rocks came a muffled roar. Shere Khan was shouting, “That cub belongs to me. Give him here. What business do the Free People have with a man’s cub?” Not even Akela’s ears moved. He merely said, “Look closely, O Wolves! What business do the Free People have taking orders from anyone but the Free People? Look closely!”

Deep growls rose all around. A young wolf in his fourth year threw Shere Khan’s question back at Akela: “What business do the Free People have with a man’s cub?” Now the Law of the Jungle says that whenever a cub’s right to join the Pack is disputed, at least two members of the Pack must speak in his favor, and neither of those two may be his father or his mother.
“Who will speak for this cub?” Akela asked. “Who among the Free People will speak?” No one answered. Mother Wolf prepared for a fight that, she knew, would be her last if it came to fighting.

Then the one other creature permitted to attend the Pack Council stood on his hind legs and grunted. This was Baloo, the drowsy brown bear who teaches the wolf cubs the Law of the Jungle: old Baloo, free to go wherever he likes because he feeds on nothing but nuts, roots, and honey.

“A man’s cub--a man’s cub?” he said. “I will speak for the man’s cub. A man’s cub can do no harm. I’m no fine speaker, but what I say is true. Let him join the Pack on its runs and be accepted along with the rest. I will teach him myself.”
“One more voice is needed,” Akela said. “Baloo, who teaches our young cubs, has spoken for him. Who else will speak after Baloo?”

A black shape dropped into the circle: Bagheera the Black Panther. He was black as ink from end to end, though certain lights caught the panther spots on his coat like the rippling pattern in watered silk. Everyone knew him, and no one wanted to get in his way. He had Tabaqui’s cunning, the wild buffalo’s courage, and the recklessness of a wounded elephant. Yet his voice was soft as wild honey dripping from a tree, and his fur was softer than down.

“O Akela, and you Free People,” he purred, “I have no standing in this gathering. But the Law of the Jungle says that when there is a dispute over a new cub, and it is not a matter involving a killing, that cub’s life can be bought for a price. The Law puts no restriction on who may pay it. Is that correct?”
“Good! Good!” cried the young wolves, who are forever hungry. “Hear what Bagheera says. A price can be paid for the cub. That is the Law.”
“Since I have no right to address you here, I ask your permission.”
“Go on, speak,” twenty voices cried.

“Killing a defenseless naked cub is shameful. Besides, when he has grown up he may offer you better sport. Baloo has already spoken for him. I will add to Baloo’s promise a bull--a fat bull, freshly killed, less than half a mile away--if you accept the man’s cub under the Law. Is that so difficult?”

Dozens of voices broke out together: “Why should we care? The winter rains will kill him. The sun will burn him up. How can a naked frog hurt us? Let him join the Pack’s runs. Where did you leave the bull, Bagheera? Accept him.” Over the noise rose Akela’s deep call: “Look closely--look closely, O Wolves!”

The pebbles still held all Mowgli’s attention; he never noticed the wolves coming forward, one after another, to examine him. Eventually they all headed downhill to the bull’s carcass. Only Akela, Bagheera, Baloo, and Mowgli’s own family of wolves stayed behind. Shere Khan’s roaring still sounded through the darkness: he was furious that they had refused to give him Mowgli.
“Yes, go on roaring,” Bagheera muttered beneath his whiskers. “Unless I know nothing about man, a day will come when this naked little creature gives you something quite different to roar about.”
“We have done well,” Akela said. “Men and their cubs are very clever. In time, he might prove useful to us.”
“Useful indeed, when help is needed; no one can expect to remain leader of the Pack forever,” Bagheera replied.

Akela made no reply. His thoughts were on the fate awaiting every leader of every pack: strength drains away, weakness grows and grows, until the wolves finally kill him and another leader takes his place--only to be killed himself when his turn comes.
“Take him home,” he told Father Wolf, “and give him the training that one of the Free People should have.”
So Mowgli became a member of the Seeonee Wolf Pack, bought with a bull and backed by Baloo’s word.

Now you will have to let ten or eleven whole years pass by, and imagine for yourself the wonderful life Mowgli had among the wolves. Telling it all would fill any number of books. He grew up alongside the cubs, although of course they were adult wolves almost before he had reached childhood. Father Wolf taught him everything he needed to know and showed him what things in the jungle meant. Soon a rustle of grass, a breath of warm night air, an owl’s cry overhead, the scraping of a bat’s claws as it settled in a tree for a rest, or the splash of a tiny fish leaping in a pool spoke to him as plainly as the business of an office speaks to the man who works there. Between lessons he lay in the sunshine and slept, ate, and fell asleep again. If he was hot or dirty, he swam in the forest pools. If he wanted honey--Baloo had explained that honey and nuts tasted just as good as raw meat--he climbed to fetch it, using the skills Bagheera taught him. Bagheera would stretch out on a branch and call, “Come on, Little Brother.” At first Mowgli clung to the tree like a sloth; later he hurled himself from branch to branch almost as fearlessly as a gray ape. He also sat at the Council Rock when the Pack gathered. There he found that no wolf could hold his gaze: if he stared hard enough, the wolf had to look down. He took to staring at them for amusement. At other times he pulled long thorns out of his friends’ paw pads, since wolves suffer badly from thorns and from burrs caught in their coats. At night he went down the hill into the farmland and watched the villagers in their huts with great curiosity. Still, he distrusted men. Bagheera had once shown him a square box with a falling gate, hidden so cleverly in the jungle that he almost stepped inside, and explained that it was a trap. What Mowgli loved most was going deep into the warm, dark forest with Bagheera, sleeping through the whole drowsy day, then watching him kill at night. Whenever he grew hungry, Bagheera killed whatever came his way, and Mowgli did the same--with one exception. As soon as the boy could understand, Bagheera told him never to harm cattle, because a bull’s life had paid for his place in the Pack. “The whole jungle belongs to you,” Bagheera said, “and you may kill anything you have the strength to kill. But remember the bull that bought your place: you must never kill cattle or eat them, whether young or old. That is the Law of the Jungle.” Mowgli kept that rule faithfully.
He grew steadily bigger and stronger, as a boy is bound to do when he never realizes that he is being taught, and has nothing in all the world to worry about except what to eat.

Once or twice Mother Wolf warned him that Shere Khan could not be trusted and that one day he would have to kill him. A young wolf would have kept that warning in mind every hour of the day. Mowgli forgot it: he was just a boy--although, had he known any human language, he would have told you he was a wolf.

He kept coming across Shere Khan in the jungle. As Akela’s age and weakness increased, the lame tiger had made close friends with the Pack’s younger wolves. They trailed after him for leftovers--something Akela would certainly have forbidden, had he dared exercise his full authority. Shere Khan flattered them, asking how such splendid young hunters could bear to follow a dying wolf and a man’s cub. “I hear,” he would say, “that at Council you don’t dare look him in the eye.” Then the young wolves growled, their fur rising.

With his eyes and ears everywhere, Bagheera had learned something of all this. Once or twice he told Mowgli outright that Shere Khan would one day kill him. Mowgli only laughed. “I have the Pack, and I have you,” he answered. “Even lazy Baloo might land a blow or two to help me. What reason have I to be afraid?”

On one very hot day, something Bagheera had heard gave him a new idea. Perhaps the news had come from Ikki the Porcupine. Deep in the jungle, with the boy resting his head on the panther’s lovely black coat, Bagheera said, “Little Brother, how many times have I warned you that Shere Khan is your enemy?”

“As many times as that palm has nuts,” Mowgli replied; naturally, he had never learned to count. “Why does it matter? I’m tired, Bagheera. Shere Khan is nothing but a long tail and a noisy voice--just like Mao, the Peacock.”
“Yet this is no moment to sleep. Baloo understands that, and so do I, and so does the Pack. Even those silly, silly deer understand. Tabaqui has warned you as well.”

“Ho! ho!” Mowgli laughed. “Not long ago Tabaqui came and insulted me, saying I was a naked man’s cub who wasn’t even fit to dig pig-nuts. I grabbed him by the tail and swung him against a palm-tree twice, to give him a lesson in manners.”

“That was a foolish thing to do. Tabaqui causes trouble, certainly, but he would have told you something that affects you very closely. Open your eyes, Little Brother. Shere Khan does not dare kill you here in the jungle. Remember, though, that Akela has grown very old. Soon he will fail to bring down his buck, and that will end his leadership. Many of the wolves who inspected you at your first Council are old now too. The younger ones have learned Shere Khan’s lesson: a man-cub does not belong in the Pack. Before long, you yourself will be a man.”

“What is so different about a man that he cannot run beside his brothers?” Mowgli asked. “The jungle is where I was born. I have kept the Law of the Jungle. There isn’t a single wolf of ours whose paws I haven’t freed from thorns. Of course they are my brothers!”
Bagheera stretched his body right out and let his eyelids droop. “Little Brother,” he said, “put your hand beneath my jaw.”
Mowgli raised his strong brown hand. Beneath Bagheera’s soft, silky chin, where sleek fur covered the great shifting muscles, his fingers found a small patch without any hair.

“No creature in the jungle knows that I, Bagheera, bear that mark--the scar of a collar. But I was born among men, Little Brother, and among men my mother died, in the cages at the king’s palace in Oodeypore. That is why I bought your life at the Council when you were a little naked cub. Yes, my birthplace too was among men. I had never laid eyes on the jungle. Behind bars, they fed me from an iron dish. Then one night I felt that I was Bagheera--the Panther--not a toy for any man. A single stroke of my paw smashed their ridiculous lock, and I left. Knowing the ways of men made me more feared in the jungle than Shere Khan. Isn’t that true?”
“It is,” Mowgli said. “Every creature in the jungle fears Bagheera--every one except Mowgli.”

“Oh, you are a man’s cub,” the Black Panther said with great tenderness. “I returned to my jungle, and in the same way you must eventually return to men--the men who are your brothers--unless you are killed at the Council first.”
“Why, though--why would anyone want me dead?” Mowgli asked.
“Look into my eyes,” Bagheera said. Mowgli met his gaze without wavering. Within half a minute the great panther had to turn his head aside.

“There is your reason,” he said, moving one paw over the leaves. “Even I cannot hold your gaze, though I was born among men and love you, Little Brother. The others hate you because they cannot meet your eyes; because you are clever; because you have taken thorns from their paws--because you are a man.”
“No one told me any of this,” Mowgli said sulkily, his thick black eyebrows drawing together in a frown.

“What does the Law of the Jungle say? Strike before you make a sound. Your very lack of caution tells them you are a man. Be clever now. I feel certain that when Akela next fails to make his kill--and every hunt makes it harder for him to hold down the buck--the Pack will turn on both him and you. They will summon a jungle Council at the Rock, and then--and then--I know!” Bagheera sprang to his feet. “Hurry down to the men’s huts in the valley. Bring back some of the Red Flower they grow there. When the moment arrives, you will have a friend stronger even than me, or Baloo, or any wolves of the Pack who love you. Bring the Red Flower.”
The Red Flower was Bagheera’s name for fire. No creature of the jungle will speak fire’s true name: they all live in mortal terror of it and find a hundred other names to use instead.
“The Red Flower?” Mowgli asked. “I see it growing outside their huts at dusk. I’ll bring some back.”
“Now that is a man’s cub speaking,” Bagheera said proudly. “Keep in mind that it grows in small pots. Fetch a pot quickly and keep it close, ready for when you need it.”
“Good!” Mowgli said. “I’ll go. But are you certain, my Bagheera”--he put his arm around that magnificent neck and searched the great eyes--“are you certain Shere Khan is behind all of this?”
“I swear by the Broken Lock that set me free: I am certain, Little Brother.”
“Then I swear by the Bull that paid for me: Shere Khan will get full payment for this, and perhaps a little extra,” Mowgli said, bounding off.
“There is a man for you. A man through and through,” Bagheera murmured as he lay back down. “Oh, Shere Khan, no hunt ever brought worse fortune than your frog-hunt ten years ago!”

By now Mowgli was far away, racing through the forest with a burning heart. As evening mist began to rise, he reached the cave, stopped for breath, and gazed down the valley. The cubs were away. But Mother Wolf, lying at the back of the cave, could tell from the sound of his breathing that something was troubling her frog.
“What’s troubling you, my son?” she asked.

“Just some bat’s chatter about Shere Khan,” he called in reply. “Tonight I’m hunting down in the plowed fields.” He rushed through the bushes toward the stream on the valley floor. There he stopped short. The Pack’s hunting cries rang out, followed by the bellow of a Sambhur they were pursuing, then a snort as the buck turned to defend himself. The young wolves burst into cruel, spiteful howls: “Akela! Akela! Let’s see the Lone Wolf’s strength. Make way for the leader of the Pack! Leap, Akela!”
The Lone Wolf must have leaped and failed to get a grip: Mowgli heard his jaws snap shut, then a yelp as the Sambhur struck him down with a front hoof.
Mowgli waited no longer. He raced ahead, leaving the cries to fade behind him as he reached the fields surrounding the villagers’ homes.
“Bagheera told the truth,” he gasped, settling into a pile of cattle feed beside a hut’s window. “Tomorrow will be the same day of reckoning for Akela and for me.”

He brought his face up to the window to watch the fire burning on the hearth. During the night, he saw the farmer’s wife rise and feed black lumps into it. Morning came, with the mist cold and white, and he watched the man’s child pick up a wicker pot lined with a coating of earth. The child filled it with pieces of glowing charcoal, tucked it beneath his blanket, and went outside to look after the cows in their shed.

“Is that all there is to it?” Mowgli said. “If a cub can manage it, there’s nothing to be afraid of.” He walked boldly around the corner, faced the boy, took the pot straight from his hand, and vanished into the mist, leaving the boy howling in terror.

“They’re very much like me,” Mowgli said, blowing into the pot just as he had watched the woman do. “Unless I feed it, this thing will die.” He dropped dry bark and twigs onto the glowing coals. Halfway up the hillside he found Bagheera, with drops of morning dew gleaming on his coat like moonstones.
“Akela failed to make his kill,” the Panther said. “They would have killed him last night, only they wanted you as well. They searched the hill for you.”
“I was down in the plowed fields. I’m ready for them. Look!” Mowgli raised the pot of fire.
“Good! I have watched men poke a dry branch into that stuff, and soon the Red Flower blooms on its tip. Doesn’t it frighten you?”
“No. What is there to be afraid of? It comes back to me now--unless I dreamed it--that before I became a Wolf I used to lie beside the Red Flower. It felt warm and pleasant.”

Mowgli spent the entire day in the cave looking after his pot of fire. He tried putting dry branches into it to see what happened, until he found one he liked. That evening Tabaqui arrived and informed him, very rudely, that he was required at the Council Rock. Mowgli laughed so hard that Tabaqui fled. He was still laughing when he set off for the Council.

Akela the Lone Wolf lay beside his rock, showing that the Pack no longer had a leader. Shere Khan openly paraded back and forth with the wolves he had fed on scraps, enjoying their flattery. Bagheera settled beside Mowgli, who kept the fire pot between his knees. Once everyone had assembled, Shere Khan started to address them--something he would never have dared while Akela was still in his full strength.
“He has no right to speak,” Bagheera whispered. “Tell him so. That son of a dog will take fright.”
Mowgli jumped up. “Free People,” he called, “is Shere Khan now the Pack’s leader? What business does a tiger have in choosing who leads us?”
“As no leader has yet been chosen, and I have been invited to speak--” Shere Khan started.
“Invited by whom?” Mowgli demanded. “Have we all become jackals, groveling before this butcher of cattle? Only the Pack decides who will lead the Pack.”

Cries rang out: “Be quiet, you man’s cub!” and “Let him speak. He has obeyed our Law.” Finally the older wolves thundered, “Let the Dead Wolf speak.” Once a Pack leader fails to make his kill, he is known as the Dead Wolf for the rest of his life--which will be short.
Wearily, Akela lifted his aging head:--

“Free People--and you too, Shere Khan’s jackals--I have led you out to the kill and home again for twelve seasons. In all those years, not one of you has been caught in a trap or crippled. Now I have failed to make my kill. You know who planned it and how. You know how you set me against a buck whose strength had not been tested, to expose my weakness. A clever trick. You have the right to kill me here, now, on the Council Rock. So I ask: who will step forward and finish the Lone Wolf? Under the Law of the Jungle, I have the right to face you one at a time.”

Silence lasted a long while; none of the wolves wanted to face Akela alone in a fight to the death. At last Shere Khan roared, “Bah! Why concern ourselves with this toothless fool? He is going to die anyway! The one who has lived too long is the man-cub. Free People, he was my prey from the beginning. Give him up to me. I have had enough of this nonsense about a man being a wolf. For ten seasons he has disturbed the jungle. Hand over the man-cub, or I shall hunt here forever and leave you not a single bone. He is a man, the child of a man, and I hate him from the very marrow of my bones!”
More than half the wolves shouted back, “A man! A man! What does a man have in common with us? Send him back where he belongs.”
“So that he can turn every villager against us?” Shere Khan shouted. “No, hand him over to me. He is a man, and not one of us can meet his eyes.”
Lifting his head once more, Akela said, “Our food has been his food. He has slept beside us. He has driven prey toward us. Not a single word of the Law of the Jungle has he broken.”
“And when you accepted him, I paid a bull for him,” Bagheera added in his softest voice. “A bull may not be worth much. But Bagheera’s honor might be worth enough for him to fight over.”
“A bull you paid ten years back!” the wolves snarled. “Why should a heap of ten-year-old bones matter to us?”
“Or a promise?” Bagheera asked, drawing back his lip to show his white teeth. “You certainly deserve the name Free People!”
“A man’s cub cannot run alongside the jungle people,” Shere Khan howled. “Hand him over to me!”

“Except for his blood, he is our brother in every way,” Akela continued, “yet you would kill him here! I really have lived too long. Some of you feed on cattle. Of others I hear that Shere Khan has taught you to creep out on dark nights and steal children from villagers’ doorsteps. I know, then, that you are cowards, and cowards are whom I am addressing. My death is certain. My life has no value now; otherwise I would offer it in exchange for the man-cub’s. But there is the Honor of the Pack--that small thing you have forgotten since losing your leader. For its sake I promise this: let the man-cub return to his own place, and when my time to die arrives, I will not bare a single tooth against you. I will let you kill me without a fight. At least three lives in the Pack will be spared by that. It is all I can offer. Accept it, and I can save you the disgrace of murdering an innocent brother--one who had voices raised for him and whose place in the Pack was bought in accordance with the Law of the Jungle.”
“A man--a man--that is what he is!” the wolves snarled. Most of them started clustering around Shere Khan, whose tail had begun to lash.
“It rests with you now,” Bagheera told Mowgli. “There is nothing else we can do for you except fight.”

Mowgli rose to his full height, holding the fire pot. He stretched his arms and yawned straight at the Council, although rage and grief were burning inside him. True to their wolf nature, the wolves had never let him know they hated him. “Listen to me!” he shouted. “Enough of this yapping like dogs. You have said so many times tonight that I am a man--though I would gladly have remained a wolf beside you all my life--that I feel you must be right. So I will call you my brothers no longer. I call you sag [dogs], as a man should. You do not get to decide what you will or will not do. That decision belongs to me. To make everything perfectly clear, I, the man, have brought a little of the Red Flower that frightens you dogs.”
He hurled the pot to the ground. A few glowing coals caught in a clump of dry moss, which blazed up at once. The entire Council shrank back in fear as the flames leaped before them.
Mowgli pushed his dry branch into the flames until the twigs crackled and caught fire. Then, standing among the cringing wolves, he swung it over his head.
“You are their master now,” Bagheera murmured. “Spare Akela’s life. He has always stood by you as a friend.”

Akela, that fierce old wolf who had never once begged for mercy, turned a single pleading look on Mowgli. The boy stood naked before him, his long black hair flying about his shoulders in the burning branch’s light, while the shadows leaped and trembled around him.

“Good!” Mowgli said, slowly looking around them. “I can see now that you are dogs. I am leaving you for my own people--if they really are my people. The jungle has closed its doors to me. I must forget your language and your friendship. But I will show more mercy than you have shown. Since I was your brother in everything except blood, I promise that when I live as a man among men I will not betray you to them as you have betrayed me.” He kicked at the fire, sending sparks upward. “There will be no war among any of us who belong to the Pack. But before I leave, I have a debt to settle.” He walked straight up to Shere Khan, who sat blinking foolishly at the fire, and seized the tuft beneath his chin. Bagheera came after him, ready in case anything went wrong. “Stand up, dog!” Mowgli shouted. “Stand when a man addresses you, or I’ll burn that coat of yours!”
With the burning branch so close to him, Shere Khan flattened his ears against his head and squeezed his eyes shut.

“This cattle butcher said he would kill me here at the Council because he failed to kill me as a cub. Well, this is how men beat dogs--like this, and like this. Move one whisker, Lungri, and I’ll stuff the Red Flower down your throat!” He struck Shere Khan’s head with the branch. In sheer torment of fear, the tiger whimpered and whined.

“Pah! You scorched jungle cat--get going! And remember this: the next time I come to the Council Rock, I will come as a man should, wearing Shere Khan’s hide on my head. As for the rest of you, Akela is free to live however he chooses. You will not kill him: I forbid it. And I don’t imagine you will stay here any longer with your tongues hanging out, as if you were important creatures instead of dogs for me to drive away--like this! Go!” The branch’s end was blazing fiercely. Mowgli lashed out on every side of the circle, and the wolves fled howling, their fur scorched by sparks. Finally only Akela, Bagheera, and perhaps ten wolves who had supported Mowgli remained. Then a pain unlike anything he had ever felt began to ache inside him. His breath caught, he sobbed, and tears streamed over his cheeks.
“What is happening? What is happening?” he asked. “I don’t want to leave the jungle, and I don’t understand this feeling. Bagheera, am I dying?”

“No, Little Brother. Those are only tears, the sort that men shed,” Bagheera told him. “Now I know you are a man, no longer a man’s cub. From this moment the jungle really is closed to you. Let them come, Mowgli. They are nothing but tears.” And Mowgli sat weeping as if his heart would break, though he had never wept once in his whole life until then.

“Now,” he said, “I will go and live with men. First, though, I must say goodbye to my mother.” He returned to the cave she shared with Father Wolf and wept against her fur, while the four cubs howled in misery around him.
“You won’t forget about me, will you?” Mowgli asked.

“Not as long as we can still follow a trail,” the cubs answered. “When you are a man, come down to the foot of our hill and we will talk with you. At night we will come into the fields to play with you too.”
“Come back soon!” Father Wolf said. “Oh, clever little frog, don’t stay away long. Your mother and I are getting old.”
“Come back soon, my little naked son,” Mother Wolf said. “Listen to me, child of man: I loved you even more than I ever loved my own cubs.”
“I promise I’ll return,” Mowgli said. “And when I do, I will spread Shere Khan’s hide across the Council Rock. Don’t forget me! Tell everyone in the jungle that they must never forget me!”
The first light of dawn was showing as Mowgli walked alone down the hillside to meet the mysterious creatures known as men.
Hunting-Song of the Seeonee Pack

As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur called
Once, twice and again!
And a doe leaped up, and a doe leaped up
From the pond in the wood where the wild deer drink.
This I saw as I scouted alone,
Once, twice and again!

As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur called
Once, twice and again!
And a wolf slipped back, and a wolf slipped back
To carry the word to the waiting pack,
And we searched and we found and we bayed on his track
Once, twice and again!

As the dawn was breaking the Wolf Pack yelled
Once, twice and again!
Feet in the jungle that leave no mark!

Eyes that can see in the dark--the dark!
Cry--cry out to it! Listen! Oh, listen!
Once, twice and again!

chapters.title: Kaa's Hunting
paragraphs: His spots delight the Leopard: his horns are the Buffalo’s pride. Keep clean, for a hunter’s strength is known by the shine of his hide. If you find that the Bullock can toss you, or the heavy-browed Sambhur can gore; You need not stop work to inform us: we knew it ten seasons before.

Do not bully the stranger’s cubs, but greet them as Sister and Brother,
For though they are little and chubby, it may be the Bear is their mother.
“There is no one like me!” says the Cub in the pride of his earliest kill;
But the jungle is large and the Cub he is small. Let him think and be still.
_Maxims of Baloo_

Everything in this story took place before Mowgli was driven out of the Seeonee Wolf Pack, and before he took his revenge on Shere Khan the tiger. Baloo was still teaching him the Law of the Jungle then. The large, solemn old brown bear loved having such a quick learner. Young wolves learn only the parts of the Law of the Jungle that concern their own pack and tribe; the moment they can recite the Hunting Verse, they run off: “Feet that move without a sound; eyes that see in darkness; ears that hear the winds in their dens; and sharp white teeth--these are the signs of all our brothers, except Tabaqui the Jackal and the Hyaena, whom we hate.” Mowgli, though, was a man-cub, and needed to learn far more. Sometimes Bagheera the Black Panther wandered over through the jungle to see how his favorite was doing. He would lean his head against a tree and purr while Mowgli repeated the day’s lesson to Baloo. By then, climbing came almost as easily to the boy as swimming, and swimming almost as easily as running. So Baloo, the Teacher of the Law, instructed him in the Wood and Water Laws. He learned to recognize rotten branches and strong ones, to address wild bees politely when he found their hive fifty feet up a tree, to speak to Mang the Bat if he woke him in the branches at noon, and to warn the water-snakes before jumping into their pools. No Jungle People enjoy being disturbed, and any of them will readily attack an intruder. Mowgli also learned the Strangers’ Hunting Call. Whenever one of the Jungle-People hunts outside his own territory, he must call it aloud, repeating it until someone answers. Translated, it says, “Allow me to hunt here, for I am hungry.” The reply is, “Then hunt to feed yourself, but not for pleasure.”

You can see from all this how much Mowgli had to memorize. Saying the same thing a hundred times and more made him thoroughly tired. But one day, after Mowgli had been slapped and had stormed off, Baloo told Bagheera, “A man’s cub is still a man’s cub. He has to learn the whole Law of the Jungle.”
“Remember how little he is,” the Black Panther replied. Left to himself, he would have spoiled Mowgli completely. “How do you expect that small head to hold all those long speeches of yours?”
“Is any creature in the jungle too small to be killed? No. That is the reason I teach him all this, and the reason I give him a very gentle slap when he forgets.”
“Gentle!” Bagheera grunted. “What would you know about being gentle, old Iron-feet? Today his face is covered in bruises from your--gentleness. Ugh.”

“Far better for me to bruise him from head to foot, because I love him, than for him to get hurt because he knows no better,” Baloo said with deep earnestness. “I am teaching him the Master Words of the Jungle now. They will keep him safe among the birds, the Snake People, and every four-footed hunter outside his own pack. If only he remembers the words, he can claim protection from everyone in the jungle. Surely that is worth a few blows?”

“Then make certain you don’t kill the man-cub while you’re teaching him. He isn’t a tree trunk for sharpening those blunt claws of yours. But what are these Master Words? Usually I give help instead of asking for it”--Bagheera extended a paw and admired its steel-blue claws, sharp as chisels that could rip things apart--“but I would still like to hear them.”
“I’ll call Mowgli over and let him repeat them--if he chooses to. Come here, Little Brother!”

“My head is buzzing like a tree full of bees,” a sulky little voice said above them. Mowgli slid down a tree trunk, full of anger and resentment. As his feet touched the earth, he added, “I’m coming for Bagheera’s sake, not yours, fat old Baloo!”
“It makes no difference to me,” Baloo said, though it saddened and wounded him. “Tell Bagheera the Master Words of the Jungle, then--the ones I taught you today.”
“Which people’s Master Words?” Mowgli asked, pleased to have a chance to show off. “There are many languages in the jungle, and I know every one.”

“You know a little, and no more than a little. You see, Bagheera, they never thank the one who teaches them. Not a single little wolf has ever returned to thank old Baloo for what he learned. Give us the Hunting-People’s words, then, great scholar.”
“We are of one blood, you and I,” Mowgli said, speaking in the Bear accent shared by all the Hunting People.
“Good. Give us the birds’ words.”
Mowgli said the words again, finishing the sentence with the whistle of a Kite.
“And now the Snake-People’s words,” Bagheera said.

Mowgli replied with a hiss impossible to describe. He kicked his heels up behind him, clapped his hands to applaud his own performance, and leaped onto Bagheera’s back. Sitting sideways there, he drummed his heels against the shining coat and pulled the ugliest faces he could imagine at Baloo.

“There, there! Surely that was worth a small bruise,” the brown bear said affectionately. “One day you will remember me.” Turning to Bagheera, he explained how he had begged the Master Words from Hathi the Wild Elephant, an expert in all such matters. Hathi had then taken Mowgli to a pool to learn the Snake Word from a water-snake, since Baloo could not make the sound. Now Mowgli was fairly well protected against mishaps throughout the jungle: no snake, bird, or beast would harm him.
“So there is no one left for him to fear,” Baloo concluded, proudly patting his large, furry belly.
“Except his own tribe,” Bagheera murmured. Then he raised his voice to Mowgli: “Mind my ribs, Little Brother! Why are you bouncing about like that?”

Mowgli had been tugging at the fur on Bagheera’s shoulders and kicking hard, trying to get their attention. When they finally listened, he was yelling at full volume, “And then I’ll have a tribe of my very own and lead them through the treetops all day.”
“What silly new notion have you dreamed up now, little dreamer?” Bagheera asked.
“Yes, and I’ll throw dirt and branches at old Baloo,” Mowgli continued. “They’ve promised I can. Ah!”
“Whoof!” With one great paw Baloo swept Mowgli off Bagheera’s back. Lying between those enormous front paws, the boy could see how angry the Bear was.
“Mowgli,” Baloo said, “you have been speaking to the Bandar-log--to the Monkey People.”
Mowgli glanced toward Bagheera, wondering whether the Panther was angry as well. His eyes had gone hard as pieces of jade.
“You have been among the Monkey People--the gray apes, who live without any law and eat anything at all. You should be deeply ashamed.”
“When Baloo hurt my head,” Mowgli said, still lying on his back, “I went off on my own. The gray apes climbed down and felt sorry for me. Nobody else cared.” He gave a small sniffle.
“The Monkey People’s pity!” Baloo snorted. “As peaceful as a mountain stream! As cool as the summer sun! What happened next, man-cub?”

“Then--then they gave me nuts and nice things to eat. And they--they held me in their arms and took me right to the treetops. They told me I was their blood brother, only without a tail, and that one day I ought to lead them.”
“They have no one to lead them,” Bagheera said. “That is a lie. Lying is what they have always done.”

“They treated me very kindly and invited me back. Why has no one ever taken me to meet the Monkey People? They stand upright on their feet like me. They don’t slap me with hard paws. They spend the whole day playing. Let me stand up! Baloo, you’re cruel--let me up! I’m going back to play with them.”

“Listen to me, man-cub,” the Bear said, his voice rumbling like thunder on a sultry night. “I have taught you the whole Law of the Jungle, for every jungle people--except the Monkey-Folk up in the trees. They have no law at all. They are outcasts. They have no language of their own; they steal the words they overhear as they lurk in the branches overhead, listening and peering down. Their ways are different from ours. No one leads them. They remember nothing. They chatter and boast, imagining themselves a mighty people about to accomplish mighty deeds in the jungle. Then a nut falls, they start laughing, and it all slips their minds. We jungle people have nothing to do with them. We never drink at their drinking places, never go where they go, never hunt where they hunt, never die where they die. Before today, have you ever once heard me mention the Bandar-log?”
“No,” Mowgli whispered. Now that Baloo had stopped speaking, the forest seemed utterly quiet.

“The Jungle-People neither speak of them nor think about them. There are crowds of them, all wicked, filthy, and without shame. If they can hold on to any wish at all, it is the wish to make the Jungle People notice them. We refuse to notice, even when they pelt our heads with nuts and filth.”

The words were hardly out of his mouth before nuts and twigs rattled down among the branches. High overhead, in the slender treetops, they heard coughing, howling, and the sounds of angry monkeys leaping about.
“The Jungle-People must have nothing to do with the Monkey-People,” Baloo said. “It is forbidden. Remember that.”
“Forbidden,” Bagheera agreed. “All the same, I think Baloo ought to have warned you about them.”
“Me--me? How could I possibly know he would play with such filthy creatures? The Monkey People! Faugh!”

Another shower rained on their heads. The two animals trotted off with Mowgli between them. Everything Baloo had said about the monkeys was true. They lived in the treetops, and since beasts rarely look upward, there was ordinarily no reason for the Monkey People and the Jungle-People to meet. Whenever the monkeys came upon a sick wolf, however, or an injured tiger or bear, they tormented him. They threw nuts and sticks at any animal for amusement, hoping someone would pay attention. They howled and screeched meaningless songs, challenged the Jungle-People to climb their trees and fight, or launched savage battles among themselves over nothing, leaving the dead where the Jungle-People could see them. They were forever about to choose a leader and establish their own laws and customs. It never happened: they could not remember their plans from one day to the next. Instead they settled for a saying they had invented: “What the Bandar-log think today, the jungle will think tomorrow.” It gave them a great deal of comfort. No other beasts could get at them; equally, no other beasts would take any notice of them. That was why they had been so delighted to play with Mowgli, and so pleased to hear Baloo's anger.

They had planned nothing further--the Bandar-log never really plan anything. But one monkey thought of what seemed to him a wonderful scheme. He told the others that Mowgli would be useful in their tribe because he knew how to weave sticks into shelters against the wind. Capture him, and they could make him teach them. Being a woodcutter’s child, Mowgli had naturally inherited all kinds of instincts. He built little huts out of fallen branches without ever wondering how he knew what to do. To the Monkey-People watching from above, these games seemed marvelous. This time, they declared, they truly would have a leader and become the cleverest people in the jungle--so clever that everyone else would notice and envy them. Silently they followed Baloo, Bagheera, and Mowgli through the forest until the hour for a midday sleep. Thoroughly ashamed of himself, Mowgli fell asleep between the Bear and the Panther, determined never to mix with the Monkey People again.

The next thing he knew, little hands--hard, powerful hands--were gripping his arms and legs. Branches swept across his face. Then he was looking down through swaying limbs while Baloo’s deep shouts woke the jungle and Bagheera raced up the tree trunk, baring every tooth. Howling in triumph, the Bandar-log scrambled higher, onto branches where Bagheera dared not venture. “He has noticed us!” they shouted. “Bagheera has noticed us. All the Jungle-People admire our cleverness and skill.” Then they fled. No one can properly describe the flight of the Monkey-People through their world of trees. They have established roads and crossroads over hills and valleys, all suspended fifty, seventy, or a hundred feet above the earth. They can follow these routes even in darkness when they need to. Two especially strong monkeys seized Mowgli beneath his arms and swung away with him, covering twenty feet with each leap through the treetops. Without him they could have traveled twice as fast, but his weight slowed them. Though dizzy and sick, Mowgli could not help taking pleasure in that wild headlong rush. The glimpses of ground far below frightened him, though, and each dreadful jolt as a swing over empty space stopped short sent his heart into his mouth. His captors raced him up a tree until he felt its thin top branches bending and crackling beneath them. Then, with a cough and a whoop, they hurled themselves outward and down, catching the lower branches of the next tree with their hands or feet. Sometimes he could see mile after mile of silent green jungle, just as a man at a masthead sees miles of open sea. Then leaves and branches whipped his face, and he and his two guards plunged almost to the ground again. Leaping, crashing, whooping, and yelling, the entire Bandar-log tribe swept along the roads in the trees with Mowgli captive among them.

At first he feared they would drop him. Next he felt angry, though he had the sense not to struggle. Finally he began to think. He must get a message to Bagheera and Baloo: at this speed, the monkeys would soon leave his friends far behind. Looking down was no use; the upper surfaces of branches blocked his view. He looked up instead. Far away in the blue sky, Rann the Kite hovered and circled, watching over the jungle for something to die. Seeing that the monkeys were carrying a burden, Rann dropped several hundred yards to discover whether it was something edible. He gave a startled whistle as Mowgli was hauled to a treetop and cried out in the Kite’s language, “We are of one blood, you and I.” The waving branches swallowed the boy again, but Rann glided across to the next tree and caught sight of the small brown face reappearing. “Follow my trail!” Mowgli shouted. “Tell Baloo of the Seeonee Pack and Bagheera of the Council Rock.”
“Whose name shall I give them, Brother?” Rann had heard about Mowgli, naturally, but had never seen him before.
“Mowgli, the Frog. They call me the man-cub! Follow my trail!”

He screamed the last words as the monkeys swung him through the air. Rann nodded, then climbed until he seemed as tiny as a dust speck. There he hovered, his telescope-sharp eyes following the restless treetops as Mowgli’s captors sped onward.

“They never get very far,” he chuckled. “They never finish what they set out to do. The Bandar-log are forever pecking at something new. Unless my eyesight is failing, this time their pecking has brought them trouble. Baloo is no fledgling, and I know Bagheera can kill bigger things than goats.”
Drawing his feet up beneath him, he balanced gently on his wings and waited there.

Meanwhile, fury and grief had seized both Baloo and Bagheera. Bagheera climbed more fiercely than he ever had, but the slender branches snapped under him. He slid back down, his claws clutching handfuls of bark.

“Why didn’t you warn the man-cub?” he roared at poor Baloo, who was lumbering into a trot, hoping to catch up with the monkeys. “What good did it do to beat him half to death if you never warned him?”
“Hurry! Oh, hurry! We--we might still catch them!” Baloo gasped.

“At that pace! You wouldn’t wear out an injured cow. Teacher of the Law--beater of cubs--a mile of that waddling would split you open. Sit down and think! Work out a plan. Chasing is no use now. Follow too closely, and they may drop him.”

“Arrula! Whoo! Perhaps they have dropped him already, tired of his weight. Who would ever trust the Bandar-log? Pile dead bats on my head! Feed me black bones! Roll me into wild bees’ nests so they can sting me to death, and bury me beside the Hyaena, for no bear was ever more miserable than I am! Arulala! Wahooa! Oh, Mowgli, Mowgli! Why did I batter your head instead of warning you against the Monkey-Folk? Perhaps I have beaten today’s lesson right out of his mind. He may be all alone in the jungle now, unable to remember the Master Words.”
Pressing his paws against his ears, Baloo rocked from side to side and groaned.

“At any rate, he recited every Word correctly to me just a little while ago,” Bagheera said impatiently. “Baloo, you have neither a memory nor any dignity. What would the jungle say if I, the Black Panther, rolled into a ball like Ikki the Porcupine and started howling?”
“Why should I care about the jungle’s opinion? By now he could be dead.”

“Unless they throw him out of a tree for fun, or kill him out of sheer boredom, I am not afraid for the man-cub. He is clever and well instructed. Above all, he has the eyes that frighten the Jungle-People. But the terrible thing is that the Bandar-log hold him, and because their home is in the trees, they are afraid of none of us.” Bagheera considered this as he licked a front paw.

“What a fool I am! Oh, what a fat brown fool, grubbing for roots,” Baloo cried, suddenly uncurling. “Hathi the Wild Elephant speaks the truth when he says, ‘Each has his own fear.’ The Bandar-log fear Kaa the Rock Snake. He climbs just as well as they do, and at night he carries off the young monkeys. Merely whisper his name and their wicked tails go cold. We must find Kaa.”
“Why would he help us? He has no feet, so he is not one of our tribe--and those eyes of his are thoroughly evil,” Bagheera said.
“He is ancient and very crafty,” Baloo answered hopefully. “Best of all, he is forever hungry. Offer him plenty of goats.”
“After a meal he sleeps an entire month. He could be sleeping now. And even if he is awake, what if he prefers catching his own goats?” Knowing little about Kaa, Bagheera was naturally wary of him.
“If it comes to that, old hunter, you and I together might persuade him to be sensible.” Baloo rubbed his faded brown shoulder against the Panther, and the two set out to find Kaa the Rock Python.

They discovered him sunning himself on a warm rock shelf that afternoon, admiring his splendid new skin. He had spent the previous ten days out of sight, shedding the old one, and now looked magnificent. His great blunt head darted along the earth while he looped all thirty feet of his body into extraordinary curves and knots, licking his lips at the thought of his next dinner.

“His belly is empty,” Baloo grunted with relief at the sight of the handsome brown-and-yellow mottled skin. “Watch out, Bagheera! His sight is always a little poor just after shedding, and he strikes very quickly.”

Kaa had no venom; in fact, he rather looked down on venomous snakes as cowards. His power was in his crushing embrace. Once those massive coils wrapped around a creature, there was nothing more to discuss. “Good hunting!” Baloo called, sitting upright on his hindquarters. Like others of his kind, Kaa was somewhat deaf and missed the first greeting. Then he drew himself into coils, lowered his head, and prepared for anything.

“Good hunting to all of us,” he replied. “Oho, Baloo, what brings you here? Good hunting to you, Bagheera. At least one of us is hungry. Have you heard of any game about? A doe, perhaps, or even a young buck? I’m hollow as a well gone dry.”
“We’re out hunting,” Baloo answered casually. He knew better than to rush Kaa: the snake was much too large for that.

“Let me join you,” Kaa said. “An extra blow or two makes no difference to either of you, Bagheera or Baloo. But I--I must lie for days and days beside a forest path, then spend half the night climbing for the mere chance of catching a young ape. Psshaw! Tree branches have changed since I was young. Every one of them is a rotten twig or a dried-up limb.”
“Perhaps that great weight of yours has a part in it,” Baloo suggested.

“I am reasonably long--reasonably long,” Kaa said with a touch of pride. “Even so, the blame lies with this newly grown wood. On my last hunt I nearly fell--very nearly indeed. My tail wasn’t wound tightly enough around the tree, and when I slipped, the noise woke the Bandar-log. They called me some extremely nasty names.”
“Yellow earthworm without any feet,” Bagheera muttered through his whiskers, as if searching his memory for something.
“Sssss! Is that something they have called me?” Kaa asked.

“They shouted something like that to us last moon, but we paid them no attention. They will say absolutely anything--even that all your teeth have fallen out and you won’t tackle anything larger than a kid, because--these Bandar-log really have no shame--because a he-goat’s horns frighten you,” Bagheera went on in his sweetest voice.
Snakes seldom let their anger show, especially cautious old pythons like Kaa. Still, Baloo and Bagheera saw the great muscles used for swallowing swell and ripple along both sides of his throat.
“The Bandar-log have moved elsewhere,” he said calmly. “When I came out to bask today, I could hear their whooping in the treetops.”

“Those--those are the creatures we are following,” Baloo said. The admission almost choked him. As far back as he could remember, no Jungle-Person had ever confessed to taking an interest in the monkeys’ activities.

“Then surely it must be a serious matter, to send two such hunters--leaders in their own jungle, I have no doubt--after the Bandar-log,” Kaa replied politely, though curiosity was swelling inside him.
“Well,” Baloo began, “I am only the old and sometimes very foolish Teacher of the Law to the Seeonee wolf-cubs. As for Bagheera here--”

“He is Bagheera,” the Black Panther said, snapping his jaws shut. Humility was not something he believed in. “Here is our difficulty, Kaa. Those stealers of nuts and pluckers of palm leaves have carried off our man-cub. Perhaps you have heard of him.”

“Ikki told me something--those quills make him far too bold--about a man-creature being admitted into a wolf pack. I didn't believe him. Ikki is always repeating stories he has only half heard, and telling them extremely badly.”

“It is true, though,” Baloo said. “There has never been another man-cub like him. He is the finest, cleverest, bravest of them all--my own pupil, who will make Baloo’s name famous in every jungle. Besides, Kaa, I--we--love him.”
“Ts! Ts!” Kaa said, swaying his head from side to side. “I too have known love. I could tell you tales that--”

“Would need a clear night and full stomachs before we could properly appreciate them,” Bagheera broke in quickly. “Our man-cub is a prisoner of the Bandar-log at this very moment. We know that of all the Jungle-People, Kaa is the only one they fear.”

“They fear no one else. And they have good cause to fear me,” Kaa said. “What chattering, foolish, vain creatures monkeys are--vain, foolish, chattering creatures. Still, a man-creature in their keeping is unfortunate. They pick nuts, tire of them, and fling them away. For half a day they carry a branch, planning wonderful things to do with it; then they break it in half. I would not envy that man-creature his position. And they called me--‘yellow fish,’ wasn’t it?”
“Worm--worm--earthworm,” Bagheera corrected him. “And other things I am too ashamed even to repeat.”
“They need reminding how to speak of their master respectfully. Aaa-ssp! We shall have to help those wandering memories of theirs. Now, which way did they take the cub?”
“Only the jungle knows,” Baloo replied. “Westward, I think, toward the sunset. We were hoping you could tell us, Kaa.”
“How should I know? I catch them when they happen to cross my path. I don’t go hunting for Bandar-log, any more than for frogs--or the green slime on a water-hole, for that matter.”
“Up, Up! Up, Up! Hillo! Illo! Illo, look up here, Baloo of the Seeonee Wolf Pack!”

Baloo lifted his eyes toward the voice. Rann the Kite was gliding down, sunlight catching the raised edges of his wings. It was almost his bedtime, but he had searched the whole jungle for the Bear, failing to spot him under the dense leaves.
“What news have you?” Baloo asked.

“I found Mowgli with the Bandar-log. He asked me to bring you word, and I kept watch. They have carried him over the river to the monkey city--the Cold Lairs. They might remain an hour, a night, or ten nights. I have asked the bats to watch during the dark hours. That is what I came to tell you. Good hunting to everyone down there!”
“May you eat your fill and sleep soundly, Rann,” Bagheera called. “At my next kill I’ll remember you and save the head for you alone, best of all kites!”
“It was nothing, nothing at all. The boy knew the Master Word. There was no less I could do.” Rann wheeled upward again toward his roost.
“He remembers how to use his voice,” Baloo chuckled proudly. “Imagine someone so young remembering even the birds’ Master Word while they were dragging him through the treetops!”
“The lesson was certainly hammered home,” Bagheera said. “Still, I am proud of him too. Now we have to make for the Cold Lairs.”

All three knew the place, but few Jungle People ever visited it. The Cold Lairs, as they called it, was an ancient abandoned city, hidden and swallowed up by forest. Animals rarely settle where men have lived before them. Wild boar do, but the hunting tribes avoid such places. Besides, the monkeys lived there--as much as they lived anywhere. No animal with any self-respect would go within sight of it, except during a drought, when a little water remained in the partly ruined tanks and reservoirs.
[Illustration: The “Cold Lairs”]
“Getting there will take half the night, even at our fastest,” Bagheera said. Baloo’s face grew grave. “I’ll go as quickly as I possibly can,” he promised anxiously.
“We cannot risk waiting for you, Baloo. Follow us. Kaa and I must travel at a run.”

“Whether I have feet or not, I can match all four of yours,” Kaa replied sharply. Baloo tried to quicken his pace, but soon had to sit and gasp for breath. They left him to follow later, and Bagheera raced ahead at a panther’s brisk canter. Kaa said nothing. However hard Bagheera pushed himself, the enormous Rock-python stayed beside him. At the hill streams Bagheera pulled ahead, leaping across while Kaa swam with his head and two feet of neck above the surface. Back on level ground, though, Kaa closed the gap.
“By the Broken Lock that set me free,” Bagheera exclaimed as dusk settled, “you certainly know how to move!”
“My stomach is empty,” Kaa said. “And they called me a speckled frog.”
“A worm--an earthworm, a yellow one at that.”
“It makes no difference. On we go.” Kaa seemed to flow over the earth, his unwavering gaze picking out the most direct route and holding to it.

At the Cold Lairs, the Monkey-People gave no thought at all to Mowgli’s friends. They had carried the boy into the Lost City and, for the moment, were thoroughly pleased with themselves. Mowgli had never seen an Indian city. Although this one was little more than ruins, it struck him as astonishing and splendid. Long ago a king had built it on a small hill. The stone roads up to the broken gateways were still visible, and the last shreds of wooden gates clung to worn, rusty hinges. Trees grew through the walls, pushing in and out of them. The battlements had crumbled and collapsed, and thick clumps of wild creepers dangled from the windows of the towers along the walls.

On the hilltop stood a vast palace with no roof. The marble of its courtyards and fountains was cracked and blotched with red and green. In the courtyard once used to house the king’s elephants, grass and saplings had forced even the paving stones upward and apart. From the palace you could look over row upon row of roofless city houses, like empty honeycombs full of darkness. At the square where four streets met stood a misshapen stone that had once been an idol. Hollows and pits at street corners marked the old public wells, and wild fig trees sprouted from the sides of shattered temple domes. The monkeys claimed it as their own city and pretended to scorn the Jungle-People for living in the forest. Yet they had no idea what the buildings were for or how to use them. They sat in circles in the king’s council hall, scratching at fleas and playing at being men. Or they dashed through the roofless houses, piling scraps of plaster and old bricks into a corner, then forgetting where they had put them. They fought and shrieked in jostling crowds, only to abandon the quarrel and play along the terraces of the royal garden, shaking rose trees and orange trees for the fun of watching flowers and fruit fall. They explored every passage and dark tunnel in the palace, and its hundreds of small, unlit rooms. But they never remembered which places they had already seen. So they wandered around alone, in pairs, or in crowds, assuring each other that they were behaving just like men. They drank from the tanks, muddying the water, then quarreled over it. Afterward they rushed together in mobs and shouted, “No one in the jungle is as wise, as good, as clever, as strong, or as gentle as the Bandar-log.” Then they started all over again, until they tired of the city and returned to the treetops, still hoping the Jungle-People would take notice.

Raised under the Law of the Jungle, Mowgli neither understood nor liked this way of living. The monkeys hauled him into the Cold Lairs late that afternoon. Instead of sleeping after the long journey, as he would have done, they clasped hands, danced around, and sang their ridiculous songs. One stood up to make a speech. He announced that capturing Mowgli was a new chapter in Bandar-log history: the boy would teach them to weave sticks and canes into shelters from the rain and cold. Mowgli gathered some creepers and began weaving them back and forth. The monkeys tried to copy him, but within minutes they grew bored and began yanking one another’s tails or coughing and bouncing on all fours.
“I need something to eat,” Mowgli told them. “This part of the jungle is strange to me. Either bring me food or allow me to hunt here.”

Twenty or thirty monkeys leaped off to fetch nuts and wild pawpaws. On the way, however, they began fighting. Carrying back whatever fruit survived seemed too much bother. Aching, angry, and hungry, Mowgli wandered the deserted city, calling out the Strangers’ Hunting Call every so often. No reply came. He began to feel that he had arrived in a truly dreadful place. “Baloo was right about every bit of it,” he thought. “The Bandar-log have no Law, no Hunting Call, no leaders--only silly talk and little hands that snatch and steal. If I starve or die here, I’ll have nobody to blame but myself. Somehow I must get back to my own jungle. Baloo is bound to beat me, but even that is better than running after silly rose leaves with the Bandar-log.”

As soon as he reached the city wall, monkeys dragged him back. They told him he failed to appreciate his good fortune and pinched him to make him feel grateful. He clenched his teeth without a word and followed the shouting throng to a terrace overlooking red sandstone reservoirs, still half full of rainwater. At the center of the terrace stood a ruined white-marble summer-house, built for queens who had been dead a hundred years. Half its dome had collapsed, blocking the underground passage from the palace through which the queens once came. Its walls, though, were screens of carved marble--lovely milky-white lacework set with agates, cornelians, jasper, and lapis lazuli. When the moon rose behind the hill, its light passed through the openings and patterned the earth with shadows like embroidery in black velvet. Tired, hungry, and sore though he was, Mowgli had to laugh when twenty Bandar-log at once began explaining how great, wise, strong, and gentle they were, and how foolish he was to want to leave. “We are great. We are free. We are wonderful. No people in the jungle are more wonderful than we are! We all agree, so it must be true,” they cried. “You are a fresh listener, and you can repeat our words to the Jungle-People so that they will pay attention to us from now on. Therefore we shall tell you everything about our excellent selves.” Mowgli did not argue. Hundreds upon hundreds of monkeys crowded onto the terrace to hear their speakers praise the Bandar-log. Whenever a speaker ran out of breath, the whole crowd shouted, “It is true; we all agree.” Mowgli nodded and blinked, answering “Yes” whenever they questioned him, while his head reeled from the din. “Tabaqui the Jackal must have bitten every one of them,” he thought, “and now they are mad. This must be _dewanee_, the madness. Don’t they ever sleep? There is a cloud coming over the moon now. If it were only large enough, I could try escaping in the dark. But I am so tired.”

Two faithful friends were watching that very cloud from the ruined ditch beneath the city wall. Bagheera and Kaa understood the danger of the Monkey-People in a crowd and were taking no chances. Monkeys will fight only with odds of a hundred to one on their side, and few jungle creatures relish facing that.
“I shall take the western wall,” Kaa whispered, “and come swiftly downhill, with the slope helping me. They won’t pile onto my back by the hundred, but--”

“I understand,” Bagheera replied. “If only Baloo were with us. Still, we must manage as best we can. Once the cloud hides the moon, I’ll reach the terrace. They seem to be holding some kind of council over the boy.”

“Good hunting,” Kaa said sternly, and slid toward the west wall. Unfortunately, it was better preserved than the others, and the great snake had to search a while before finding a route up the stones. The cloud passed over the moon. As Mowgli wondered what might happen next, he heard Bagheera’s soft tread on the terrace. The Black Panther had come racing up the slope almost silently. Now he struck out on every side--he knew not to waste precious time biting--at the monkeys sitting fifty and sixty rows deep around Mowgli. Fear and fury burst into a howl. Then Bagheera stumbled on the bodies kicking and rolling beneath him, and a monkey cried, “There’s only one of them! Kill him! Kill.” A struggling mass closed over the Panther, biting, clawing, tearing, and tugging. Meanwhile five or six monkeys seized Mowgli, hauled him up the summer-house wall, and shoved him through the gap in its shattered dome. A boy raised by men would have been badly bruised by that fifteen-foot fall. Mowgli, however, fell the way Baloo had taught him and landed upright on his feet.
“Stay in there,” the monkeys called, “until we’ve killed your friends. Then we’ll play with you--provided the Poison-People let you live that long.”
“We are of one blood, you and I,” Mowgli said at once in the Snake’s Call. Rustles and hisses sounded from the rubble all around. To be certain, he repeated the Call.

“Yesss, indeed! Lower your hoods, everyone!” murmured half a dozen voices. Sooner or later every Indian ruin becomes a home for snakes, and the old summer-house swarmed with cobras. “Keep still, Little Brother. Those feet of yours could hurt us.”

Mowgli held as still as he could, peering through the carved openings and listening to the battle raging around the Black Panther. Shrieks, chattering, and scuffling mingled with Bagheera’s deep, rough cough as he backed, bucked, twisted, and lunged beneath piles of enemies. Never before in his life had Bagheera needed to fight simply to stay alive.
“Baloo must be close by. Bagheera would never have come alone,” Mowgli thought. Then he shouted, “Head for the tank, Bagheera. Roll toward the water tanks. Roll and dive! Make for the water!”

Hearing Mowgli’s voice and knowing the boy was safe gave Bagheera fresh courage. Desperately, inch by inch, he fought toward the reservoirs, stopping from time to time without a sound. Then Baloo’s rumbling battle cry rose from the broken wall nearest the jungle. The old Bear had done everything he could, but had been unable to arrive sooner. “Bagheera,” he called, “I’ve come. I’m climbing! I’m hurrying! Ahuwora! These stones slide under my paws! Just wait till I reach you, you disgraceful Bandar-log!” He gasped his way onto the terrace and vanished up to his head beneath a wave of monkeys. Planting himself firmly on his hindquarters, he spread his front paws, gathered as many monkeys into his arms as he could hold, and struck in a steady bat-bat-bat, like the slapping blades of a paddle wheel. Mowgli heard a crash and a splash: Bagheera had reached the tank, beyond the monkeys’ reach. The Panther lay panting with his head barely above the surface. On the red steps the monkeys crowded three deep, jumping up and down in fury, ready to attack him from every direction if he emerged to help Baloo. Then Bagheera raised his dripping chin and, in desperation, made the Snake’s Call for protection: “We are of one blood, you and I.” He thought Kaa had fled at the last moment. Even Baloo, nearly suffocating under the monkeys at the terrace edge, could not resist a chuckle at the sound of the Black Panther begging for help.

Kaa had only just crossed the western wall. As he landed, a wrench of his body sent a stone from the wall’s top tumbling into the ditch. Determined to keep every advantage the ground offered, he coiled and uncoiled once or twice, testing that every foot of his long body worked properly. All this time Baloo was still fighting, the monkeys were yelling around Bagheera in the tank, and Mang the Bat was flitting back and forth, spreading word of the great battle through the jungle. Even Hathi the Wild Elephant trumpeted. Far away, scattered Monkey-Folk awoke and came springing along the tree-roads to help their friends at the Cold Lairs. The uproar woke every daytime bird for miles. Then Kaa drove straight forward, swift and eager to kill. A python fights by striking with his head, putting his whole body’s strength and weight behind the blow. Imagine a lance, a battering ram, or a hammer weighing nearly half a ton, directed by a calm, unhurried mind lodged in its handle. That will give you some idea of Kaa in battle. Even a four- or five-foot python can knock a man down with a direct blow to the chest; Kaa, as you know, measured thirty feet. His first strike went into the middle of the throng surrounding Baloo. Mouth shut, utterly silent, he drove it home. There was no need to strike again. The monkeys scattered, screaming, “Kaa! It's Kaa! Run! Run!”

For generations, older monkeys had frightened the young into behaving by telling stories about Kaa, the thief of the night. They told how he moved along branches as silently as moss grows and carried away the strongest monkey alive.
