They told of old Kaa disguising himself as a dead branch or rotten stump, fooling even the wisest until the branch seized them. He stood for everything the monkeys feared in the jungle. Not one knew how far his power reached; not one could meet his gaze; not one had ever survived his embrace. So they fled to the walls and rooftops, stammering in terror. Baloo let out a long breath of relief. His coat was much thicker than Bagheera’s, but the fighting had hurt him badly. For the first time Kaa opened his mouth, uttering a single long, hissing word. Far away, the monkeys rushing to defend the Cold Lairs froze where they were and cowered until the crowded branches bent and crackled beneath their weight. Those on the walls and roofless houses fell silent too. In the hush over the city, Mowgli heard Bagheera shake the water from his sides as he climbed out of the tank. Then the uproar started again. Monkeys scrambled farther up the walls, clung to the necks of huge stone idols, and shrieked as they leaped along the battlements. Inside the summer-house, Mowgli danced, pressed an eye to the marble openings, and hooted between his front teeth like an owl, mocking them to show his contempt.
“Free the man-cub from that trap; I have nothing left in me,” Bagheera panted. “Let us get him and leave. They might come at us again.”

“Until I command them, they will not move. Keep sssstill!” Kaa hissed. Once again the city fell quiet. Turning to Bagheera, he added, “I could not arrive sooner, Brother, but I believe I heard you calling.”
“I--perhaps I did shout during the fight,” Bagheera replied. “Baloo, have you been injured?”

“I’m not certain they haven't pulled me apart into a hundred small bears,” Baloo said solemnly, shaking each leg in turn. “Wow! Everything hurts. Kaa, I think you have saved both our lives--mine and Bagheera’s.”
“Never mind that. Where is the little man?”
“Over here, caught in a trap. I can’t climb out,” Mowgli shouted. The broken dome curved inward above his head.
“Get him out of here,” the cobras inside complained. “He dances about like Mao the Peacock. He will trample our young.”
“Hah!” Kaa chuckled. “This little man seems to find friends wherever he goes. Step back, little man. And you Poison People, get under cover. I am going to smash the wall.”

Kaa examined the carved marble until he spotted a stained crack marking a weak place. Two or three gentle taps of his head measured the distance. Then he raised six feet of his body off the ground and hurled his nose forward in half a dozen crushing blows at full strength. The screen shattered, collapsing in a cloud of rubble and dust. Mowgli jumped through the opening and threw himself between Baloo and Bagheera, putting an arm around each great neck.
“Did they hurt you?” Baloo asked, holding him gently in his arms.
“I ache, I’m hungry, and I have plenty of bruises. But, oh, my Brothers, look what they have done to you! You’re bleeding.”
“So are others,” Bagheera replied. He licked his lips and glanced at the dead monkeys lying across the terrace and beside the tank.
“None of that matters, none of it, as long as you are safe, my finest little frog!” Baloo whimpered.

“We shall decide about that later,” Bagheera said dryly, in a tone Mowgli disliked very much. “But here is Kaa. We owe him our victory, and you owe him your life. Give him our customary thanks, Mowgli.”
Turning around, Mowgli saw the huge Python’s head swaying a foot higher than his own.

“So here is the little man,” Kaa said. “What soft skin he has. And he looks rather like the Bandar-log. Be careful, little man, or one evening after I have shed my skin I may take you for a monkey in the twilight.”
“We are of one blood, you and I,” Mowgli replied. “You have given me my life tonight. If you ever go hungry, Kaa, whatever I kill will be yours.”
“Many thanks, Little Brother,” Kaa said, a twinkle in his eyes. “And what does this bold hunter bring down? I ask so that I can follow him the next time he sets out.”

“I’m still too small to kill anything. But I can drive goats toward someone who has a use for them. When you are hungry, come and find out whether I mean what I say. I’m quite clever with these [he held out his hands]. If you ever get caught in a trap, I might repay what I owe you, and Bagheera, and Baloo here. Good hunting to all of you, my masters.”

“Spoken well,” Baloo growled, pleased by Mowgli’s graceful thanks. For a moment the Python rested his head lightly on the boy’s shoulder. “A courageous heart and a polite tongue,” he said. “Those will take you far in the jungle, little man. Now hurry away with your friends. Go and sleep. The moon is setting, and you ought not to see what happens after it goes.”

The moon was descending behind the hills. Rows of trembling monkeys huddled on walls and battlements, looking like ragged fringes shaking in the air. Baloo went down to drink from the tank. Bagheera began grooming his coat. Meanwhile Kaa slid to the terrace’s center and snapped his jaws together so loudly that every monkey turned to look.
“The moon is going down,” he said. “Can you still see in the light that remains?”
A moan drifted from the walls like wind through high branches: “We can see, O Kaa.”
“Good. Now the dance begins--the Dance of the Hunger of Kaa. Remain still and watch.”

He moved around in a wide circle two or three times, his head swaying left and right. Then his body formed loops, figures of eight, and soft, flowing triangles that dissolved into squares, five-sided shapes, and heaped coils. He never rested or hurried, and his low, humming song went on without a pause. The darkness deepened until the sliding, shifting coils could no longer be seen, though the rustling of his scales was still audible.
Baloo and Bagheera were motionless as stone, growling low in their throats, the fur on their necks standing up. Mowgli stared in wonder.
“Bandar-log,” Kaa’s voice said at last, “can you move a hand or a foot unless I command it? Answer me!”
“Unless you command it, O Kaa, we cannot move a hand or a foot!”
“Good! Each of you, take one step toward me.”
Helplessly the rows of monkeys swayed toward him. Baloo and Bagheera moved with them, each taking one rigid step.
“Closer!” Kaa hissed. Once more, every one of them moved.
Mowgli put a hand on each of his friends to lead them away. Both great animals jolted as if suddenly waking out of a dream.
“Leave your hand on my shoulder,” Bagheera whispered. “Don't take it away, or I will have to return--have to go back to Kaa. Aah!”
“It’s only old Kaa drawing circles in the dust,” Mowgli said. “Come on, let’s leave.” The three slipped through an opening in the walls and back into the jungle.
“Whoof!” Baloo exclaimed when they were safely beneath the quiet trees. “I shall never ask Kaa to be my ally again.” He gave his whole body a shake.
“He understands things we don’t,” Bagheera said, shaking. “If I had stayed a moment longer, I would have walked straight into his throat.”
“Before the moon comes up again, plenty will take that path,” Baloo replied. “He will enjoy good hunting--in his own way.”

“What did it all mean, though?” Mowgli asked. He knew nothing of a python’s power to hold others spellbound. “All I saw was a large snake tracing silly circles until it grew dark. And his poor nose was sore all over. Ho! Ho!”

“Mowgli,” Bagheera said sharply, “you are the reason his nose was hurt. You are also the reason my ears, sides, and paws are bitten, and Baloo’s neck and shoulders too. For days to come, neither Baloo nor I will be able to enjoy hunting.”
“That hardly matters,” Baloo replied. “Our man-cub is back with us.”

“Yes, but consider what he has cost us: time we could have spent on good hunting, wounds, fur--half the hair has been torn from my back--and, finally, our honor. Remember this, Mowgli: I, the Black Panther, had to beg Kaa to protect me. His Hunger Dance made Baloo and me as witless as small birds. Every bit of that happened because you chose to play with the Bandar-log, man-cub.”
“Yes, it’s all true,” Mowgli said miserably. “I’m a wicked man-cub, and I feel sick with sorrow inside.”
“Mf! Baloo, what does the Law of the Jungle say?”
Baloo wanted to spare Mowgli further trouble, but the Law was not his to alter. He muttered, “Being sorry does not cancel punishment. Only remember how small he is, Bagheera.”
“I will keep that in mind. But he has caused harm, and now he must take his blows. Mowgli, do you have anything to say for yourself?”
“No. What I did was wrong, and both you and Baloo were hurt. The punishment is fair.”

Bagheera struck him six times--gentle little love-taps, by a panther’s standards, barely enough to wake one of his own cubs. To a seven-year-old boy, though, they were as harsh a beating as anyone could wish to escape. Once it was finished, Mowgli sneezed and got to his feet without saying anything.
“Now climb onto my back, Little Brother,” Bagheera told him, “and we will make our way home.”
One fine feature of Jungle Law is that punishment wipes out every debt. Once it is over, nobody nags.
Resting his head against Bagheera’s back, Mowgli fell into such a deep sleep that being laid down in the family cave did not wake him.
Road-Song of the Bandar-Log

Here we go in a flung festoon,
Half-way up to the jealous moon!
Don’t you envy our prancing bands?
Don’t you wish you had extra hands?
Wouldn’t you like if your tails were--so--
Curved in the shape of a Cupid’s bow?
Now you’re angry, but--never mind,
_Brother, your tail hangs down behind!_

Here we sit in a branchy row,
Thinking of beautiful things we know;
Dreaming of deeds that we mean to do,
All complete, in a minute or two--
Something noble and wise and good,
Done by merely wishing we could.
We’ve forgotten, but--never mind,
_Brother, your tail hangs down behind!_

All the talk we ever have heard
Spoken by bat or beast or bird--
Hide or fin or scale or feather--
Jabber it quickly and all together!
Excellent! Wonderful! Once again!

Now we are talking just like men!
Let’s pretend we are ... never mind,
_Brother, your tail hangs down behind!_
This is the way of the Monkey-kind.

_Then join our leaping lines that rush wildly through the pines,
That rocket by where, light and high, the wild grape swings.
By the rubbish in our wake, and the noble noise we make,
Be sure, be sure, we’re going to do some splendid things!_

chapters.title: "Tiger! Tiger!"
paragraphs:
What of the hunting, hunter bold?
Brother, the watch was long and cold.
What of the prey you went to kill?
Brother, he grazes in the jungle still.
Where is the power that made your pride?
Brother, it drains from my flank and side.
Why do you hurry so swiftly by?
Brother, I go to my lair--to die.

We must return now to the first story. After the confrontation with the Pack at the Council Rock, Mowgli left the wolves’ cave and went down to the farmland around the village. He would not stay there, though. It lay too close to the jungle, and he knew the Council had left him with at least one dangerous enemy. He hurried onward along the rough valley road, keeping up a steady trot for almost twenty miles until he reached unfamiliar country. Here the valley spread into a broad plain, scattered with rocks and sliced by ravines. A little village stood at one end. At the other, thick jungle swept down to the pasture and ended abruptly, as if someone had chopped it away with a hoe. Cattle and buffaloes grazed across the plain. The little boys minding them saw Mowgli, shouted, and fled, while the yellow pariah dogs found around every Indian village began barking. Hungry, Mowgli kept walking. At the village entrance he saw that the great thorn-bush used to block the gate at dusk had been dragged aside.

“Umph!” he said. During his nighttime searches for food he had encountered several such barriers. “Men here are afraid of the People of the Jungle too.” He sat beside the gate. When a man emerged, Mowgli stood up, opened his mouth, and pointed into it to show his hunger. The man stared, then raced back along the village’s only street, shouting for the priest--a large, fat man in white clothing with a red-and-yellow mark on his forehead. The priest came to the gate, followed by at least a hundred people. They stared, chattered, shouted, and pointed at Mowgli.
“These Men Folk have no manners at all,” Mowgli thought. “Only a gray ape would act like this.” He tossed his long hair back and scowled at the crowd.
“Why be frightened?” the priest asked. “Look at those marks on his legs and arms: wolf bites. He is simply a wolf-child who has wandered out of the jungle.”

Of course the cubs, playing with Mowgli, had often nipped harder than they meant to. White scars covered his limbs. He would never have described them as bites, though: he understood what it meant to be truly bitten.

“Arre! Arre!” two or three women exclaimed at once. “The poor child, bitten by wolves! What a fine-looking boy he is. His eyes glow like red fire. Upon my honor, Messua, he looks rather like the son the tiger took from you.”
“Let me see him,” said a woman wearing heavy copper bracelets and anklets. Shading her eyes with her hand, she studied Mowgli. “Yes, he does. He is thinner, but he has exactly my boy’s look.”

The priest was shrewd. He knew Messua’s husband was the wealthiest man in the village. After gazing skyward for a moment, he pronounced solemnly, “The jungle has returned what it once took away. Bring the child into your home, my sister, and remember to honor the priest who sees so deeply into men’s lives.”
“By the Bull that paid for me,” Mowgli thought, “all this chatter is like being inspected by the Pack again! Well, if I am a man, I must learn to be one.”

The people moved aside as the woman motioned him toward her hut. Inside stood a red-lacquered bed frame and a large earthenware grain chest decorated with curious raised patterns. There were six copper cooking pots, a Hindu god’s image in a small recess, and, hanging on the wall, a real mirror of the kind sold at country fairs.

She gave Mowgli plenty of milk to drink and some bread. Then she rested a hand on his head and searched his eyes, wondering whether this could truly be her son, returned from the jungle where the tiger had carried him. “Nathoo, oh, Nathoo!” she said. The name meant nothing to Mowgli. “Don’t you remember when I gave you your new shoes?” She felt his foot; it was nearly as hard as horn. “No,” she said sadly. “These feet have never had shoes on them. But you are so like my Nathoo, and I will make you my son.”

Having never been beneath a roof, Mowgli felt uncomfortable. Looking up, though, he saw that he could rip through the thatch whenever he wanted to escape; the window had no latch either. Finally he thought, “What use is a man who cannot understand other men’s speech? I am as helpless and foolish here as a man would be among us in the jungle. I have to learn their language.”

His years with the wolves had taught him more than tricks for amusement when he learned to copy a buck’s challenge and a small wild pig’s grunt. As soon as Messua spoke a word, he could reproduce it almost exactly. By nightfall he knew the names of many objects in the hut.

Bedtime caused trouble. Mowgli refused to sleep beneath a roof that looked so much like a panther trap. When they closed the door, he climbed out of the window. “Let him do as he wants,” Messua’s husband said. “Remember, he cannot ever have slept in a bed before tonight. If he has truly been sent to replace our son, he will not leave us.”
Mowgli lay down in a patch of tall, clean grass beside the field. Before his eyes had shut, a soft gray muzzle nudged him beneath the chin.

“Phew!” said Gray Brother, the oldest of Mother Wolf’s cubs. “Some reward for tracking you all twenty miles. You smell of cattle and wood smoke--just like a man already. Wake up, Little Brother. I have news for you.”
“Is everyone in the jungle well?” Mowgli asked, putting his arms around him.

“Everyone except the wolves scorched by the Red Flower. Listen to this: Shere Khan has gone hunting in a distant place while his coat grows back. He was badly burned. He swears that when he comes back he will leave your bones in the Waingunga.”

“I have something to say about that. I made a small promise too. Still, it is always good to hear news. Tonight I’m tired--all these unfamiliar things have worn me out, Gray Brother--but always bring me word of what happens.”
“You won’t forget you’re a wolf?” Gray Brother asked worriedly. “These men won’t make you forget?”
“Not ever. I will always know that I love you and everyone in our cave. I will also always remember that the Pack drove me away.”

“Remember too that another pack might drive you away. Men are merely men, Little Brother. Their chatter is like frogs croaking in a pool. When I next come down, I’ll wait among the bamboos beside the pasture for you.”

For the next three months Mowgli scarcely passed beyond the village gate: learning human habits and customs kept him too busy. First they made him wrap a cloth around himself, which irritated him terribly. Then came lessons about money, which made no sense to him at all, and plowing, whose purpose he could not see. The village children, too, made him furious. Fortunately, the Law of the Jungle had taught him to master his anger, because in the jungle both food and life depend on self-control. But when the children mocked his refusal to play games or fly kites, or laughed at his mistakes in speaking, only his knowledge that killing small naked cubs was against fair sporting rules stopped him from grabbing them and snapping them in half.
He had no sense of his own power. Among the jungle beasts he had known himself to be weak. Here, people told him he had the strength of a bull.

Mowgli also understood nothing of the distinctions caste draws between one man and another. When the potter’s donkey slipped into the clay pit, he pulled it out by its tail and helped load the pots for the trip to Khanhiwara’s market. This shocked everyone too: the potter belonged to a low caste, and his donkey ranked lower still. The priest scolded Mowgli, who threatened to put him on the donkey as well. The priest then advised Messua’s husband to find work for the boy immediately. The village head-man told him he must take the buffaloes out the following day and watch over them at pasture. No one could have been happier than Mowgli. That evening, now something like an appointed village servant, he joined the group that gathered nightly on a stone platform beneath a great fig-tree. It was the village club. The head-man, watchman, barber--who knew every scrap of village gossip--and old Buldeo, the local hunter with his Tower musket, met there to smoke. Monkeys sat chattering in the upper branches. Below the platform a cobra lived in a hole; because he was sacred, he received a small dish of milk each evening. Around the tree the old men talked and drew smoke from their great huqas, or water-pipes, long into the night. They told marvelous stories about men, gods, and ghosts. Buldeo told still more marvelous stories about the jungle beasts, until the children outside the circle stared with their eyes almost popping out. Animals were the subject of most tales: the jungle lay on their doorstep. Deer and wild pigs dug up the fields, and sometimes, at dusk, a tiger carried off a man within sight of the village gates.

Naturally Mowgli knew something about their subject. As Buldeo went from one extraordinary tale to the next, his Tower musket resting on his knees, Mowgli had to hide his face to conceal his laughter. His shoulders shook.

Buldeo explained that the tiger which had stolen Messua’s boy was a ghost-tiger. Inside it lived the spirit of a wicked old money-lender who had died years earlier. “I can be certain of it,” he declared, “because Purun Dass always walked with a limp after being struck in the riot when his account books were burned. This tiger limps as well: the prints left by his paws do not match.”
“Yes, yes, that must be right,” the bearded elders agreed, all nodding their gray heads.

“Are all your stories made of cobwebs and moonshine?” Mowgli asked. “Everyone knows the tiger limps because he was born lame. Talking about a money-lender’s soul inside a beast with less courage than a jackal is nonsense fit for children.”
For a moment surprise struck Buldeo dumb. The head-man simply stared at Mowgli.

“Oho! So the jungle brat is speaking, is he?” Buldeo said. “If you know so much, take that tiger’s hide to Khanhiwara. The Government offers a hundred rupees for his death. Better yet, keep quiet while your elders are talking.”

Mowgli got up to leave. Over his shoulder he said, “I have spent the whole evening lying here listening. Except on one or two occasions, Buldeo has not told the truth about the jungle, though it is right outside his door. Why should I believe him about the ghosts, gods, and goblins he claims to have seen?”
“It’s high time that boy started herding,” the head-man said. Buldeo snorted and spluttered at Mowgli’s impudence.

In most Indian villages, a few boys lead the cattle and buffaloes to pasture early each morning and return with them after dark. The same cattle that would trample a white man to death submit to being hit, pushed about, and shouted at by children scarcely tall enough to reach their noses. As long as the boys stay with their animals, they are safe: even a tiger will not rush a herd of cattle. But a boy who wanders off to collect flowers or catch lizards may be carried away. At dawn Mowgli rode through the village on Rama, the herd’s great bull. One by one the slate-blue buffaloes left their sheds and followed, their fierce eyes beneath long horns curving backward. Mowgli made sure his fellow herders understood that he was in charge. He drove the buffaloes with a long, smooth bamboo stick. He told one boy, Kamya, to take the cattle to graze separately while he went on with the buffaloes, and warned him firmly not to wander away from his herd.

Indian pasture is a maze of rocks, scrub, clumps of grass, and small ravines; scattered among them, a herd can vanish from view. Buffaloes usually stay near pools and muddy hollows, where they wallow or bask for hours in the warm mud. Mowgli took them to the far side of the plain, where the Waingunga emerged from the forest. Sliding down from Rama’s neck, he trotted toward a bamboo thicket and found Gray Brother there. “Ah,” the wolf said, “I have been waiting for days and days. What are you doing, herding cattle?”
“I was told to,” Mowgli answered. “For the moment I’m one of the village herders. What have you heard about Shere Khan?”
“He returned to this part of the country and waited a long time for you. Game is scarce, so he has left again. But he is determined to kill you.”

“Good,” Mowgli said. “While he is away, you or one of the four brothers should sit up on that rock where I can see you as I leave the village. Once he returns, meet me in the ravine beside the _dhâk_ tree in the middle of the plain. There is no reason to walk straight into Shere Khan’s jaws.”

After that Mowgli chose a shady spot and slept, with the buffaloes grazing around him. Few occupations are lazier than herding in India. The cattle shuffle along, chew, lie down, and wander on again. They do not even moo, but merely grunt. Buffaloes hardly make a sound. One after another they lower themselves into the muddy pools and burrow down until only their noses and staring china-blue eyes remain visible; then they lie still as logs. Heat from the sun makes the rocks shimmer and dance. Overhead, almost beyond sight, the children hear a single kite whistling--never more than one. They know that if a child or a cow died, that kite would swoop down. Another kite miles off would see the descent and follow, then another, and another, until almost before death arrived, twenty hungry kites would appear from nowhere. The children doze, wake, and doze again. They weave dry grass into tiny baskets and fill them with grasshoppers, or catch two praying mantises and set them fighting. They thread red-and-black jungle nuts into necklaces, watch a lizard sunning on a rock, or follow a snake pursuing a frog by the mud pools. They sing very long songs with the strange, wavering native notes at the end. The day seems longer than most people’s entire lives. Perhaps they build a mud castle, make mud figures of men, horses, and buffaloes, and put reeds into the men’s hands. They pretend to be kings commanding these armies, or gods receiving worship. Eventually evening arrives. The children call, and the buffaloes heave themselves from the sticky mud, making a succession of sounds like gunshots. All of them trail across the gray plain toward the village’s flickering lights.

Every day Mowgli took the buffaloes to their muddy pools. Every day, a mile and a half across the plain, he saw Gray Brother’s back and knew Shere Khan had not returned. And every day he lay in the grass, listening to the sounds around him and remembering his former jungle life. On those long, silent mornings, he would have heard it if Shere Khan had stumbled on his lame paw in the forests beside the Waingunga.

One day, at last, Gray Brother was absent from the lookout rock. Mowgli laughed and steered the buffaloes toward the ravine near the dhâk tree, now covered in golden-red blossom. Gray Brother waited there, every hair along his back bristling.
“He kept hidden for a month to make you stop watching,” the Wolf panted. “Last night he crossed the ranges with Tabaqui, following close on your trail.”
Mowgli drew his brows together. “Shere Khan doesn’t frighten me. But Tabaqui is a clever one.”

“No need to worry,” Gray Brother said, giving his lips a small lick. “I found Tabaqui at dawn. He’s sharing his wisdom with the kites now. Before I broke his back, though, he told me everything. Shere Khan means to wait at the village gate this evening for you--you alone. Just now he is resting in the Waingunga’s big dry ravine.”
“Has he fed today, or is his belly empty for the hunt?” Mowgli asked. His own life or death depended on the reply.
“At dawn he killed a pig, and he has drunk as well. You know Shere Khan: he could never go without food, not even for revenge.”

“Oh! What a fool, what a fool! He’s more childish than a cub! He has eaten and drunk, and now he expects me to wait while he sleeps! Where exactly is he resting? With just ten of us, we could bring him down where he lies. These buffaloes won’t charge until they smell him, and I don’t know their language. Can we come onto his trail from behind, so they pick up his scent?”
“To prevent that, he swam a long way down the Waingunga,” Gray Brother replied.

“That was Tabaqui’s advice, I’m certain. He could never have thought of it himself.” Mowgli put a finger in his mouth and considered. “The large ravine beside the Waingunga opens onto the plain less than half a mile away. I could circle through the forest with the herd, reach its upper end, and sweep down it. But he would escape through the bottom. We have to block that exit. Gray Brother, can you separate the herd into two?”

“Perhaps I cannot--but I brought someone wise to help.” Gray Brother trotted away and vanished into a hollow. Then a great gray head, very familiar to Mowgli, rose above it. Through the hot air rang the loneliest sound in all the jungle: a wolf’s hunting howl at noon.

“Akela! Akela!” Mowgli cried, clapping. “I should have known you would remember me. We have important work ahead. Divide the herd, Akela. Keep the mothers and their calves in one group; put the bulls and plowing buffaloes in the other.”

Like dancers weaving through a ladies’ chain, the two wolves darted in and out among the buffaloes. The animals snorted, tossed their heads, and split into two groups. In one, the mothers surrounded their calves, glaring and scraping the ground. If a wolf stood still for even a moment, they were ready to charge and stamp him to death. In the other group, adult and younger bulls stamped and snorted. They looked fiercer but were much less dangerous, with no calves to defend. Even six men working together could not have divided the animals so neatly.
“Your orders!” Akela panted. “They're trying to come back together.”
Mowgli climbed onto Rama. “Take the bulls off to the left, Akela. Gray Brother, after we leave, keep the mothers together and drive them into the ravine’s lower entrance.”
“How far inside?” Gray Brother asked between gasps and snaps.

“Until the walls rise too high for Shere Khan to leap out,” Mowgli shouted. “Hold them there until we arrive from above.” Akela bayed, and the bulls rushed away. Gray Brother planted himself before the mothers. When they charged, he ran just ahead of them to the ravine’s mouth, while Akela drove the bulls well over to the left.

“Excellent! One more rush will get them properly moving. Be careful now, Akela, careful. Snap once too often and the bulls will turn on you. Hujah! This is much wilder than driving black-buck. Did you ever imagine animals like these could run so fast?” Mowgli shouted.
“I have--have hunted these creatures myself before now,” Akela gasped through the dust. “Do you want them turned toward the jungle?”
“Yes! Turn them. Turn them quickly! Rama is wild with anger. Oh, if only I could explain what I want him to do today.”

This time the bulls turned right and plunged into the thick undergrowth. Half a mile away, the other boys watched from beside their cattle. Then they ran for the village as fast as they could, shouting that the buffaloes had gone mad and escaped.

Mowgli’s scheme was straightforward. He meant to make a wide uphill circuit to the top of the ravine, then drive the bulls down it, trapping Shere Khan between them and the mothers below. A tiger full of food and water, he knew, could neither fight effectively nor scramble up the steep walls of the ravine. He was calming the buffaloes with his voice now. Far behind, Akela gave only an occasional whine to hurry the stragglers. They took a very wide circle, keeping clear of the ravine so as not to alert Shere Khan. Eventually Mowgli gathered the confused herd on a grassy patch above the ravine’s head, where the ground fell sharply into it. From there a person could look over the treetops to the plain below. Mowgli, however, studied the ravine walls. To his great satisfaction, they were almost vertical. A tiger trying to climb out would get no support from the vines and creepers trailing over them.
“Give them a moment to breathe, Akela,” he said, raising his hand. “They haven’t caught his smell yet. Let them rest. I must tell Shere Khan who is coming. He’s caught in our trap now.”
He cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted into the ravine. It was like calling down a tunnel: the sound echoed from one rock face to another.
A long pause followed. Then came the slow, drowsy snarl of a well-fed tiger only just roused from sleep.
“Who’s calling?” Shere Khan demanded. A magnificent peacock burst screeching from the ravine, beating its wings upward.
“Mowgli calls. Cattle thief, your time has come to visit the Council Rock! Drive them down, Akela--quickly! Down you go, Rama, down!”

For a moment the buffaloes hesitated at the slope’s edge. Then Akela let out his full hunting cry, and they plunged over one by one, like steamships shooting down rapids, spraying sand and stones around them. Once in motion they could not possibly halt. Before they had fully reached the ravine floor, Rama caught Shere Khan’s scent and bellowed.

“Ha! Ha!” Mowgli laughed from his back. “Now you understand!” A torrent of black horns, foaming mouths, and staring eyes swept down the ravine like boulders in a flood. Weaker animals were shoved against the walls, tearing through the creepers. They knew what lay ahead: the dreadful rush of a buffalo herd that no tiger can withstand. Shere Khan heard the hooves thunder. He got up and lumbered down the gully, glancing right and left for an escape. But the walls rose straight up. Heavy with his meal and drink, he could only keep running, ready to try anything to avoid a fight. The herd splashed through the pool he had just left, its bellows resounding in the narrow channel. An answering bellow reached Mowgli from below. He saw Shere Khan turn: the tiger knew that, if forced to choose, bulls were a better prospect than mothers defending calves. Rama tripped, stumbled over something soft, and surged onward. With the bulls close behind, he crashed headlong into the other herd. The collision lifted the weaker buffaloes entirely off their feet. Both groups burst out onto the plain, goring, stamping, and snorting. Mowgli waited for his chance, slid off Rama’s neck, and struck about him with his stick.
“Hurry, Akela! Split them apart. Scatter them before they begin fighting each other. Drive them off, Akela. Hai, Rama! Hai, hai, hai! my children. Gently now, gently! It’s over.”

Akela and Gray Brother darted back and forth, nipping at buffalo legs. Once the herd wheeled as if to charge back up the ravine, but Mowgli got Rama turned around. The others followed their bull toward the mud pools.
There was no need to trample Shere Khan again. He lay dead, and already the kites were gathering.

“That was the death of a dog, Brothers,” Mowgli said, reaching for the knife he now always wore in a sheath around his neck, as men did. “But he would never have stood and fought. His skin will look fine on the Council Rock. We must work quickly.”

No boy brought up among men would have thought of skinning a ten-foot tiger by himself. Mowgli, though, understood better than anyone how an animal’s hide fits its body and how to remove it. Even so, it was difficult work. For an hour he cut, tugged, and grunted, while the wolves panted with their tongues out or came forward to pull wherever he directed. Then a hand touched his shoulder. Looking up, he found Buldeo standing there with his Tower musket. The children had brought news of the stampede to the village, and Buldeo had angrily set out, eager to punish Mowgli for neglecting the herd. The wolves had slipped from sight the moment they noticed the man approaching.

“What foolishness is this?” Buldeo snapped. “Imagine thinking you know how to skin a tiger! Where did the buffaloes kill him? And it’s the Lame Tiger himself, with a hundred rupees offered for his head. Well, well, we can overlook your allowing the herd to escape. When I’ve taken the hide to Khanhiwara, perhaps I’ll give you one rupee out of the reward.” He searched his waist cloth for his flint and steel, then bent to burn off Shere Khan’s whiskers. Most native hunters always singe a dead tiger’s whiskers so that its ghost will not haunt them.

“Hum!” Mowgli muttered as he peeled the skin from a front paw. “So you’ll take the hide to Khanhiwara, collect the reward, and perhaps let me have one rupee? As it happens, I want this skin for something of my own. Heh! Keep that fire away, old man!”

“Is that how you address the village’s chief hunter? You have only killed him through luck and the stupidity of your buffaloes. His stomach was full, or he would be twenty miles away by now. You can’t even skin him correctly, you little beggar brat, yet you dare tell me, Buldeo, not to burn his whiskers. You’ll get no reward from me, Mowgli, not one anna--only a sound beating. Step away from that carcass!”
“By the Bull that paid for me,” Mowgli said, working toward the shoulder, “am I supposed to spend all midday chattering with an old ape? Akela, come here. This man is bothering me.”
Still bent over Shere Khan’s head, Buldeo suddenly found himself flat on the grass beneath a gray wolf. Mowgli continued removing the hide as calmly as if he were the only person in India.

“Ye-es,” he said through his teeth. “Exactly right, Buldeo. You will never pay me a single anna of that reward. This lame tiger and I have been fighting a war for a long time--a very long time. And I have won it.”

To be fair to Buldeo, ten years earlier he would have faced his chances against Akela if they had met in the woods. But this was no ordinary wolf: it obeyed a boy who waged private wars against man-eating tigers. To Buldeo that could only mean sorcery, magic of the most dreadful sort. He wondered if the charm hanging at his neck would save him. He lay absolutely still, expecting Mowgli himself to change into a tiger at any moment.
“Maharaj! Great King,” he finally whispered, his voice rough and faint.
“Yes?” Mowgli answered with a small chuckle, without bothering to look around.
“I am old. I had no idea you were more than a boy tending cattle. Will you allow me to get up and leave, or is your servant going to tear me apart?”
“Go in peace. Just remember next time to leave my kill alone. Akela, let the man go.”

Buldeo limped back to the village as quickly as he could, repeatedly glancing over his shoulder in case Mowgli transformed into some terrifying creature. On arriving he told a story so full of magic, spells, and sorcery that the priest’s expression grew solemn.
Mowgli returned to the job. Even with the wolves helping, it was nearly dusk before they had pulled the huge, brightly patterned skin free from the carcass.
“We must hide this now and get the buffaloes back home! Help me round them up, Akela.”

They gathered the herd in the hazy evening light. Near the village Mowgli could see lights and hear the blowing of conches and clanging of bells at the temple. Half the villagers seemed to be waiting by the gate. “They’ve come because I killed Shere Khan,” he thought. Instead, a volley of stones whistled past his ears. The villagers screamed, “Sorcerer! Wolf’s brat! Jungle demon! Leave us! Get away at once, or the priest will change you back into a wolf. Fire, Buldeo, fire!”
The old Tower musket fired with a bang. One of the young buffaloes roared in pain.
“More witchcraft!” the villagers cried. “He makes bullets change direction. That was your buffalo, Buldeo.”
“What is happening now?” Mowgli asked in confusion as still more stones came flying toward him.
“These brothers of yours are much like the Pack,” Akela observed, sitting down calmly. “Unless I misunderstand what bullets mean, I believe they intend to drive you out.”
“Wolf! Cub of a wolf! Be gone!” the priest cried, brandishing a sprig of sacred tulsi.
“Once again? Before, they sent me away for being a man. Now they send me away for being a wolf. Come on, Akela.”

A woman came running toward the buffaloes: Messua. “Oh, my son, my son!” she cried. “They say you are a sorcerer who can become an animal whenever he wishes. I don’t believe it. But leave now, or they’ll kill you. Buldeo calls you a wizard, but I know you have taken revenge for Nathoo’s death.”
“Get back here, Messua!” the crowd shouted. “Come back or we’ll throw stones at you too.”

A stone struck Mowgli’s mouth, and he gave a brief, harsh laugh. “Go back to them, Messua. This is just another silly tale like those they tell beneath the big tree at dusk. At least I have avenged your son’s death. Goodbye. Run quickly--I’m going to send the herd through faster than they throw their broken bricks. I’m no wizard, Messua. Goodbye!”
“One more time, Akela,” he called. “Drive the buffaloes through the gate.”
The buffaloes already wanted nothing more than to get home. Akela scarcely needed to call before they swept through the gate like a whirlwind, scattering villagers to either side.

“Count them!” Mowgli shouted contemptuously. “Perhaps I have stolen one. Count them carefully: you won’t have me herding for you again. Goodbye, children of men. You can thank Messua that I do not bring my wolves into the village and hunt you back and forth along your street.”

Turning away, he walked off beside the Lone Wolf. He looked at the stars and felt glad. “No more sleeping in traps, Akela. Let’s collect Shere Khan’s hide and leave. No, we won’t harm the village. Messua treated me kindly.”

When moonlight spread across the plain, turning it milky white, the terrified villagers saw Mowgli trotting over it with a bundle on his head and two wolves behind. He moved at the steady wolf’s pace that devours miles like fire. The temple bells clanged and the conches sounded louder than ever. Messua wept. Buldeo added more and more flourishes to his jungle adventure, until he was claiming that Akela had risen onto his hind legs and spoken like a man.
As the moon began to set, Mowgli and his two companions reached the hill beneath the Council Rock. They paused at Mother Wolf’s cave.
“Mother, the Man-Pack has driven me away,” Mowgli called. “But I’ve brought Shere Khan’s hide, just as I promised.”
Mother Wolf stepped stiffly out of the cave, the cubs following behind. Her eyes lit up at the sight of the hide.
“On the day he pushed his head and shoulders into this cave to take your life, Little Frog, I warned him. I told him the hunter would become the hunted. You have done well.”

“Well done, Little Brother,” said a deep voice from the bushes. “The jungle was lonely without you.” Bagheera ran up to Mowgli’s bare feet. Together they climbed the Council Rock. Mowgli laid the skin across the flat stone that had once been Akela’s seat and pinned it down with four strips of bamboo. Akela stretched himself on it and gave the old summons to Council: “Look--look closely, O Wolves.” It was the same call he had made when Mowgli first came there.

Since Akela’s removal, the Pack had had no leader. Each wolf hunted and fought as he chose. Habit still brought them to the call. Some limped from traps, others from gunshot wounds. Some had developed mange from bad food. Many never came at all. But every survivor arrived at the Council Rock. They saw Shere Khan’s striped skin spread over the stone, its enormous claws hanging from the limp, empty feet. A song rose in Mowgli’s throat, coming to him without effort. He shouted it out, jumping on the rustling hide and beating the rhythm with his heels until his breath gave out. Between the verses, Gray Brother and Akela howled.
“Look closely, O Wolves. Have I done what I promised?” Mowgli asked. The wolves bayed their “Yes,” and one ragged wolf cried out:
“Be our leader once more, Akela. Lead us again, Man-cub. We have had enough of life without law and long to be the Free People again.”

“No,” Bagheera purred. “That cannot happen. Once your bellies are full, the madness might seize you again. You deserve your name, the Free People. Freedom was what you fought for, and now you have it. Feed on it, O Wolves.”
“The Man-Pack rejected me, and so did the Wolf-Pack,” Mowgli said. “From now on, I shall hunt by myself in the jungle.”
“Then we will come hunting beside you,” the four cubs replied.
Mowgli left with the four cubs, and from that day they hunted together in the jungle. He did not remain alone forever, however. Years later he grew into a man and married.
That, however, is a tale meant for grown-ups.
Mowgli’s Song

THAT HE SANG AT THE COUNCIL ROCK WHEN HE
DANCED ON SHERE KHAN’S HIDE

The Song of Mowgli—I, Mowgli, am singing. Let the jungle listen to the
things I have done.
Shere Khan said he would kill—would kill! At the gates in the twilight
he would kill Mowgli, the Frog!
He ate and he drank. Drink deep, Shere Khan, for when will you drink
again? Sleep and dream of the kill.
I am alone on the grazing-grounds. Gray Brother, come to me! Come to
me, Lone Wolf, for there is big game about!
Bring up the great bull buffaloes, the blue-skinned herd bulls with the
angry eyes. Drive them back and forth as I order.
Are you still sleeping, Shere Khan? Wake, oh, wake! Here I come, and the
bulls are behind.
Rama, the King of the Buffaloes, stamped with his foot. Waters of the
Waingunga, where did Shere Khan go?
He is not Ikki to dig holes, nor Mao, the Peacock, that he should fly.
He is not Mang the Bat, to hang in the branches. Little bamboos that
creak together, tell me where he ran?
_Ow!_ He is there. _Ahoo!_ He is there. Under the feet of Rama lies the
Lame One! Up, Shere Khan!
Up and kill! Here is meat; break the necks of the bulls!
_Hsh!_ He is asleep. We will not wake him, for his strength is very
great. The kites have come down to see it. The black ants have come up
to know it. There is a great gathering in his honor.
_Alala!_ I have no cloth to wrap me. The kites will see that I am
naked. I am ashamed to meet all these people.
Lend me your coat, Shere Khan. Lend me your bright striped coat so I may
go to the Council Rock.
By the Bull that bought me I made a promise—a little promise. Only your
coat is missing before I keep my word.
With the knife, with the knife that men use, with the knife of the
hunter, I will bend down for my gift.
Waters of the Waingunga, Shere Khan gives me his coat for the love that
he feels for me. Pull, Gray Brother! Pull, Akela! Heavy is the hide of
Shere Khan.
The Man Pack are angry. They throw stones and talk child’s talk. My
mouth is bleeding. Let me run away.
Through the night, through the hot night, run swiftly with me, my
brothers. We will leave the lights of the village and go to the low
moon.
Waters of the Waingunga, the Man-Pack have cast me out. I did them no
harm, but they were afraid of me. Why?
Wolf Pack, you have cast me out too. The jungle is shut to me and the
village gates are shut. Why?
As Mang flies between the beasts and birds, so I fly between the
village and the jungle. Why?
I dance on the hide of Shere Khan, but my heart is very heavy. My mouth
is cut and wounded with the stones from the village, but my heart is
very light, because I have come back to the jungle. Why?
These two things fight together in me as the snakes fight in the
spring. The water comes out of my eyes; yet I laugh while it falls.
Why?
I am two Mowglis, but the hide of Shere Khan is under my feet.
All the jungle knows that I have killed Shere Khan. Look—look closely, O
Wolves!
_Ahae!_ My heart is heavy with the things that I do not understand.

chapters.title: The White Seal
paragraphs:
Oh! hush now, my baby, the night is behind us,
And black are the waters that sparkled so green.
The moon, above breakers, looks downward to find us
At rest in the hollows that rustle between.
Where billow meets billow, let soft be your pillow,
Ah, weary wee flipperling, curl at your ease!
The storm shall not wake you, nor shark overtake you,
Asleep in the arms of the slow-swinging seas!
Seal Lullaby

This all happened years ago at Novastoshnah, or North East Point, on St. Paul Island, far away in the Bering Sea. Limmershin the Winter Wren told me about it after the wind blew him onto the rigging of a steamer bound for Japan. I brought him into my cabin and kept him warm and fed for two days, until he could fly back to St. Paul’s. Limmershin is an odd little bird, but he tells the truth.

People visit Novastoshnah only on business, and seals are the only people with regular business there. Hundreds upon hundreds of thousands arrive from the cold gray sea each summer. No beach anywhere in the world offers seals better quarters than Novastoshnah.

Sea Catch knew that. Every spring, wherever he happened to be, he swam straight for Novastoshnah like a torpedo-boat, then spent a month fighting other seals for a good rocky spot close to the water. Fifteen years old, he was an enormous gray fur seal, with something like a mane around his shoulders and long, vicious canine teeth. Raised on his front flippers, he stood over four feet high. Anyone brave enough to weigh him would have found he weighed nearly seven hundred pounds. Fierce battles had scarred his whole body, yet he was always willing to fight once more. He tilted his head as though afraid to meet his opponent’s eyes, then darted it forward like lightning. Once his teeth locked onto another seal’s neck, that seal could escape if he could manage it; Sea Catch would offer no help.

He never pursued a defeated seal, however: the Rules of the Beach forbade it. He wanted only a nursery beside the water. But forty or fifty thousand others wanted the same thing every spring, and their whistles, bellows, roars, and snorts made a dreadful uproar.

From little Hutchinson’s Hill you could see three and a half miles of ground packed with fighting seals. Everywhere in the surf, seal heads hurried ashore to join the battles. They fought in the breaking waves, on the sand, and over the nurseries’ smooth basalt rocks, as stupid and unwilling to compromise as men. Their wives waited until late May or early June to arrive; they had no wish to be torn apart. Younger seals, aged two, three, and four, had no households yet. They passed through the fighters and went half a mile inland, where enormous crowds played on the dunes and rubbed away every growing green thing. These were the holluschickie--the bachelors. Novastoshnah alone held perhaps two or three hundred thousand.

One spring Sea Catch had just finished his forty-fifth battle when his wife Matkah emerged from the sea, soft and sleek, with gentle eyes. He grabbed her by the neck and dumped her on his patch. “Late again,” he growled. “Where have you been?”

Sea Catch followed the seal custom of eating nothing at all throughout the four months he spent on the beaches, and so he was usually in a bad temper. Matkah knew not to argue. Looking around, she cooed, “How considerate. You’ve secured our old place again.”
“Of course I have,” Sea Catch replied. “Just look at me!”
Scratches bled in twenty places. One eye was nearly torn out, and strips of flesh hung along his sides.
“Oh, you men, you men!” Matkah sighed, fanning herself with a back flipper. “Why not behave sensibly and agree on your places peacefully? You look as if you’ve been battling the Killer Whale.”

“I’ve done nothing except fight since mid-May. This season the beach is disgracefully full. At least a hundred seals from Lukannon Beach have been here looking for homes. Why won’t people stay where they belong?”
“I often think we’d be happier coming ashore at Otter Island, away from this crowd,” Matkah said.
“Bah! Otter Island is for holluschickie. Go there, and everyone would call us cowards. Appearances must be maintained, my dear.”

Proudly sinking his head between his broad shoulders, Sea Catch pretended to nap, though he remained alert for another fight. Now that the seals and their wives were ashore, their racket carried miles out to sea, even above the fiercest gales. At least a million crowded the beach: old seals, mothers, tiny babies, and holluschickie, all fighting, jostling, bleating, crawling, and playing. Down to the water and back up again they went in gangs and regiments. They sprawled over every inch of ground as far as anyone could see, while whole brigades skirmished through the fog. Novastoshnah is nearly always foggy. Occasionally the sun appears and briefly makes everything gleam with pearly rainbow colors.

Matkah’s baby Kotick was born amid all that turmoil. Like every small seal, he was mostly head and shoulders, with pale, watery-blue eyes. Something about his fur, though, made his mother examine him closely.
At last she said, “Sea Catch, our baby is going to be white!”
“Empty clam-shells and dry seaweed!” Sea Catch snorted. “There has never been a white seal anywhere in the world.”
“That’s not my fault,” Matkah replied. “There will be one now.” She began the quiet, crooning lullaby all mother seals sing to their young:

You must not swim till you’re six weeks old,
Or your head will be sunk by your heels;
And summer gales and Killer Whales
Are bad for baby seals.

Are bad for baby seals, dear rat,
As bad as bad can be;
But splash and grow strong,
And you can’t go wrong.
Child of the Open Sea!

At first, of course, the baby understood none of it. He paddled and scrambled beside his mother, learning to scuttle out of danger when his father fought another seal and the two rolled roaring over the slippery rocks. Matkah went to sea for food, so Kotick fed only every other day. But when feeding time finally came, he ate as much as his small stomach would hold and grew strong on those meals.

His first expedition was a crawl inland. There he found tens of thousands of babies his age. They romped like puppies, slept on clean sand, and resumed their games. The adults in the nurseries ignored them, the holluschickie stayed on their own grounds, and the babies enjoyed a wonderful time.

Returning from deep-sea fishing, Matkah went directly to the playground. She called like a ewe seeking her lamb and waited for Kotick’s answering bleat. Then she headed straight toward him, swinging her front flippers and sending babies tumbling on either side. At any moment, a few hundred other mothers would also be searching the playgrounds for their own children, so the little seals had plenty to keep them lively and on the move. Matkah told Kotick, “Avoid lying in muddy water and catching mange, don’t rub coarse sand into any scratch or cut, and never swim in rough seas. Follow those rules and nothing here will hurt you.”

Baby seals know no more about swimming than children do, but feel miserable until they learn. On Kotick’s first visit to the water, a wave swept him beyond his depth. Down went his heavy head; up flew his little rear flippers, exactly as Matkah’s song warned. Without the next wave throwing him back, he would have drowned.

After that he practiced in a shallow beach pool, letting the wash cover and lift him while he paddled, always watching for dangerous bigger waves. For two whole weeks he worked at learning how to use his flippers. Throughout that time, each attempt brought him farther toward understanding what his flippers were for. He floundered in and out, coughed, grunted, crawled ashore for naps on the sand, then tried again. Finally he discovered that the water was truly his home.

Imagine the fun he and his friends had then: diving beneath rollers, riding a breaking wave ashore in a splash and splutter as it surged up the beach, standing on their tails and scratching their heads like adults, or playing “I’m the King of the Castle” on slippery, weed-covered rocks barely above the wash. Occasionally a narrow fin, like a large shark’s, cruised near shore. Kotick knew it belonged to the Killer Whale, the Grampus, who caught young seals whenever possible. He shot toward the beach like an arrow, while the fin drifted slowly away as though its owner were not looking for anything at all.

By late October, families and tribes were leaving St. Paul’s for the deep waters of the open ocean. Fighting over nursery grounds ended, and holluschickie played wherever they wanted. “Next year you’ll be a holluschickie,” Matkah told Kotick. “This year you must learn to fish.”

Together they crossed the Pacific. Matkah taught him to sleep floating on his back, flippers tucked beside him, only his small nose above water. No cradle rocks more comfortably than the Pacific’s long swells. When prickling spread over his skin, she explained that he was developing the “feel of the water.” That tingling warned of approaching bad weather: he must swim hard to escape it.

“Soon you’ll know which direction to take,” she said. “For now, we’ll follow wise Sea Pig, the Porpoise.” A whole school of porpoises was diving and racing ahead through the waves, and little Kotick followed behind as fast as he could swim. “How do you know where to go?” he gasped. The leader rolled his white eye and dived. “My tail prickles, youngster. There’s a gale behind me. Keep coming! South of the Sticky Water [he meant the Equator], a prickling tail means the gale is ahead, so turn north. Keep coming! This water feels wrong.”

This was only one of the many things Kotick learned, for he was continually discovering something new and there was always another lesson to learn. Matkah showed him how to track cod and halibut along underwater banks and haul rockling from their weedy holes; how to sweep around wrecks a hundred fathoms down, shooting through one porthole and out another like a rifle bullet after fleeing fish; how to dance on waves beneath a lightning-filled sky, politely waving a flipper to the short-tailed Albatross and Man-of-war Hawk as they rode the wind. He learned dolphin-like leaps three or four feet clear of the sea, flippers tucked and tail curved; to avoid bony flying fish; to bite a cod’s shoulder at full speed ten fathoms down; and never to linger near a boat or ship, especially a rowing boat. After six months, anything he didn't know about deep-sea fishing scarcely mattered. Throughout those months he never once touched land.

One day, half asleep in warm water off Juan Fernandez Island, Kotick felt weak and restless, rather as humans do when spring stirs in their legs. He remembered Novastoshnah’s firm beaches seven thousand miles away, his friends’ games, seaweed smells, roaring seals, and battles. At that very moment he turned his nose northward and began swimming steadily toward home. As he continued on his way, more and more of his companions came into sight. Dozens of companions joined him, heading the same way. “Greetings, Kotick!” they called. “We’re all holluschickie this year. We can dance the Fire-dance in Lukannon’s surf and play on the fresh grass. Where did you find that coat?”

His fur was nearly pure white now, and he was very proud of it. But he answered only, “Hurry! Every bone in me longs for land.” Together they reached their birthplace and heard their fathers, the old seals, battling in drifting mist.

That night Kotick joined the yearlings’ Fire-dance. On summer nights the sea glows all the way between Novastoshnah and Lukannon. Every seal trails what looks like burning oil, flashes like flame when leaping, and swims among waves breaking in luminous streaks and spirals. Afterward they rolled through fresh wild wheat on the holluschickie grounds inland, exchanging stories of their travels. They talked about the vast Pacific quite as familiarly as a group of boys would talk about a wood where they had gone together to gather nuts. Anyone understanding them could have drawn an unrivaled chart of that ocean. Three- and four-year-old holluschickie romped down Hutchinson’s Hill, calling, “Make way, youngsters! The sea is deep; you haven’t discovered everything in it yet. Wait until you round the Horn. Hey, yearling, where did that white coat come from?”

“I didn’t find it,” Kotick answered. “It grew.” He was about to bowl the speaker over when two men appeared behind a dune, black-haired, with flat red faces. Never having seen a man, Kotick coughed and lowered his head. The other holluschickie shuffled a few yards away and stared stupidly. These were Kerick Booterin, chief of the island’s seal-hunters, and his son Patalamon. They lived in the little village less than half a mile from the nurseries. Now they were choosing seals to drive like sheep to the killing pens, where their journey toward becoming sealskin jackets would begin.
“Ho!” Patalamon exclaimed. “Look! A white seal!”

Beneath his coating of smoke and oil, Kerick Booterin went almost pale. He was an Aleut, and Aleuts are not clean people. Murmuring a prayer, he said, “Leave him alone, Patalamon. There hasn’t been a white seal since--since my birth. Perhaps that’s old Zaharrof’s ghost. The great gale took him last year.”
“I’ll keep away,” Patalamon replied. “He brings bad luck. Could he really be Zaharrof returned? I still owe him money for gulls’ eggs.”

“Don’t stare at him,” Kerick said. “Cut off those four-year-olds. The men should skin two hundred today, but the season is just starting and they aren’t used to the work yet. A hundred is enough. Hurry!”

Patalamon shook two seal shoulder bones before a group of holluschickie. They halted, snorting and puffing. When he approached, they moved; Kerick steered them inland, and none tried rejoining their friends. Hundreds of thousands watched the driving but continued their games. Kotick alone wanted to know what was happening and began asking all his companions about it. Not one could explain where the seals were going or what the men meant to do. His companions knew nothing beyond the fact that men did this for six weeks or two months every year.
“I’m following them,” he announced. As he shuffled along behind the departing herd, he stared after them with such wide eyes that they almost seemed to pop out of his head.
“That white seal is following us,” Patalamon cried. “No seal has ever gone to the killing-grounds by himself before.”
“Hsh! Don’t turn around,” Kerick warned. “That’s Zaharrof’s ghost! I must speak with the priest about this.”

The killing-grounds lay just half a mile away, but getting there took an hour. Kerick knew that rushing overheated seals, making their fur fall out in patches during skinning. Slowly they passed Sea Lion’s Neck and Webster House, reaching the Salt House beyond the beach seals’ view. Panting and puzzled, Kotick followed. He felt he had reached the world’s end, though the distant nursery roared like a train inside a tunnel. Kerick sat on the moss, produced a heavy pewter watch, and allowed thirty minutes for the seals to cool. While the men waited and the seals cooled, Kotick could hear the tiny drops of moisture gathered from the fog falling one after another from the brim of Kerick’s cap. Ten or twelve men arrived carrying iron-bound clubs three or four feet long. Kerick indicated a few seals that were overheated or bitten. Wearing heavy boots of walrus-throat skin, the men kicked those aside. After pointing out these unsuitable animals and seeing them kicked clear of the drove, Kerick finally gave the order. “Let go!” he shouted, and they clubbed the others’ heads as fast as possible.

Ten minutes later Kotick no longer recognized his friends. Their skins had been slit from nose to rear flippers, stripped away, and piled on the ground. He could bear no more. He turned and galloped seaward--seals can gallop remarkably fast for short distances--his newly grown little mustache stiff with horror. At Sea Lion’s Neck, where huge sea lions sit beside the surf, he plunged headfirst into cool water and rocked there, gasping in misery. “What’s going on?” a sea lion growled; sea lions generally mind their own business.
“Scoochnie! Ochen scoochnie!” (“I’m lonely, terribly lonely!”) Kotick cried. “They’re killing every holluschickie on every beach!”
The Sea Lion looked ashore. “Rubbish!” he said. “Your friends are just as noisy as always. You’ve seen old Kerick finish off a group. He’s been doing that for thirty years.”
“It’s dreadful,” Kotick replied, paddling backward beneath a wave. Twisting his flippers, he steadied himself and stopped upright within barely three inches of the jagged edge of a rock.

“Fine work for a yearling!” said the Sea Lion, an admirer of skillful swimming. “From your viewpoint I suppose it is unpleasant. But you seals keep returning every year, so naturally men learn about it. Unless you find an island men never visit, you will always be driven by them.”
“Doesn’t an island like that exist?” Kotick asked.

“I’ve hunted poltoos [halibut] for twenty years without finding one. Still, you seem to enjoy addressing your elders and betters. Why not visit Walrus Islet and ask Sea Vitch? He might know. Don’t go rushing away like that. It’s six miles across. In your place, little one, I’d go ashore and sleep first.”

Kotick accepted this sensible advice. He swam to his own beach and slept ashore for half an hour, twitching as seals do. Then he headed straight toward Walrus Islet, a low rocky island almost northeast of Novastoshnah, crowded with ledges and gull nests. The walruses lived there apart from everyone else.

He landed beside sleeping old Sea Vitch, whose rear flippers lay partly in the surf. This enormous North Pacific walrus was ugly, swollen, pimply, thick-necked, and long-tusked, with no manners at all except while asleep.
“Wake up!” Kotick barked above the clamor of the gulls.

“Hah! Ho! Hmph! What is it?” Sea Vitch grunted. He swung his tusks at the walrus lying next to him and woke him with a blow. That walrus struck his neighbor in turn, and the blows passed down the line until all were awake, looking everywhere except in the right direction.
“Hi! Over here,” Kotick called, bobbing like a tiny white slug in the waves.

“Well! I’ll be--skinned!” Sea Vitch exclaimed. All the walruses regarded Kotick like a club of sleepy old gentlemen confronted by a small boy. At that particular moment Kotick had no wish to hear another word about skinning; he had already seen more of it than he could bear. He called, “Is there somewhere seals can live where men never come?”
“Find out for yourself,” Sea Vitch replied, closing his eyes. “Go away. We have things to do.”

Kotick leaped dolphin-fashion and shouted at full volume, “Clam-eater! Clam-eater!” For all Sea Vitch’s fierce pretensions, Kotick knew he had never caught a fish, only rooted about for clams and seaweed. The Chickies, Gooverooskies, and Epatkas--Burgomaster Gulls, Kittiwakes, and Puffins--never miss a chance for rudeness. All of them eagerly took up the cry and shouted it back at the walrus, each bird trying to make itself heard above the others. Limmershin told me that for nearly five minutes a gunshot would have been inaudible on Walrus Islet. Everyone screamed, “Clam-eater! Stareek [old man]!” Sea Vitch rolled back and forth, coughing and grunting.
“Will you answer me now?” Kotick demanded, completely breathless.
“Ask Sea Cow,” Sea Vitch said. “If he’s still alive, he should be able to tell you.”
“How will I recognize Sea Cow?” Kotick asked, beginning to swim away.
“The only sea creature uglier than Sea Vitch,” a Burgomaster gull shrieked, circling beneath the walrus’s nose. “Uglier, and even ruder! Stareek!”

Leaving the gulls screaming, Kotick returned to Novastoshnah. Nobody there supported his search for a peaceful seal home. Men had always driven holluschickie, they said; it was everyday business. If he disliked horrible sights, he shouldn't have visited the killing-grounds. But his friends had never witnessed the killing. None of the other seals had actually seen their friends being killed. That knowledge, which he alone possessed, made all the difference between Kotick and the companions who refused to understand him. Besides, Kotick was a white seal.

After hearing his adventures, Sea Catch said, “Grow into a great seal like your father and establish your nursery here. Then they’ll leave you alone. In five years you should be able to fight your own battles.” Even gentle Matkah told him, “You cannot stop the killing. Go and play in the water, Kotick.” So Kotick went off into the sea and joined in the Fire-dance with the others, but as he danced his little heart felt terribly heavy.

That autumn he left as early as possible, alone, with an idea lodged in his round head. He would find Sea Cow, if such a creature existed, and a peaceful island with firm beaches beyond men’s reach. He searched the Pacific from north to south, sometimes swimming three hundred miles in twenty-four hours. He explored and explored entirely by himself, from the northern Pacific right down to its southern waters. More things happened to him on those journeys than there is room to tell here. Basking Shark, Spotted Shark, and Hammerhead almost caught him. He encountered the unreliable ruffians prowling the oceans, ponderous polite fish, and scarlet-spotted scallops anchored for hundreds of years to one place and immensely proud of it. But throughout all these journeys he never met Sea Cow, and never found an island that he could imagine as the home he wanted for the seals.

Whenever he found firm beaches with slopes for playing, a whaler’s smoke marked the horizon: men rendering blubber. Kotick knew exactly what the smoke meant and understood why such a beach would be no refuge for seals. Elsewhere, signs showed that seals had lived there and been slaughtered. He knew that men who had visited once would return.

An old short-tailed albatross recommended Kerguelen Island as a haven of peace. Kotick went there, only to nearly smash himself against vicious black cliffs during a sleet-storm full of thunder and lightning. Struggling back against the gale, he saw that even this place had once held seal nurseries. He found the same discouraging evidence on every other island he visited: none of them offered the untouched home he was searching for.

Limmershin listed many islands. Kotick searched for five seasons, he said, resting four months yearly at Novastoshnah while the holluschickie mocked his imaginary refuges. At the Gallapagos, a dreadful dry place on the Equator, he nearly roasted alive. He visited the Georgia Islands, the Orkneys, Emerald Island, Little Nightingale Island, Gough’s Island, Bouvet’s Island, the Crossets, and even a tiny island south of the Cape of Good Hope. At every one of these places he spoke with the People of the Sea, and everywhere they gave him the same discouraging answer: seals had once come, but men killed them all. Returning from Gough’s Island, he swam thousands of miles beyond the Pacific to Cape Corrientes. Even there, a few hundred mangy seals crowded a rock and told him men visited.

Nearly heartbroken, he turned around the Horn toward home. Heading north, he landed on an island covered with green trees. There he came upon a very, very old seal who was dying. Kotick caught fish to feed him and told him everything that had made his journeys so sorrowful. “I’m returning to Novastoshnah,” he said. “If they drive me to the killing-pens with the holluschickie, I won’t care.”

“Make one more attempt,” the old seal urged. “I’m the last survivor of the Lost Rookery of Masafuera. When men slaughtered us by the hundred thousand, the beaches had a story: someday a white seal would come from the North and lead our people to safety. I’m too old to see it happen, but others will. Try again.”
Kotick curled his splendid mustache. “I am the only white seal ever born on these beaches,” he declared, “and the only seal, black or white, ever to think of searching for new islands.”

The thought greatly encouraged him. Back at Novastoshnah that summer, Matkah begged him to marry and settle down. No longer a holluschick, he was a mature sea-catch, with a curly white mane, matching his father in weight, size, and fierceness. “Allow me one more season,” he answered. “Remember, Mother: the seventh wave always reaches farthest up the beach.”

As it happened, another seal also decided to postpone marriage a year. The evening before his final expedition, Kotick danced the Fire-dance beside her along Lukannon Beach. This time he headed west, following a huge shoal of halibut. Keeping himself fit required at least a hundred pounds of fish daily. He chased the fish until he was tired, then curled his body up to sleep. The long ocean swell rolling toward Copper Island carried him along in its hollows as he rested. He knew this coast well. Around midnight, feeling a gentle bump against seaweed, he murmured, “Hm, strong tide tonight.” He rolled underwater, slowly opened his eyes, and stretched. Then he jumped like a cat: enormous creatures were nosing about the shallows, grazing on thick weed fringes.
“By the Great Combers of Magellan!” he muttered through his mustache. “Who in the Deep Sea are these creatures?”

They resembled no walrus, sea lion, seal, bear, whale, shark, fish, squid, or scallop he knew. Twenty to thirty feet long, they lacked rear flippers. Their shovel-shaped tails looked carved from wet leather. Their heads were the most foolish-looking things you could ever hope to see anywhere in the sea. When not grazing, they balanced on their tails in deeper water, solemnly bowing and waving front flippers like fat men waving arms.

“Ahem!” Kotick said. “Good hunting, gentlemen?” They bowed and waved like the Frog Footman. As they resumed feeding, he saw their upper lips split into halves that opened about a foot apart, then closed around a bushel of seaweed. They tucked the great bundles of weed into their mouths and went on chewing, as solemnly as if feeding were a very serious business.

“A messy way to eat,” Kotick observed. More bows followed, testing his patience. “Very well. An extra joint in your front flippers is no reason to show off. Your bows are elegant, I admit, but what are your names?” Their divided lips twitched, their glassy green eyes stared, and no answer came.
“Well!” Kotick exclaimed. “I’ve never met anyone uglier or worse-mannered than Sea Vitch--until now.”

Suddenly he remembered the Burgomaster gull’s cries when he was a yearling at Walrus Islet. Remembering those words, he tumbled backward in the water in surprise, realizing that at last he had discovered Sea Cow.

The sea cows kept slurping and chewing seaweed while Kotick tried every language learned on his journeys. In all his travels he had picked up a great many languages, for the Sea People have almost as many different ways of speaking as human beings do. But Sea Cow cannot speak. His neck has six bones instead of seven; undersea folk say this leaves him unable to talk even to his companions. As you know, however, his front flipper has an extra joint. Waving it up, down, and around, he communicates through a clumsy sort of telegraph code.

By dawn Kotick’s mane bristled and his patience had gone where dead crabs go. The Sea Cows slowly headed north, occasionally stopping for ridiculous councils of bows. Kotick followed patiently enough in his movements, though not in his thoughts, saying to himself as he watched their solemn bows, “Such idiots would have been killed ages ago unless they knew a safe island. A place good enough for Sea Cow will suit Sea Catch. But I wish they would move faster.”

Following them was exhausting. They covered only forty or fifty miles daily, stayed close inshore, and at night stopped traveling so that they could feed. Kotick swam around, above, and below them without speeding them up even half a mile. Farther north, their bowing councils happened every few hours. He nearly bit his mustache off in frustration, until he noticed they were following a warm current. Once he understood that, he began to have rather more respect for them.

One night they dropped like stones through the glimmering water and, for the first time, began swimming fast. Kotick followed, astonished: he had never imagined Sea Cow could swim well. They approached a coastal cliff plunging into deep water and entered a dark hole twenty fathoms beneath the surface. They led him through a dark underwater tunnel, and swimming along it seemed to take a very, very long time. Before emerging from its darkness, Kotick desperately needed another breath.
“My wig!” he exclaimed, bursting into open water, gasping and puffing. “That was certainly a long dive to make, but it was well worth all the effort.”

The sea cows had spread out to graze lazily beside the finest beaches he had ever seen. Smooth rock stretched for miles, perfectly suited to seal nurseries. Behind lay firm sandy playgrounds sloping inland. There were great rolling waves where seals could dance, long stretches of grass where they could roll about, and sandy dunes to climb up and down. Best of all, the water’s feel--which never misleads a true sea-catch--told Kotick that no man had ever reached this place.

Before doing anything else, he made certain that the fishing in these waters was good and that there would be plenty of food for seals to catch. Then he swam along the shores, counting delightful low sandy islands partly hidden by beautiful drifting fog. Northward, a chain of sandbars, shallows, and rocks would keep ships at least six miles from the beaches. Between mainland and islands, deep water reached the sheer cliffs. Somewhere beneath them lay the tunnel entrance.

“Another Novastoshnah, only ten times better,” Kotick declared. “Sea Cow is wiser than I supposed. Even if men lived here, they couldn't descend those cliffs. Offshore shallows would smash their ships. If anywhere in the ocean is safe, this place is.”

He remembered the seal waiting at home. Eager as he was to return to Novastoshnah, he explored his discovery thoroughly so that when the others questioned him about the place, he would be able to answer everything they might want to know.

He dived, fixed the tunnel entrance in his memory, and sped south through it. No one except a sea cow or a seal would have dreamed that such a hidden place could exist beneath those cliffs. Looking back, even Kotick scarcely believed he had swum beneath those cliffs.

Despite his speed, reaching home took six days. He landed above Sea Lion’s Neck and immediately met the seal who had waited for him. She looked into his eyes and knew at once, without waiting for his story, that he had found the island he had been seeking.

But his father Sea Catch, the holluschickie, and every other seal laughed at him when he told them the story of everything he had discovered. A young male about his age objected, “All very nice, Kotick, but you can’t arrive from who knows where and order us to leave. We've fought for our nurseries, something you never bothered to do. You preferred roaming the ocean.”
The others laughed, and the young male twisted his head from side to side. Newly married that year, he considered it an extremely important achievement.
“I have no nursery worth fighting over,” Kotick replied. “I want to show everyone a safe place to live. Why should that require a fight?”
“Oh, if you’re looking for an excuse to retreat, I’ve nothing further to say,” the young seal chuckled nastily.
“If I beat you, will you follow?” Kotick asked. Green flashed in his eyes; being forced into a fight made him furious.
“All right,” the youngster answered carelessly. “Beat me, and I’ll go with you.”

Before he could reconsider, Kotick darted forward and buried his teeth in the blubber around his neck. Bracing on his hindquarters, Kotick dragged him down the beach, shook him, and flung him over. Then he roared at the others, “I've worked for you for five seasons. I've found an island where you'll be safe. Yet unless someone pulls your heads off your foolish necks, you won't believe it. Now I'll teach you. Watch yourselves!”

Limmershin watches ten thousand large seals fight every year. Yet never in his little life, he told me, had he witnessed anything like the charge Kotick made as he flung himself straight into the crowded nurseries. Kotick hurled himself at the largest sea-catch available, seized his throat, choked, battered, and thumped him until he begged for mercy, then tossed him aside and attacked another. Unlike the big seals, Kotick had never fasted for four months annually. Ocean voyages kept him perfectly fit, and, best of all, he had never fought before. His white curls stood rigid with rage, his eyes blazed, and his long teeth gleamed: a magnificent sight. Sea Catch watched his son drag grizzled elders around like halibut and scatter young bachelors everywhere. Roaring, he cried, “Fool he may be, but no seal fights better! Spare your father, son! I'm on your side!”

Kotick roared back. Mustache bristling, Sea Catch waddled into battle, puffing like a locomotive. Matkah and Kotick’s future wife crouched together, admiring their menfolk. It was a splendid battle to watch, with both of them fighting at their very best. Father and son continued until no seal dared raise his head. Then they marched side by side along the beach, bellowing grandly.
That night, as Northern Lights flickered through the mist, Kotick climbed a bare rock. Below lay scattered nurseries and bleeding, battered seals. “Now,” he announced, “you have had your lesson.”
