“My wig!” Sea Catch said, hauling his badly mauled body stiffly upright. “The Killer Whale couldn't have hurt them worse. Son, you make me proud. I'll even follow you to that island--if such a place really exists.”
“Listen, you fat sea-pigs. Who will follow me through Sea Cow’s tunnel? Answer me, or I will teach you another lesson,” Kotick roared.
A murmur rippled along the beaches like the tide. Thousands of tired voices all along the shore answered him, “We'll come. We will follow Kotick, the White Seal.”

Proudly Kotick lowered his head between his shoulders and closed his eyes. From nose to tail he was now red rather than white. Yet he would have despised himself for examining or touching a single wound.

A week later he led his army north: nearly ten thousand holluschickie and older seals bound for Sea Cow’s tunnel. Those remaining at Novastoshnah called them fools. But when they met again near the Pacific fishing banks next spring, the travelers described their new beaches so wonderfully that increasing numbers deserted Novastoshnah. Of course, it did not all happen in one season or all at once, for changing the habits of so many seals was slow work. Seals are not especially clever and consider things slowly. Year after year, however, more left Novastoshnah, Lukannon, and the other nurseries for those peaceful, sheltered shores. There Kotick spends each summer, growing larger, fatter, and stronger every year, while holluschickie play around him in seas untouched by men.
Lukannon
This is the great ocean song sung by all St. Paul seals returning to their summer beaches. It serves as a kind of seal National Anthem, and a very sorrowful one.

I met my mates in the morning (and, oh, but I am old!) Where roaring on the ledges the summer ground-swell rolled; I heard them raise the chorus that drowned the breakers’ song— The Beaches of Lukannon—two million voices strong.

_The song of pleasant homes beside the salt lagoons,
The song of snorting squadrons that shuffled down the dunes,
The song of midnight dances that churned the sea to flame—
The Beaches of Lukannon—before the sealers came!_

I met my mates in the morning (I’ll never meet them more!); They came and went in legions that darkened all the shore. And over foam-flecked waters as far as voice could reach We greeted landing-parties and we sang them up the beach.

_The Beaches of Lukannon—the winter wheat so tall—
The dripping, wrinkled lichens, and the sea-fog drenching all!
The platforms of our playground, all shining smooth and worn!
The Beaches of Lukannon—the home where we were born!_

I met my mates in the morning, a broken, scattered band. Men shoot us in the water and club us on the land; Men drive us to the Salt House like foolish sheep and tame, And still we sing Lukannon—before the sealers came.

_Wheel down, wheel down to southward; oh, Gooverooska, go!
And tell the Deep-Sea Viceroys the story of our woe;
Before, empty as the shark’s egg the tempest flings ashore,
The Beaches of Lukannon shall know their sons no more!_

chapters.title: "Rikki-Tikki-Tavi"
paragraphs:
At the hole where he went in
Red-Eye called to Wrinkle-Skin.
Hear what little Red-Eye says:
“Nag, come up and dance with death!”

Eye to eye and head to head,
(_Keep the rhythm, Nag._)
This will end when one is dead;
(_At your pleasure, Nag._)
Turn for turn and twist for twist—
(_Run and hide now, Nag._)
Hah! The hooded Death has missed!
(_Trouble finds you, Nag!_)

Here is the story of Rikki-tikki-tavi’s great war, fought almost entirely alone through the bathrooms of a large bungalow in Segowlee cantonment. Darzee the Tailorbird helped, and Chuchundra the muskrat offered advice. Chuchundra always creeps along walls, never venturing into the middle of a floor. The actual fighting, however, fell to Rikki-tikki.

He was a mongoose, with fur and tail rather like a small cat’s, but a weasel’s head and habits. His eyes were pink, and so was the tip of his constantly moving nose. Any of his four legs could scratch whatever part of himself he chose. He could puff his tail into a bottle brush, and as he dashed through tall grass his battle cry rang out: “Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!”

A summer flood swept him from the burrow he shared with his parents and carried him down a roadside ditch, kicking and clucking. He gripped a small clump of floating grass until he fainted. When he woke, he lay soaking and bedraggled in hot sunlight in the middle of a garden path. A little boy was saying, “Here’s a dead mongoose. Let's give him a funeral.”
“No,” his mother answered. “Let's bring him inside and dry him off. He may still be alive.”

Inside the house, a large man lifted him between finger and thumb. He wasn't dead, the man said, only half suffocated. They wrapped him in cotton wool and warmed him beside a small fire. Soon his eyes opened, and he sneezed.
“Now, don't scare him,” the man said--an Englishman newly arrived at the bungalow. “Let's watch and see what he does.”

Scaring a mongoose is almost impossible: curiosity fills him from nose to tail. “Run and find out” is the entire mongoose family's motto, and Rikki-tikki was true to his kind. He looked closely at the cotton wool and decided that it was certainly not anything he could eat, circled the table, sat up to groom himself, scratched, and leaped onto the boy’s shoulder.
“Don't worry, Teddy,” his father said. “He's simply trying to make friends with you.”
“Ouch! He's tickling me beneath my chin,” Teddy said.
Rikki-tikki peered between collar and neck, sniffed the boy’s ear, and climbed to the floor, where he sat rubbing his nose.
“Good gracious,” Teddy’s mother exclaimed, “a wild animal behaving like that! Perhaps our kindness has made him tame.”
“That's how all mongooses behave,” her husband replied. “Provided Teddy doesn't grab his tail or cage him, he'll spend all day running in and out. We ought to give him something to eat.”

He thoroughly enjoyed the little piece of raw meat they offered. Afterward he went onto the veranda, settled in the sunshine, and fluffed his fur so it could dry right down to the roots. That made him feel better.
“This house holds more things to investigate,” he thought, “than my whole family could discover in their entire lives. I shall certainly remain here and find out about them.”

Throughout that whole day he roamed and explored the house. He almost drowned in bathtubs, dipped his nose in ink on the writing table, then burned it against the man’s cigar after climbing onto his lap to study writing. At dusk he visited Teddy’s nursery to see how kerosene lamps were lit. When Teddy got into bed, Rikki-tikki joined him. He made a restless bedfellow: throughout the night, every sound demanded that he get up and discover its cause. His parents came for a final look at Teddy and found Rikki-tikki awake on the pillow. “I dislike that,” his mother said. “He might bite our child.” “Nothing of the kind,” his father replied. “That creature guards Teddy better than a bloodhound could. Suppose a snake came into the nursery--”
But Teddy’s mother refused to imagine anything quite so dreadful.

Early next morning he rode Teddy’s shoulder to breakfast on the veranda, where he received banana and boiled egg. In turn he sat on everyone’s lap. All properly raised mongooses hope to become household mongooses someday, with rooms to explore. His mother, who had lived in the general’s house at Segowlee, had carefully instructed him how to behave if he met white men.

Then he explored the garden. Only half of its large grounds were cultivated. Marshal Niel rose bushes grew as big as summer-houses; there were lime and orange trees, bamboo clumps, and thickets of tall grass. Rikki-tikki licked his lips. “What magnificent hunting grounds,” he said, his tail swelling like a bottle brush. He darted about, sniffing everywhere, until mournful voices reached him from a thorn-bush.

Darzee the Tailorbird and his wife were weeping there. They had drawn two large leaves together, sewn the edges with fibers, and lined the lovely nest with cotton and soft down. Sitting on its rim, they cried while it swayed beneath them.
“What has happened?” Rikki-tikki asked them.
“We're terribly unhappy,” Darzee replied. “Yesterday a baby fell from our nest, and Nag swallowed him.”
“H’m!” Rikki-tikki said. “That's very sad. But I've only just arrived here--who is this Nag?”

Neither bird answered. They crouched into their nest as a low hiss rose from the thick grass below: a dreadful, chilling sound that sent Rikki-tikki leaping two feet backward. Then, inch by inch, the head of Nag rose slowly out of the thick grass, with his broad hood already spread wide. The great black cobra measured five feet from tongue to tail. Raising a third of his length above ground, he swayed like a dandelion head in the breeze. He watched Rikki-tikki with those wicked snake eyes whose expression never changes, whatever thoughts lie behind them.
“Who is Nag?” he repeated. “I am Nag. The mighty God Brahm marked our entire people after the first cobra shaded the sleeping god from the sun with his hood. Look at me, and fear!”

His hood opened still wider, revealing the spectacle-mark behind it, shaped exactly like the eye of a hook-and-eye fastening. For a moment Rikki-tikki felt afraid. But a mongoose cannot remain frightened long. Though he had never encountered a living cobra, his mother had fed him dead ones, and he knew a grown mongoose’s life's work was fighting and eating snakes. The cobra Nag knew perfectly well that this was so, too. Deep within that cold heart, the cobra felt fear.
“Well,” Rikki-tikki said, his tail puffing again, “marked or unmarked, do you consider it right to steal young birds out of their nest and eat them?”

Nag considered his answer while watching the slightest movements in the grass behind Rikki-tikki. Sooner or later, he knew, mongooses here would mean death for his family. For now he needed this one unwary. He lowered his head slightly and tilted it aside.
“Let's discuss it,” he said. “You eat eggs yourself. Why shouldn't I eat birds?”
“Behind you! Watch behind you!” Darzee called.

Rikki-tikki wasted no time looking. He sprang as high as possible, and Nagaina’s head flashed beneath him. Nag’s wicked wife had crept up while he talked, intending to kill him. He heard her furious hiss at missing. Coming down, he landed almost across her back. An experienced mongoose would have known to break it with one bite immediately. But Rikki-tikki was still a young mongoose, and he was afraid of the terrible counterstroke the cobra could make as she lashed back toward him. He did bite, yet released too soon, leaping away from the lashing tail and leaving Nagaina wounded and enraged.
“Wicked, wicked Darzee!” Nag cried, striking upward toward the thorn-bush nest as high as he could. Darzee had built beyond snakes’ reach, however, and it merely swung back and forth.

Heat reddened Rikki-tikki’s eyes--red eyes mean an angry mongoose. Sitting on his hind legs and tail like a miniature kangaroo, he scanned his surroundings and chattered furiously. Both cobras had vanished into the grass. A snake that misses never announces its next move or gives a hint of its intentions. Rikki-tikki had no wish to follow them into that grass, because he could not feel certain of being able to deal with two snakes attacking him at once. He trotted to the gravel path beside the house and sat considering this serious problem.

Old natural-history books claim that a mongoose bitten in battle seeks out a herb to cure himself. That story simply is not true, however often those old books repeat it. Victory comes from sharp eyes and swift feet: the mongoose’s leap against the snake’s strike. No human eye can track a striking snake’s head; that makes the feat more wonderful than any magical plant. Knowing his youth, Rikki-tikki felt especially pleased to have avoided an attack from behind. Thinking it over, he felt more and more confidence in himself and in his ability to do what a mongoose ought to do. When Teddy ran down the path, he was quite ready for some petting.

As Teddy bent down, something stirred in the dust. “Take care. I am Death!” a tiny voice warned. This was Karait, the little dusty-brown snake that prefers dusty ground. His bite is as deadly as a cobra’s. Being so small, he goes unnoticed and therefore harms all the more people.

Rikki-tikki’s eyes reddened again. He approached Karait in the rocking, swaying dance inherited from his family. It looks comical, but balances a mongoose perfectly for springing in any direction--a useful advantage against snakes. Unknowingly, he faced greater danger than with Nag. Karait’s small size allowed such quick turns that, unless seized just behind the head, he could strike back into Rikki’s lip or eye. But Rikki-tikki did not know how much greater the danger was. He had no experience to tell him what fighting so small and quick a snake might mean. Red-eyed, he rocked and searched for a place to grip. Karait lunged. Rikki leaped sideways, trying to dart in, but the wicked little gray head whipped within a hair of his shoulder. He jumped across the snake’s body, its head following close behind his heels.

“Look here!” Teddy shouted toward the house. “Our mongoose is killing a snake.” His mother screamed. His father rushed out carrying a stick, but Karait had already lunged once too far. Rikki-tikki sprang onto his back, tucked his head between his front legs, bit as high on the spine as he could, and rolled clear. That bite left Karait completely paralyzed. Rikki was about to eat him tail first, his family’s customary dinner method, when he remembered that full stomachs slow mongooses. To keep all his speed and strength available, he must remain lean.

He went to bathe in dust under the castor-oil bushes while Teddy’s father battered the dead snake. “What's the point?” Rikki-tikki wondered. “I've dealt with everything already.” Teddy’s mother scooped him from the dust and hugged him, crying that he had saved her son’s life. His father called him a providence; Teddy stared with frightened, enormous eyes. Rikki found the commotion amusing without understanding it. She might equally well have praised Teddy for playing in dust. As far as Rikki was concerned, he was enjoying himself immensely.

At dinner he walked among the wine-glasses on the table, where he could have filled himself three times with delicious food. He remembered the two cobras, though. Although he thoroughly enjoyed being stroked and petted by Teddy’s mother and sitting up on the boy’s shoulder, his eyes periodically reddened and his long battle cry burst out: “Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!”

Teddy brought him to bed and insisted he sleep beneath his chin. Too polite to bite or scratch, Rikki-tikki waited until the boy slept, then began his nightly inspection. In the dark he encountered Chuchundra the muskrat creeping beside a wall. A miserable little creature, Chuchundra whimpers and squeaks all night, trying to gather courage to cross the room. But he never actually manages to reach its center.
“Please don't kill me,” Chuchundra almost sobbed. “Don't kill me, Rikki-tikki!”
“Would a killer of snakes bother killing muskrats?” Rikki-tikki asked contemptuously.
“Snake-killers are killed by snakes,” Chuchundra said even more miserably. “How can I know Nag won't mistake me for you on some dark night?”
“You're in no danger of that,” Rikki-tikki replied. “Anyway, Nag lives in the garden, and you never venture there.”
“Chua, my cousin the rat, told me something--” Chuchundra began, then broke off.
“What did he tell you?”
“Hush! Nag is everywhere, Rikki-tikki. You ought to have spoken with Chua out in the garden.”
“Well, I didn't. You'll have to explain. Hurry, Chuchundra, or I'll bite!”

Chuchundra sat weeping until tears dripped from his whiskers. “I'm such a poor creature,” he sobbed. “I've never even had the courage to cross to the middle of a room. Hush! I mustn't say anything. Can't you hear it, Rikki-tikki?”

Rikki-tikki listened. The house was utterly silent, yet he thought he heard the tiniest scratch-scratch, scarcely louder than a wasp’s feet crossing window glass. It was the dry scraping of snake scales against bricks.
“Nag or Nagaina,” he thought. “He's entering through the bathroom drain. Chuchundra was right: I should have talked with Chua.”

He crept into Teddy’s bathroom and found it empty, then tried his mother's. A missing brick at the foot of its smooth plaster wall provided a drain for bathwater. Slipping beside the raised masonry surrounding the bath’s place, Rikki-tikki heard Nag and Nagaina whisper outside in the moonlight.

“Once the house has no people,” Nagaina told her husband, “he'll have to leave. Then the garden will belong to us again. Enter quietly. Bite the big man first--the one who killed Karait. Come out afterward and tell me, and together we'll hunt Rikki-tikki down.”
“Are you certain killing the people will actually help us?” Nag asked her.

“It will solve everything. Before people occupied the bungalow, did any mongoose live in our garden? With the house empty, we rule here as king and queen. And remember, our eggs in the melon bed may hatch tomorrow. Our children will need peace and space.”

“I hadn't considered that,” Nag replied. “I'll go. But afterward we won't need to pursue Rikki-tikki. I'll kill the man, his wife, and, if possible, their child, then quietly leave. With the bungalow empty, Rikki-tikki will have to go somewhere else.”

Rikki-tikki shook with hatred and fury. Nag’s head slid through the drain, followed by five feet of cold body. Despite his anger, the mongoose felt terrified at the cobra’s size. Nag curled himself up and raised his head, examining the dark bathroom. His eyes glittered where Rikki could see them.
“If I kill him here, Nagaina will know,” Rikki-tikki-tavi thought. “If I attack on the open floor, he'll have the advantage. What should I do?”

Nag swayed, then drank from the largest jar used for filling the bath. Rikki-tikki heard him say, “That is good. The man carried a stick when he killed Karait. Perhaps he still has it. But when he bathes tomorrow morning, he won't be carrying it. I'll wait for him. Nagaina, can you hear? I'm staying in this cool place until daylight.”

No answer came, so Rikki-tikki knew Nagaina had left. Coil by coil, Nag settled around the water jar’s bulging base. The mongoose remained perfectly motionless. An hour later he began inching toward it, moving one muscle at a time. Nag slept. Rikki studied his broad back, choosing where to grip. “Unless the first leap breaks his spine, he can fight back. And if he does--oh, Rikki!” He examined the thick neck just beneath the hood, but it was much too large for him to get his teeth properly around. Biting near the tail would merely enrage the cobra.
“It will have to be his head,” he finally decided, “the part above the hood. Once I have taken hold there, I must never let go.”

He sprang. Nag’s head lay slightly away from the jar beneath its curve. As his teeth closed, Rikki pressed his back against the red earthenware bulge to pin the head down. This gave him one second’s leverage, and he used it fully. Then the cobra began battering him back and forth, just as a dog shakes a rat it has caught in its mouth: across the floor, up and down, around in sweeping circles. Red-eyed, he clung on as the body lashed like a whip, overturning the tin dipper, soap dish, and flesh brush, and crashing against the tin bath. Expecting to be beaten to death, he tightened his jaws for his family's honor: they should find him with his teeth still locked. Dizzy and aching, feeling shaken apart, he heard a thunderclap behind him. Heat knocked him unconscious; red fire scorched his fur. Awakened by the racket, the man had fired both shotgun barrels into Nag just below his hood.

Eyes closed, Rikki-tikki still gripped him, certain now that he was dead himself. But the head stopped moving. The man lifted the mongoose. “It's him again, Alice. The little fellow has saved all our lives this time.”

White-faced, Teddy’s mother entered and saw Nag’s remains. Rikki-tikki dragged himself into the boy’s room. For half the remaining night he gently shook himself, checking whether he really had broken into forty pieces, as it felt he had.

When morning arrived he felt very stiff all over, yet he was thoroughly pleased with what he had accomplished during the night. “Nagaina is next. She'll be worse than five Nags, and those eggs could hatch at any moment. Goodness! I must speak to Darzee.”

Without even waiting for breakfast, he rushed to the thorn-bush. Darzee was singing triumphantly at full volume. Everyone in the garden knew Nag was dead: the sweeper had tossed his body onto the rubbish heap.
“You foolish bundle of feathers!” Rikki-tikki snapped. “Is this any time for singing?”

“Nag is dead--is dead--is dead!” Darzee sang. “Brave Rikki-tikki seized his head and wouldn't release him. The man fetched the bang-stick, and Nag broke in two! He'll never swallow another baby of mine.”
“Quite true. But where is Nagaina?” Rikki-tikki asked, cautiously studying everything around him.

“Nagaina called to Nag at the bathroom drain,” Darzee continued, “and out he came on a stick. The sweeper lifted him on its end and flung him onto the rubbish heap. Let us praise mighty red-eyed Rikki-tikki!” Darzee drew breath and poured out more song.

“If I could reach that nest, I'd tip your babies out!” Rikki-tikki cried. “You never know when to do what’s needed. You're safe up there; down here I'm fighting a war. Stop singing for a moment, Darzee.”
“For wonderful, magnificent Rikki-tikki, I shall be silent,” Darzee replied. “What do you need, Slayer of dreadful Nag?”
“For the third time, where has Nagaina gone?”
“She's beside the stables, mourning Nag on the rubbish heap. Mighty is white-toothed Rikki-tikki.”
“Forget my white teeth! Do you know where she has hidden her eggs?”
“In the melon bed, beside the wall, where sunlight falls almost all day. She put them there weeks ago.”
“And you thought that wasn't worth mentioning? The end beside the wall--is that what you said?”
“Rikki-tikki, surely you don't mean to eat her eggs?”

“Not exactly eat them, no. If you have any sense, Darzee, fly to the stables, pretend your wing is broken, and lure Nagaina after you toward this bush. I need to reach the melon bed. If I go now, she'll spot me.”

Darzee was scatterbrained, unable to keep two ideas in his head at once. Because Nagaina’s young hatched from eggs like his, he initially thought killing them unfair. His wife was more sensible: cobra eggs would soon become little cobras. She left the nest herself, leaving Darzee to warm their babies and continue praising Nag’s death. She left her husband there to continue making up his song about the death of Nag, while she attended to the work that needed doing. In certain ways Darzee was remarkably like a man.
She fluttered before Nagaina near the rubbish pile. “Oh, my wing is broken!” she cried. “The boy threw a stone and broke it.” Then she began fluttering even more desperately than before.
Nagaina raised her head and hissed, “You warned Rikki-tikki just as I meant to kill him. You have certainly chosen an unfortunate place to be crippled.” She slid over the dust toward the bird.
“A stone from the boy broke it!” Darzee’s wife screamed.

“Well! Perhaps after death you'll feel comforted to know I'll settle with that boy. My husband lies on the rubbish pile this morning. Before tonight, the child inside that house will be lying very still too. Why bother fleeing? I'm bound to catch you. Look at me, little fool!”
Darzee’s wife knew not to obey. A bird meeting a snake’s eyes becomes too frightened to move. She fluttered on without leaving the ground, crying pitifully, while Nagaina followed faster.

Hearing them pass along the path from the stables, Rikki-tikki raced to the melon patch beside the wall. Hidden cleverly in warm debris above the melons lay twenty-five eggs, each about a bantam egg’s size, with pale leathery skin instead of shell.

“Not a moment too early,” he said. Through the pale skins he could see the little cobras curled inside, and knew that as soon as they hatched each one could kill a man or a mongoose. As quickly as he could work, he bit the top off each egg and made certain to crush the baby snake within. From time to time he turned over the surrounding litter to check whether another egg lay hidden there. Finally only three remained. He began chuckling to himself, but then he heard Darzee’s wife scream:
“Rikki-tikki, I brought Nagaina toward the house. She's on the veranda now--oh, hurry--she intends to kill!”

He crushed two eggs, took the third in his mouth, tumbled backward out of the melon bed, and sprinted for the veranda. Teddy and his parents sat at early breakfast without touching their food. The three of them sat as motionless as stones, and their faces had turned quite white with fear. Beside Teddy’s chair, Nagaina lay coiled on the matting, easily within reach of his bare leg. She swayed and sang her triumph.

“Son of the man who killed Nag,” she hissed, “keep still. Not yet; I'm not ready. Wait. None of you three must move! Move, and I'll strike. Stay still, and I'll strike. Oh, foolish people who murdered my Nag!”
Teddy stared at his father, who could only whisper, “Don't move, Teddy. Stay absolutely still. Teddy, you must keep perfectly still.”
Rikki-tikki rushed up. “Face me, Nagaina. Turn around and fight!” he cried.

“In a moment,” she answered, never shifting her gaze. “Your turn will come. Look at those friends of yours: pale, frozen, terrified. They dare not move. One step closer from you, Rikki-tikki, and I strike.”
“Look at your eggs in the melon bed beside the wall,” Rikki-tikki said. “Go and look, Nagaina!”
Turning halfway, the cobra saw the egg on the veranda. “Ah-h! Give that to me,” she demanded.

With a paw on either side of it, Rikki-tikki stared blood-red-eyed. “What will you pay for a snake’s egg? A baby cobra? A young king cobra? The last one--the very last of your brood? Ants are feeding on all the others beside the melons.”

Nagaina wheeled fully toward him, forgetting everything except her remaining egg. Teddy’s father thrust out his big hand, seized the boy’s shoulder, and dragged him over the little tea-cup-covered table, safely beyond the cobra’s reach.

“Fooled! Fooled! Fooled! Rikk-tck-tck!” Rikki-tikki chuckled. “The boy is safe. And last night in the bathroom, I--I--I seized Nag’s hood.” He bounced on all four feet, keeping his head near the floor. “He tossed me everywhere but couldn't loosen my grip. Before the man shot him in two, he was already dead. I killed him! Rikki-tikki-tck-tck! Come on, Nagaina. Fight me. You won't remain a widow long.”

Nagaina realized Teddy had escaped her. The egg remained between the mongoose’s paws. Lowering her hood, she said, “Give me that egg, Rikki-tikki. Return my last egg and I'll leave forever. I won't come back.”
“You'll certainly leave and never return--because you will be going to join Nag on the rubbish heap. Fight, widow! The man has gone to fetch his gun! Fight!”

Rikki-tikki bounded around her, eyes burning like coals, staying barely beyond striking distance. Nagaina drew all her long body together, gathering herself for the blow, then flung her head straight out at him. He sprang backward and upward. Over and over she struck, each time thumping her head on the veranda matting before recoiling like a watch spring. Then Rikki-tikki danced around in a complete circle, trying to get behind the cobra; she turned to keep facing him. Her tail rustled over the matting like dry leaves blowing in wind.

He had completely forgotten the egg lying nearby. Nagaina edged toward it until, while he paused for breath, she snatched it in her mouth. Wheeling toward the steps, she shot down the path with Rikki-tikki pursuing. A cobra fleeing for her life moves like a whip flicked across a horse’s neck.

Rikki-tikki knew he had to catch her; otherwise their trouble would start again. She headed toward tall grass beside the thorn-bush, where Darzee was still singing his silly victory song. His wiser wife left the nest and beat her wings around Nagaina’s head. With Darzee’s help they might have turned her aside, but alone she merely made the cobra lower her hood and continue. That brief delay let Rikki catch up. As Nagaina plunged into the rat-hole she had shared with Nag, his little white teeth gripped her tail. Down he went after her. Few mongooses, however experienced, willingly pursue cobras underground. In that darkness he couldn't know where the tunnel might widen enough for her to turn and strike. He held fiercely, spreading his feet to brake against the warm, damp earth of the downward slope.
The grass at the entrance stopped moving. “Rikki-tikki is finished!” Darzee cried. “We must sing his funeral song. Brave Rikki-tikki is dead! Nagaina is certain to kill him down there.”

He immediately invented a mournful song. At its most touching passage, the grass stirred again. Filthy and licking his whiskers, Rikki-tikki pulled himself out, one leg at a time. Darzee stopped singing in the middle of his song and gave a little startled shout. Rikki shook dust from his coat and sneezed. “It's over,” he said. “The widow will never emerge again.” Red ants living among the grass stems heard him and marched down the hole, one after another, to test his claim.
Rikki-tikki curled up right there in the grass and slept. After such a hard day's work, he slept and slept until late afternoon.
“Time to return to the house,” he said on waking. “Tell the Coppersmith, Darzee. He'll announce Nagaina’s death throughout the garden.”

The Coppersmith’s call sounds exactly like a little hammer striking a copper pot. He keeps making it because he serves as town crier to Indian gardens, telling all the latest news to every creature in the garden who cares to stop and listen. As Rikki walked home, he heard the attention signal, like a miniature dinner gong, followed by steady calls: “Ding-dong-tock! Nag is dead--dong! Nagaina is dead! Ding-dong-tock!” Birds everywhere began singing; frogs croaked too. The cobras had eaten frogs as well as small birds.

Teddy and both parents met him outside, almost weeping. His mother remained pale after her fainting spells. That evening Rikki ate everything offered until he couldn't swallow another mouthful. He then went off to bed on Teddy’s shoulder, and his mother found him there when she looked in late that night.
“He saved us and Teddy,” she told her husband. “Think of it--he saved every one of our lives.”
Mongooses sleep lightly; Rikki-tikki startled awake at the sound of their voices.
“Oh, it's you,” he said. “Why all this fuss? Every cobra is dead. And even if one weren't, I'm here.”

He had earned his pride, but never became too proud. He guarded that garden as a mongoose should, jumping, springing, biting, and using his teeth, until not a single cobra dared raise its head within those walls.
Darzee’s Chant
(Sung in honor of Rikki-tikki-tavi)

Singer and tailor am I--
Twice the joys that I know--
Proud of my song to the sky,
Proud of the house that I sew--
Over and under, I weave my music--I weave the house that I
sew.

Sing to your fledglings again,
Mother, oh lift up your head!
Evil that plagued us is slain,
Death in the garden lies dead.
Terror that hid in the roses is powerless--flung on the dung-hill
and dead!

Who has saved us, who?
Tell me his nest and his name.
Rikki, the valiant, the true,
Tikki, with eyeballs of flame,
Rikk-tikki-tikki, the ivory-fanged, the hunter with eyeballs of
flame!

Give him the Thanks of the Birds,
Bowing with tail feathers spread!
Praise him with nightingale words--
No, I will praise him instead.
Hear! I will sing you the praise of the bottle-tailed Rikki, with
eyeballs of red!
(_At this point Rikki-tikki interrupted; the rest of the song is lost._)

chapters.title: Toomai of the Elephants
paragraphs:
I will remember what I was, I am sick of rope and chain--
I will remember my old strength and all my forest affairs.
I will not sell my back to man for a bundle of sugar-cane:
I will return to my own kind, and the wood-folk in their lairs.

I will go out until the day, until the morning breaks--
Out to the wind’s untainted kiss, the water’s clean caress;
I will forget my ankle-ring and snap my tethering stake.
I will revisit my lost loves, and playmates masterless!

Kala Nag means Black Snake. For forty-seven years he had served the Indian Government in every task an elephant could perform. He had already been twenty when captured, making him nearly seventy--a respectable age for an elephant. He remembered pushing a cannon out of deep mud with a thick leather pad protecting his forehead. That was before the Afghan War of 1842, when he had not yet reached his full strength.

His mother, Radha Pyari--Radha the darling--was captured in the same drive. Before he lost his baby tusks she told him that frightened elephants always got hurt. Experience confirmed it: his first exploding shell sent him screaming backward into stacked rifles, whose bayonets pricked all his tenderest parts. Before twenty-five he stopped being afraid. No elephant in India's Government service was more loved or better cared for. He carried twelve hundred pounds of tents on marches through Upper India. They had hoisted him into a ship on the end of a steam crane, and for days afterward he traveled across the water, far away from India. In a distant, rocky country he carried a mortar and saw Emperor Theodore dead at Magdala. After that faraway service, he came back again aboard the steamer. The soldiers said that he had earned the right to wear the Abyssinian War medal for the work he had done there. Ten years later, at Ali Musjid, he watched other elephants die from cold, epilepsy, starvation, and sunstroke. Later he traveled thousands of miles south to Moulmein’s timberyards to haul and stack enormous teak beams. There he nearly killed a rebellious young elephant that refused its share of work.

They then removed him from timber work and sent him with several dozen trained elephants to help capture wild ones in the Garo hills. The Indian Government protects elephants strictly. There is an entire Government department devoted to them. Its only business is hunting them down, catching them, training them for service, and sending them from one part of the country to another wherever work requires them.

Kala Nag measured a full ten feet at the shoulders. His tusks were shortened to five feet and capped with copper bands against splitting. Those stumps accomplished more than an untrained elephant’s pointed tusks. After weeks of cautiously driving scattered wild elephants through the hills, forty or fifty huge beasts would enter the final stockade. Behind them crashed a heavy gate made of lashed tree trunks. On command, Kala Nag entered that blazing, trumpeting chaos--usually at night, when flickering torches confused distances. From the whole crowd he would pick out the very biggest and most uncontrollable tusker. Then he would batter him and hustle him about until the wild elephant was quiet enough to be managed. Meanwhile men riding the other elephants roped and secured the smaller captives.

Wise old Black Snake knew every trick of battle. More than once he had faced a wounded tiger’s charge. Curling his vulnerable trunk safely aside, he met the leaping tiger with a swift, curved sweep of his head, a stroke he had invented himself. It knocked the beast sideways out of the air. Then Kala Nag knelt on him with those enormous knees until a gasp and howl ended his life. Only a soft, striped heap remained on the ground, ready for the elephant to drag by its tail.

“Black Snake fears no one except me,” said Big Toomai, his driver. His father Black Toomai had taken Kala Nag to Abyssinia; his grandfather, Toomai of the Elephants, had witnessed the capture. “Three generations of our family have fed and groomed him. He'll live to see a fourth.”

“He fears me too,” Little Toomai declared, standing all four feet tall in his single rag. He was only ten years old, the eldest son of Big Toomai, and he stood there wearing no more than one rag of clothing. Custom dictated that one day he would sit on Kala Nag’s neck in his father’s place, wielding the heavy iron ankus, the elephant goad polished smooth by father, grandfather, and great-grandfather before him.

He knew what he meant. Born in Kala Nag’s shadow, he played with the elephant’s trunk before learning to walk and led him to water as soon as he could. Kala Nag would never dream of resisting those shrill commands. Nor had he dreamed of harming the brown baby on the day Big Toomai carried him under the tusks and ordered the elephant to salute his future master.
“Yes, he's afraid of me,” Little Toomai repeated. Taking long strides up toward Kala Nag, he called him a fat old pig and ordered each foot lifted in turn.

“Wah! What a great elephant you are,” the boy said, shaking his fluffy head and repeating his father's words. “The Government pays, but elephants belong to us mahouts. When you grow old, some wealthy rajah will buy you for your size and good manners. Then you will have no work except to walk at the head of the King’s processions. There will be golden earrings in your ears, a gold howdah on your back, and a red cloth covered with gold hanging along your sides. I'll sit on your neck, Kala Nag, carrying a silver ankus. Men with golden staffs will run ahead, calling, ‘Make way for the King's elephant!’ That will be fine--but not as fine as hunting through these jungles.”

“Umph!” Big Toomai said. “You're a boy, wild as a buffalo calf. Racing around these hills is not the finest Government duty. I'm aging, and wild elephants don't please me. Give me brick elephant quarters, a separate stall apiece, stout tethering posts, and broad level exercise roads, rather than this endless moving of camp. Ah, Cawnpore barracks were comfortable. A bazaar nearby and only three hours of work daily.”

Remembering Cawnpore, Little Toomai kept quiet. Camp life suited him far better. He hated the wide flat roads, daily grass-cutting in the forage reserve, and idle hours spent watching Kala Nag fidget at his stakes with nothing else to do.

He loved scrambling along paths only elephants could travel, plunging into valleys, and glimpsing wild herds feeding miles away. He loved pigs and peacocks scurrying from Kala Nag’s feet, warm blinding rain that made valleys and hills steam, and lovely misty mornings with no knowing where night would find their camp. He loved the slow, careful driving of wild elephants and the final night's furious rush, blaze, and uproar. Then elephants poured into the enclosure like landslide boulders, discovered they were trapped, and hurled themselves against stout posts, only to recoil from yelling men, flaming torches, and volleys of blank cartridges.

Even a small boy could help, and Toomai did the work of three. He waved his torch and yelled as loudly as anyone. The best part began when they drove the captives out. The Keddah--the stockade--resembled the world's end. Men had to wave and make signs to one another; however loudly they spoke, they could not hear their own voices above the tremendous noise. Toomai climbed a trembling post, sun-bleached brown hair flying over his shoulders, looking like a goblin by torchlight. Whenever the uproar paused for a moment, you could hear the high-pitched voice of Little Toomai calling encouragement to Kala Nag. His shouts rose above all the trumpeting and crashing, above the noise of breaking ropes and the groaning of elephants struggling against their tethers. “Mael, mael, Kala Nag! (On, on, Black Snake!) Dant do! (Give him your tusk!) Somalo! Somalo! (Careful, careful!) Maro! Mar! (Hit him, hit him!) Watch the post! Arre! Arre! Hai! Yai! Kya-a-ah!” As Kala Nag and his wild opponent wrestled across the enclosure, sweating old elephant-catchers still found time to nod at the boy wriggling with delight above them.

He did more than wriggle. One night he slid into the enclosure between the elephants, picked up a dropped rope end, and tossed it to a driver trying to secure a kicking youngster’s leg. Calves always cause more trouble than adults. Seeing him, Kala Nag lifted him with his trunk and passed him to Big Toomai. His father slapped him immediately and returned him to the post.

Next morning his father scolded him. “Aren't decent brick quarters and carrying tents enough? Must you catch elephants on your own, you worthless little fellow? Those foolish hunters, paid less than I am, have told Petersen Sahib.” Little Toomai was frightened at the thought of that. He did not know very much about white men or their ways, but to him Petersen Sahib was the greatest white man in all the world. He directed all Keddah work, caught elephants for the Indian Government, and understood their ways better than anyone living.
“What--what will happen to me?” Little Toomai asked.

“Happen! The worst possible thing. Petersen Sahib is mad--why else pursue wild devils? He may make you an elephant-catcher, sleeping anywhere in fever-ridden forests until you're trampled to death in a Keddah. Luckily this foolish business is ending safely. Next week the catching stops and we plains men return to our stations. Smooth roads again, and no more hunting. But, my son, I am angry with you for interfering in business that is no concern of yours, work that belongs to these dirty Assamese people of the jungle. Kala Nag obeys only me, so I must enter the enclosure. Yet he's a fighter, not a roping elephant. I sit comfortably, as a mahout should--a mahout, not some ordinary hunter, a man entitled to a pension when his service ends. Must Toomai of the Elephants' family be trampled into Keddah dirt? Bad boy! Wicked boy! Worthless son! Wash Kala Nag, clean his ears, and check his feet for thorns. Otherwise Petersen Sahib will surely seize you and turn you into a wild hunter, following elephant tracks like a jungle bear. Bah! Shame! Go!”

Little Toomai left silently, but while inspecting Kala Nag’s feet he poured out his complaints. Lifting the fringe of the elephant’s huge right ear, he said, “Never mind. They've mentioned my name to Petersen Sahib, and perhaps--perhaps--perhaps--who knows? Hai! What a tremendous thorn I've pulled out!”

For several days they assembled the elephants and walked each new captive between two tame animals to prepare it for the downward journey to the plains. They also took stock of all the blankets, all the ropes, and the other supplies and equipment that had either worn out or been lost during their weeks of work in the forest.

Petersen Sahib arrived on clever Pudmini, his female elephant. With the season ending, he had been paying the other hill camps. Beneath a tree a native clerk sat at a table distributing the drivers' wages. Paid men returned to their elephants and joined the departing line. The permanent Keddah men--catchers, hunters, and beaters who lived in the jungle all year--sat on Petersen Sahib’s regular elephants or leaned against trees with guns across their arms. They made fun of the drivers who were preparing to go away to the plains. Whenever one of the newly captured elephants broke out of the waiting line and started running about, the jungle men laughed at the trouble it caused.

Big Toomai approached the clerk, his little son walking behind him. Chief tracker Machua Appa murmured to a friend, “At least there's one good future elephant man. A pity to send that young jungle-cock down to molt on the plains.”

Petersen Sahib seemed to have ears all over his body. Anyone who listens for the wild elephant, the most silent of living creatures, has to hear every small sound around him. Stretched out on Pudmini’s back, he turned. “What was that? I didn't know any plains-driver had enough sense to rope even a dead elephant.”
“Not a man--a boy. During the last drive, he entered the Keddah and threw Barmao his rope. That was when we were trying to pull the young calf with the blotch on its shoulder away from its mother.”
Machua Appa indicated Little Toomai. Petersen Sahib looked toward him, and the boy bowed down to the ground.
“He threw a rope? He's smaller than a tethering peg. What is your name, little one?” Petersen Sahib asked.

Too frightened to answer, Little Toomai gestured to Kala Nag behind him. The elephant lifted him in his trunk, holding him level with Pudmini’s forehead before the great Petersen Sahib. The boy hid his face in his hands. After all, he was only a child, and away from elephants he was as shy as any child could be.
“Oho!” Petersen Sahib said, smiling to himself underneath his mustache. “Why teach him that trick? To help you steal green corn from rooftops where the ears are laid to dry?”

“Not corn, Protector of the Poor--melons,” Little Toomai admitted. Everyone sitting nearby roared with laughter; most had taught their own elephants the same trick as boys. Suspended eight feet above ground, Little Toomai wished he were buried eight feet below it instead.
“He's my son, Toomai, Sahib,” his father said, scowling. “A very bad boy. He'll finish in prison, Sahib.”

“I doubt that,” Petersen Sahib replied. “A child his age who dares enter a full Keddah won't end in prison. Here, little one: four annas for sweets. There's a head worth something beneath that enormous mop of hair. Perhaps you'll become a hunter yourself.” His father's scowl deepened. “But remember,” Petersen Sahib added, “Keddahs are no playground for children.”
“Must I never enter one, Sahib?” Little Toomai gasped, drawing a great breath.
“You may,” Petersen Sahib said with another smile, “once you've watched the elephants dance. That's the right time. Come and tell me when you've seen their dance, and I'll admit you to every Keddah.”

Laughter roared again. Elephant-catchers know that old joke: it means never. Deep in the forests lie large, level clearings called elephants’ ballrooms. Even those places are discovered only by accident; nobody has ever watched the dance. When a driver boasts about his courage or skill, his companions ask, “And when did you see the elephants dance?”

Kala Nag lowered the boy, who bowed to the ground again and followed his father. He gave the silver four-anna coin to his mother as she nursed his baby brother. All climbed onto Kala Nag. The squealing, grunting line descended toward the plains. The new captives made it a lively journey, causing trouble at every river crossing and constantly requiring either coaxing or blows.

Still furious, Big Toomai jabbed Kala Nag spitefully. His little son was far too happy to say anything at all. Petersen Sahib had noticed and rewarded him. He felt like an ordinary soldier summoned from the ranks for praise by his commander-in-chief.
At last he quietly asked his mother, “What did Petersen Sahib mean about the elephants dancing?”
His father overheard and grunted. “He meant you must never become one of those hill-buffalo trackers. That's all. Hey, up ahead--what's blocking our way?”

An Assamese driver two or three elephants ahead turned angrily. “Bring Kala Nag and teach my youngster some manners. Why did Petersen Sahib send me down with you rice-field donkeys? Bring your beast alongside, Toomai, and have him use his tusks. By every God of the Hills, these captives are possessed--or they smell their friends in the jungle.” Kala Nag struck the young elephant’s ribs and knocked out his breath. Big Toomai said, “Our last drive cleared these hills of wild elephants. Your careless driving is the trouble. Must I keep the entire line in order?”

“Listen to him!” the driver scoffed. “We cleared the hills! Ho! Ho! Such clever plains people. Anyone but a mud-head who'd never seen a jungle would know that the elephants know this season's drives are finished. Tonight every wild elephant will--but why waste understanding on a river-turtle?”
“What will they do tonight?” Little Toomai called forward.
“Ohe, little one, you're there? I'll tell you: you have a sensible head. They'll dance. Your father, who cleared every elephant from every hill, had better double-chain his animals tonight.”
“What nonsense is this?” Big Toomai demanded. “Father and son, we've tended elephants forty years without ever hearing this moonshine about dancing.”

“Of course: a plainsman in his hut knows only its four walls. Leave your elephants loose tonight and see what happens. As for dancing, I've seen the place where--Bapree-bap! How often does the Dihang River bend? Another crossing, and these calves must swim. Stop there, you behind us.”
Talking, quarreling, and splashing across rivers, they completed the first day's march to a receiving camp for the captives. Long before arriving, they had all lost their patience.

They chained the elephants' hind legs to heavy stakes, added ropes around the newcomers, and piled food in front of them. In the afternoon light, the hill drivers returned to Petersen Sahib. They warned the plains men to be especially watchful that night, laughing whenever anyone asked why.

Little Toomai gave Kala Nag his supper. As evening approached, overflowing with happiness, he searched the camp for a tom-tom. An Indian child whose heart is full doesn't run about shouting at random; he sits and holds a private celebration. And Petersen Sahib had spoken to Little Toomai! I believe failure to find his drum might have made him ill. The sweet-seller lent him a small tom-tom, played with the flat hand. As stars appeared, he sat cross-legged before Kala Nag, drum in his lap. He beat and beat and beat it. The more he remembered his great honor, the harder he thumped, alone amid elephant fodder. There was no tune to any of it, and he sang no words along with the beating. He simply went on thumping, because the thumping itself made him happy.

The new captives pulled at their ropes, occasionally squealing or trumpeting. From the hut he heard his mother soothing his little brother with an ancient song about the great God Shiv assigning food to every animal. It is a very soothing, wonderfully calming lullaby. Its first verse goes:

Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds to blow,
Sitting at the doorways of a day of long ago,
Gave each one his portion, food and work and fate,
From the King upon the _guddee_ to the Beggar at the gate.
All things he made--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo! Mahadeo! He made all--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the cattle,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!

At every verse’s end Little Toomai added a cheerful tunk-a-tunk, until sleepiness sent him stretching out on fodder beside Kala Nag. The elephants gradually lay down, as usual. Finally only Kala Nag remained upright at the line’s right-hand end. He rocked slowly, ears forward, listening to the faint night breeze across the hills. The night air was full of all those small sounds which, when you hear them together, seem to make one enormous silence across the whole forest: bamboo clicking together, a creature rustling in undergrowth, the scratching and squawking of a half-awake bird--birds wake at night much more than we suppose--and distant falling water. Toomai slept awhile. Waking in bright moonlight, he saw Kala Nag still listening. Little Toomai turned over, making the dry fodder rustle beneath him, and lay watching the curve of Kala Nag’s huge back against the sky. It seemed to cover half the stars in heaven as the boy looked up at it. Then, immensely far away, like a pinprick through the silence, came a wild elephant’s “hoot-toot.”

Every elephant sprang up as if shot. Their grunts finally woke the mahouts, who hammered stakes deeper with heavy mallets, tightened ropes, retied knots, and restored quiet. One captive nearly uprooted its post. Big Toomai removed Kala Nag’s chain and shackled that elephant's front foot to its back foot. Instead of the iron chain, he slipped a loose loop of grass cord around Kala Nag’s leg and told the old elephant to remember that he was tied there firmly and must not go away. He, his father, and his grandfather had done this hundreds of times. Usually Kala Nag answered with a gurgle, but not now. He stood watching the great folds of the Garo hills in moonlight, head slightly raised, ears fanned wide.

“Look after him if he becomes restless,” Big Toomai told his son before returning to sleep. Little Toomai was just about to fall asleep himself when he heard a little tang beside him: the coir string had snapped. Kala Nag moved from his stakes as slowly and silently as a cloud leaves a valley. Barefoot, the boy pattered after him down the moonlit road, whispering, “Kala Nag! Kala Nag! Take me along, Kala Nag!” Soundlessly the elephant turned, came three strides back, lowered his trunk, and swung the child onto his neck. Almost before Toomai could settle his knees, they disappeared into the forest.

Furious trumpeting burst once from the tethered elephants; then silence closed behind them. Kala Nag advanced. Tall grass sometimes brushed his sides like waves against a ship. Wild-pepper vines scraped his back, or bamboo creaked against a shoulder. But in the spaces between those small noises, not a sound came from the great elephant. He drifted through the thick trees and undergrowth of the Garo forest as easily and silently as though all that forest were only smoke. They were climbing. Though Toomai watched stars through gaps in the branches, he couldn't identify their direction.

At the summit Kala Nag paused. Moonlit treetops stretched for miles, mottled and furry-looking; blue-white mist lay over the river below. Little Toomai leaned forward over the elephant’s neck and looked carefully down into the valley. He had the feeling that the whole forest below him was awake--awake, alive, and crowded with creatures moving through it. A large brown fruit bat swept past his ear. Porcupine quills rattled in nearby bushes. Between dark trunks, a hog-bear dug vigorously in warm, damp soil, snuffling as it worked.

Branches closed overhead, and Kala Nag descended into the valley. This time there was no stealth: he rushed like a runaway cannon down a steep bank. His enormous legs drove steadily as pistons, covering eight feet a stride; wrinkled elbow skin rustled. Undergrowth tore on either side like canvas. Saplings shoved aside by his shoulders snapped back against his flanks. Tangled vines dangled from his tusks as his swinging head plowed a path. Little Toomai lay down as flat as he could, pressing himself close against the elephant’s great neck. He feared that one of the branches swinging back across their path might sweep him off and throw him to the ground. He wished desperately to be back among the tethered elephants.

The grass grew wet; each enormous footfall sucked and squelched. Valley mist chilled the boy. Splashing and trampling carried them into rushing water, and Kala Nag crossed the riverbed, feeling out every step. Above the noise of the moving water as it swirled around the elephant’s legs, Little Toomai could hear still more splashing. From both upstream and downstream there came trumpeting, great deep grunts, and angry snorts from other creatures passing through the river. Around him the mist seemed full of wavering, moving shadows.
“Ai!” he murmured through chattering teeth. “The elephant people are abroad tonight. Then this must be their dance!”

Kala Nag emerged splashing, blew water from his trunk, and climbed again. Now others traveled with him, and he needed no fresh path. A six-foot-wide opening already stretched ahead, its flattened jungle grass still struggling upright. The boy could see that many elephants must have traveled along that very path only a few minutes before Kala Nag reached it. Looking back, Toomai saw a huge wild tusker rising out of the misty river, tiny piglike eyes glowing like coals. Trees hid it again. They continued upward amid trumpeting, crashes, and snapping branches on every side.

At the hilltop Kala Nag stopped between two trunks in a ring of trees enclosing an uneven clearing of three or four acres. Everywhere inside, the ground had been stamped hard as a brick floor. A few trees stood in the center, their bark rubbed away to expose white wood polished bright in patches of moonlight. Vines hung from the upper branches. Their enormous waxy white bells, like convolvulus flowers, drooped asleep. But everywhere within the boundaries of that open space the boy looked in vain for anything green growing on the ground. Not even a single blade of grass remained. There was nothing beneath the trees except the hard earth trampled by elephants.

Moonlight turned it iron-gray; the shadows beneath standing elephants were black as ink. Little Toomai held his breath as he looked, staring so hard that his eyes seemed ready to start from his head. And while he looked, more elephants, and more, and still more swung into the open between the tree trunks. He could count only to ten. Again and again he counted on his fingers, until he lost track of the tens and his head swam. Outside, elephants crashed through undergrowth while climbing the hillside. The moment they entered the ring of trees, however, their movements became ghostly silent.

The wild males carried long white tusks and fallen leaves, nuts, and twigs in their neck wrinkles and ear folds. Fat females moved slowly, restless pinkish-black calves three or four feet tall running beneath their bellies. Youngsters displayed just-emerging tusks with great pride. There were lanky, scraggy unmarried females with hollow, worried faces and trunks rough as bark, and savage old bulls scarred from shoulder to flank by ancient battles, dried mud from solitary baths crumbling off their shoulders. One had a broken tusk and the long, terrible scoring of a tiger’s full claw-stroke down his side.
Dozens upon dozens of elephants stood facing each other, crossed the clearing in pairs, or rocked and swayed alone where they stood.

Toomai knew he was safe if he remained still on Kala Nag. Even in a frantic Keddah drive, wild elephants do not reach up and drag riders from tame elephants' necks. Tonight they weren't thinking about men at all. They startled once, ears pricking at the clink of iron in the forest. But it was Petersen Sahib’s favorite Pudmini, grunting and snuffling uphill with her chain broken short. She must have escaped her stakes and come straight from his camp. Little Toomai also noticed another elephant, one he did not recognize at all. Deep sores made by ropes marked that animal’s back and breast. He too must have escaped from some camp among the surrounding hills.

Eventually no further elephants could be heard approaching through the forest. Kala Nag left his place between the trees and moved into the crowd, clucking and gurgling. Around him the whole gathering began moving and talking in its own language.

Lying flat, Toomai looked over scores of broad backs, flapping ears, tossing trunks, and rolling little eyes. Tusks clicked as they accidentally crossed; intertwined trunks rustled dryly. Enormous shoulders and sides rubbed, and great tails constantly flicked and hissed. A cloud covered the moon, leaving him in blackness. Still the quiet, steady shoving and pushing continued in exactly the same way as before. The elephants went on bustling and gurgling to one another around him, although now he could no longer see them. Elephants surrounded Kala Nag; backing out was impossible. The boy clenched his teeth and shivered. At least a Keddah had shouting men and torchlight. Here he lay alone in darkness. Once a trunk reached up and touched his knee.

One elephant trumpeted. All joined in for five or ten dreadful seconds. Dew showered from overhead trees onto invisible backs. A low booming began, at first too faint for Toomai to identify. It strengthened. Kala Nag raised one front foot, then the other, bringing them down--one-two, one-two--with the regularity of trip-hammers. Every elephant was stamping together, like a war drum sounding at a cave mouth. Dew fell until the trees had none left. The booming continued; earth shook and trembled. Toomai covered his ears, but the stamping of hundreds of heavy feet on bare ground passed through his whole body as one enormous jolt. Once or twice the herd surged several strides forward. Then the pounding became the crushing of lush green plants, before the hard-earth boom resumed a minute or two later. Nearby a tree groaned and creaked. Toomai stretched out his arm and felt the rough bark against his hand. But Kala Nag moved forward again, still bringing his feet down in the same steady rhythm, and the boy could no longer tell where he was in the clearing. The elephants themselves made no sound except once, when two or three calves squeaked together. A thump and shuffle followed; the booming went on. It lasted fully two hours. The sound and shaking had gone on for what must have been two full hours, until every nerve in Little Toomai’s body ached. Yet he knew from the smell of the night air, changing around him, that morning was finally approaching.

Behind the green hills, dawn spread across the whole sky in a single sheet of pale yellow light. At its first ray the stamping ceased as though commanded by sunrise. Before the ringing left Toomai’s ears, before he even shifted, the elephants had vanished. Only Kala Nag, Pudmini, and the rope-scarred stranger remained. No rustle, whisper, or movement down the slopes betrayed where the others had gone.

Little Toomai stared again and again. The clearing had grown overnight. More trees now stood inside it, while grass and undergrowth along its edges had been driven back. He stared again and understood. Their stamping had enlarged the ballroom. Thick grass and juicy cane became crushed debris; debris became splinters, splinters became tiny fibers, and fibers became hard-packed earth beneath those feet.
“Wah!” he murmured, his eyelids very heavy. “Kala Nag, my lord, stay beside Pudmini and take me to Petersen Sahib’s camp, or I'll fall off your neck.”
The third elephant watched them leave, snorted, turned, and followed his own route. Perhaps he belonged to a minor native king’s household fifty, sixty, or even a hundred miles away.

Two hours later Petersen Sahib was having early breakfast when his double-chained elephants began trumpeting. Pudmini, muddy to the shoulders, and Kala Nag, painfully footsore, shuffled into camp. Leaves filled Little Toomai’s dew-soaked hair; his face looked gray and pinched. He tried to salute and cried weakly, “The dance--the elephants' dance! I've seen it, and--I'm dying!” Kala Nag knelt, and the boy slid unconscious from his neck.

Native children have scarcely any nerves worth mentioning. Within two hours, Toomai lay contentedly in Petersen Sahib’s hammock, head pillowed on the Sahib’s shooting-coat. He had swallowed warm milk with a little brandy and a dash of quinine. Before him, hairy, scarred old jungle hunters sat three rows deep, regarding him like a spirit. He told his story in a child's simple, short phrases, finishing with:

“If any word is false, send men to look. They'll find that the elephant people have stamped their ballroom larger. They'll find ten tracks, and ten more, and many tens leading there. With their feet they made more room. I saw it myself. Kala Nag carried me, and I watched. And Kala Nag’s legs are terribly tired!”

He lay back and slept through the long afternoon into dusk. Meanwhile Petersen Sahib and Machua Appa followed the elephants' trail fifteen miles over the hills. In eighteen years of catching elephants, Petersen Sahib had found only one such ballroom before. Machua Appa needed neither a second glance nor a scrape of his toe across the rammed earth to understand what had happened there.
“The boy told the truth,” he said. “This was all done last night. Seventy sets of tracks cross the river. Look, Sahib--Pudmini’s leg iron scraped that tree’s bark! Yes, she was here as well.”
They looked at each other, then all around, marveling. No man, black or white, has understanding deep enough to grasp all the ways of elephants.

“For forty-five years I've followed my lord, the elephant,” Machua Appa said. “Never have I heard of any human child seeing what this boy saw. By all the Gods of the Hills, it is--what words have we?” He shook his head.

They returned at suppertime. Petersen Sahib ate alone in his tent, but ordered two sheep, several fowls, and double portions of flour, rice, and salt for everyone else. He knew quite well that the men throughout the camp would want to celebrate what had happened by holding a feast that evening.

Big Toomai had hurried up from the camp on the plains to search for his son and his elephant. Now that he had found them, he looked at both almost as though he feared them. Blazing campfires lit the feast in front of the rows of tethered elephants, and Little Toomai was the hero of the evening. The big brown elephant-catchers, trackers, drivers, and ropers, the men who understood every secret of taming the wildest elephants, passed him from one pair of arms to another. They marked his forehead with blood from the breast of a freshly killed jungle-cock, showing that he was now an initiated forester, free to enter all the jungles.

At last the flames sank. Red logs made the elephants look dipped in blood too. Machua Appa sprang up, holding the child high overhead: chief driver of every Keddah, Petersen Sahib’s other self, a man who had seen no built road in forty years, so great that Machua Appa was his only name. “Listen, brothers! And listen, my lords tethered there, for I, Machua Appa, speak. No longer Little Toomai: from now on he is Toomai of the Elephants, his great-grandfather’s name. Through the long night he witnessed what no man has seen. The elephant people and Gods of the Jungles favor him. He shall grow into a great tracker of elephants. He shall become greater than I am--greater even than I, Machua Appa! His clear eyes will follow fresh tracks, old tracks, and mingled tracks! Under wild tuskers' bellies he will run to rope them and suffer no harm. If he falls before a charging bull, that bull will recognize him and spare him. Aihai! My chained lords”--he whirled along the tethering line--“here is the child who saw your dances in your secret places, the sight no man has seen! Honor him, my lords! Salaam karo, my children. Salute Toomai of the Elephants! Gunga Pershad, ahaa! Hira Guj, Birchi Guj, Kuttar Guj, ahaa! Pudmini--you saw him at the dance, and you too, Kala Nag, my pearl of elephants!--ahaa! Together! To Toomai of the Elephants. Barrao!”

At that last fierce cry every trunk rose until its tip touched the elephant’s forehead. The full salute thundered out: the mighty trumpet fanfare normally heard only by India's Viceroy, the Keddah’s Salaamut.
All of it honored Little Toomai, who had watched what nobody had witnessed before: the elephants dancing at night, alone in the heart of the Garo hills!
Shiv and the Grasshopper
(The song Toomai’s mother sang to his baby brother)

Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds to blow,
Sitting at the doorways of a day of long ago,
Gave each one his portion, food and work and fate,
From the King upon the _guddee_ to the Beggar at the gate.
_All things he made--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo! Mahadeo! He made all,--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the cattle,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

Wheat he gave to rich folk, millet to the poor,
Broken scraps for holy men that beg from door to door;
Battle to the tiger, carrion to the kite,
And rags and bones to wicked wolves outside the wall at night.
Nothing seemed too lofty, no one seemed too low--
Parbati beside him watched them come and go;
Thought to trick her husband, making Shiv a jest--
Stole the little grasshopper and hid it in her breast.
_So she tricked him, Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo! Mahadeo! Turn and see.
Tall are the camels, heavy are the cattle,
But this was Least of Little Things, O little son of mine!_

When the gifts were given, laughingly she said,
“Master, of a million mouths, is not one unfed?”
Laughing, Shiv made answer, “All have had their part,
Even he, the little one, hidden by your heart.”
From her breast she plucked it, Parbati the thief,
Saw the Least of Little Things gnawed a new-grown leaf!
Saw and feared and wondered, offering prayers to Shiv,
Who has surely given food to all that live.
_All things he made--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo! Mahadeo! He made all,--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the cattle,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

chapters.title: Her Majesty's Servants
paragraphs:
You can work it out by Fractions or by simple Rule of Three,
But the way of Tweedle-dum is not the way of Tweedle-dee.
You can twist it, you can turn it, you can braid it till you drop,
But the way of Pilly Winky’s not the way of Winkie Pop!

For an entire month heavy rain had fallen on thirty thousand men and thousands of camels, elephants, horses, bullocks, and mules camped at Rawal Pindi. They had assembled for inspection by India's Viceroy, who was entertaining Afghanistan’s Amir, a wild king ruling a very wild country. His bodyguard numbered eight hundred men with horses, none of whom had ever seen a military camp or locomotive: savage men and horses from far beyond Central Asia. Every single night a crowd of those horses was certain to break its heel ropes and stampeded through the dark, muddy camp. Otherwise camels escaped, ran about, and tumbled over tent ropes. Imagine how delightful that was for men trying to sleep. My tent stood far from the camel lines, and I considered it safe. One night, however, a man thrust his head inside. “Out, quickly! Here they come! My tent's gone!”

Knowing who “they” meant, I pulled on boots and waterproof and hurried into the slush. My fox terrier, little Vixen, escaped through the opposite side. Roaring, grunting, and bubbling followed. I saw my tent collapse as its pole broke, then dance about like a crazed ghost. A camel had blundered inside. Wet and furious though I was, I couldn't help laughing. Then I set off running again through the dark, uncertain how many animals were loose, until I was beyond sight of camp, struggling through mud.

Eventually I tripped over the rear of a gun and realized I was near the artillery lines, where cannon were parked overnight. Tired of floundering through dark drizzle, I draped my waterproof across one gun's muzzle and propped it into a small wigwam with a few rammers I found nearby. I stretched along another gun’s tail, wondering where Vixen was and exactly where I had ended up.

As sleep approached, harness jingled and someone grunted. A mule passed, shaking wet ears. The straps, rings, chains, and fittings rattling on his saddle pad identified him as a screw-gun battery mule. These screw-guns are very small cannon made in two separate pieces. When the time comes to use them, the men screw those two pieces firmly together. Mules carry them up mountain tracks wherever their feet can find a route, making them extremely useful in rocky-country warfare.

Following behind the mule there came a camel, soft broad feet slipping and squelching, his neck bobbing like a lost hen’s. Fortunately the natives had taught me enough animal speech--camp animals' language, naturally, not wild creatures'--to understand his words.

He must have been my tent's destroyer. “What should I do? Where can I go?” he asked. “I fought a waving white thing, and it picked up a stick and struck my neck.” That was the broken pole, a discovery that pleased me considerably. “Should we keep running?”
“So it was you and your friends making all this trouble,” the mule replied. “Very well. You'll be beaten tomorrow. Meanwhile, I might as well give you an advance installment.”

Harness rattled as the mule backed up and planted two kicks in the camel’s ribs, sounding like drumbeats. “Next time,” he said, “think before charging through a mule battery at night shouting ‘Thieves and fire!’ Sit down and hold that foolish neck still.”

Folding himself up in the usual camel fashion, like a two-foot ruler, the camel sat and whimpered. Steady hooves sounded in the dark. A large cavalry horse cantered up with parade-ground precision, cleared a gun tail, and landed beside the mule.
“Disgraceful,” he snorted. “Those troublesome camels have charged through our lines for the third time this week. How can a horse stay fit without sleep? Who's here?”
“I carry the breech-piece of number two gun, First Screw Battery,” the mule answered. “The other is one of your friends. He woke me too. Who are you?”
“Number Fifteen, E troop, Ninth Lancers: Dick Cunliffe’s horse. Move over a little, please.”
“My apologies,” the mule said. “You can't see much in this darkness. Aren't these camels utterly tiresome? I left my lines hoping to find some peace here.”
“My lords,” the camel said meekly, “we had dreadful dreams and became very frightened. I'm merely a baggage camel with the 39th Native Infantry, not a brave creature like yourselves, my lords.”
“Then why not stay carrying the 39th Native Infantry’s baggage,” asked the mule, “instead of racing about the entire camp?”
“The dreams were so dreadful,” the camel replied. “I'm sorry. Listen! What's that sound? Must we run again?”

“Stay seated,” the mule ordered, “or you'll break those long stick-legs among the guns.” He raised an ear. “Bullocks! Gun bullocks. You and your friends have certainly awakened everybody. Rousing a gun-bullock takes a great deal of prodding.”

A chain scraped across the ground. Two enormous, sullen white bullocks shouldered forward together: the animals that pull heavy siege guns when elephants refuse to approach the firing any closer. Almost treading on their chain, another battery mule followed, frantically calling for “Billy.”
“One of our new recruits,” the older mule told the horse. “He's looking for me. Over here, youngster. Stop squealing. Darkness has never hurt anyone.”
Both gun-bullocks settled down together and began chewing their cud. The young mule pressed close against Billy.
“Things!” he gasped. “Terrible, horrible things, Billy! They invaded our lines while we slept. Will they kill us?”
“I ought to give you a first-class kicking,” Billy declared. “A fourteen-hand mule with your training, embarrassing our battery in front of this gentleman!”

“Easy, easy!” the horse said. “They're all like this initially. When I was a three-year-old back home in Australia, I saw my first man and ran for half a day. A camel would have kept me running forever.”
Almost all English cavalry horses come to India from Australia, whereupon the soldiers themselves train them for their work.

“Fair enough,” Billy conceded. “Stop trembling, youngster. When they first loaded my back with full harness and chains, I balanced on my front legs and kicked everything off. I hadn't learned scientific kicking yet, but the battery had never seen anything like it.”

“This wasn't harness or jingling metal,” the youngster protested. “You know that no longer bothers me, Billy. These were Things like trees, falling about the lines and bubbling. My head-rope broke. I couldn't find my driver or you, so I escaped with--with these gentlemen.”

“H’m!” Billy said. “As soon as I heard that the camels had broken loose, I came away on my own account. When a battery--a screw-gun mule--calls gun-bullocks gentlemen, he's badly rattled. Who are you two lying there?”

Still rolling their cud, both answered together, “Seventh yoke, first gun, Big Gun Battery. We were sleeping when the camels arrived. After being trampled, we got up and left. Quiet mud is better than comfortable bedding with no peace. We told this friend of yours that there was nothing at all to be afraid of. But apparently he knew so much more than we did that he insisted on thinking otherwise. Wah!”
Their chewing continued without interruption.
“That's the reward for fear,” Billy observed. “Gun-bullocks laugh at you. I hope you enjoy it, youngster.”
The youngster snapped his teeth. I heard him mutter that no old lump of beef could frighten him. The bullocks simply knocked their horns together and went on chewing.

“Don't turn angry because you've been scared,” the horse advised. “That's the worst cowardice. Anyone deserves forgiveness for fearing things they don't understand in darkness. We have broken away from our stakes again and again, all four hundred and fifty horses together because some recruit described Australia's whip snakes until we were all frightened out of our wits by nothing more than the loose ends of the ropes tied to our heads.”
“That's fine in camp,” Billy replied. “I sometimes stampede for amusement myself, after a day or two without exercise. But tell me, what do you do when you are actually on active service?”

“A completely different pair of shoes,” the horse said. “At such times I have Dick Cunliffe riding on my back, pressing with his knees. I need only watch my footing, keep my hind legs tucked well underneath, and respond correctly to the bridle.”
“What does responding to the bridle mean?” the youngster asked.

“By the Blue Gums of the Back Blocks,” the horse snorted. “Doesn't your training include that? How can you work without turning instantly when a rein touches your neck? It can mean the difference between life and death for the man riding you. Naturally, if it means life or death for him, it means life or death for you as well. The instant you feel that rein, turn, keeping your hind legs underneath. If there's no room to swing, rise a little and pivot on your back legs. That's being bridle-wise.”

“We are not trained to do things that way,” Billy answered stiffly. “We obey the man leading us: step out or in when he says. Presumably the result is the same. After all this fancy turning and rearing, which surely harms your hocks, what work do you actually do?”

“It varies,” the horse replied. “Usually I have to go right into a crowd of shouting, hairy men armed with long, gleaming knives, worse than the farrier's. Dick’s boot must just touch his neighbor’s without crushing it. I see his lance beside my right eye and know I'm safe. I wouldn't want to be the man or horse blocking us when we're in a hurry.”
“Can those knives hurt you?” the young mule asked.
“I once took a slash across the chest. That wasn't Dick’s fault, though--”
“If it hurt, I wouldn't care whose fault it was!” the youngster exclaimed.

“You have to care,” the horse replied. “Without trusting your rider, you might as well bolt immediately. Some horses do, and I don't blame them. As I said, Dick wasn't responsible. A man lay on the ground; I stretched to avoid treading on him, and he slashed upward. Next time I pass over a fallen man, I shall step squarely on him.”

“H’m!” Billy said. “That sounds foolish. Knives are unpleasant at any time. Proper fighting means climbing a mountain under a balanced saddle, clinging with all four feet and your ears too. You creep, crawl, and wriggle until you're hundreds of feet above everybody on a shelf barely wide enough for your hooves. Then you must stand there very quietly--don't ask anyone to hold your head, youngster--while the men assemble the guns. Afterward watch the little popping shells fall among treetops far, far below.”
“Do you never stumble up there?” asked the cavalry horse.

“They say you can split a hen’s ear when a mule stumbles,” Billy replied. “An unbalanced load may occasionally tip one over, but rarely. I wish you could see our work. It's beautiful.
