It took me three whole years to discover what the men really meant me to do, and to understand just what they were trying to accomplish. The crucial trick is never silhouetting yourself against the skyline: that invites shots. Remember, youngster. Stay concealed, even if it takes a mile's detour. Whenever the battery has that sort of climbing to do, I am the mule who leads the whole lot of them up the mountain.”
“Being shot at without charging the shooters!” the cavalry horse said, thinking very hard about it. “Impossible for me. I'd want to charge alongside Dick.”
“No, you wouldn't. As soon as the guns have been put in position, the guns do the charging themselves. Neat and scientific, that is. But knives--pah!”
For some time the camel had bobbed his head, desperate for a chance to speak. At last he nervously cleared his throat, and I heard:
“I--I--I've seen some fighting, though it involved neither climbing like that nor running.”
“No, now you mention it,” Billy said, “you hardly look designed for much climbing or running. Tell us, old Hay-bales, how did you manage?”
“In the proper manner,” the camel answered. “We all sat down--”
“My crupper and breastplate!” the horse muttered. “They sat down!”
“A hundred of us sat in a large square,” the camel continued. “The men stacked our packs and saddles outside it. Then they fired over our backs from all four sides.”

“Which men? Any who happened along?” the horse asked. “Riding-school lessons teach us to lie down for our riders to shoot across us. Only Dick Cunliffe could persuade me, though. It tickles my girths; besides, with my head down I can't see.”
“Why should the shooter matter?” the camel asked. “Lots of men and camels surround me, along with great clouds of smoke. Then I'm not afraid. I sit and wait quietly.”

“Yet you have bad dreams and go wrecking everybody’s camp in the middle of the night,” Billy observed. “Well, well! Before I'd lie down--never mind sit--for a man to fire over me, my heels would discuss matters with his head. Have you heard anything more dreadful?”
After nobody had spoken for a long time one bullock raised his great head. “Extremely foolish, all this,” he said. “There's only one way to fight.”
“Do tell,” Billy replied. “Don't let me stop you. Presumably you gentlemen fight balanced on your tails?”
“Only one way,” they chorused--surely they were twins. “The moment Two Tails trumpets, all twenty yoke of us are harnessed to the heavy gun.” Two Tails is the camp nickname for an elephant.
“Why does Two Tails start trumpeting?” the young mule asked.

“To announce he refuses to go closer to the smoke opposite us. A great coward, Two Tails. Then together we haul the gun--Heya--Hullah! Heeyah! Hullah! We have no need to climb about like cats, nor do we run around the place like young calves. All twenty pairs cross the flat plain until unharnessed. We graze while the guns speak across it to a mud-walled town. Chunks fall from the walls, raising dust like a crowd of homecoming cattle.”
“Oh! That's when you decide to graze?” asked the youngster.

“Then or whenever. Food is always welcome. We eat until harnessed again, then pull the gun back to waiting Two Tails. Sometimes guns inside the town answer and kill a few of us. More grass remains for the survivors. That is Fate. Still, Two Tails is a coward. Our method is the proper way of fighting. We're brothers from Hapur, sons of a sacred bull of Shiva. We have said our piece.”
“Well, tonight has taught me something,” the horse remarked. “You gentlemen belonging to the screw-gun battery--do you fancy eating under heavy artillery fire while Two Tails waits behind you?”

“As much as lying down for men to sprawl over us, or charging knives,” Billy said, stamping. “What nonsense. Give me a mountain shelf, a balanced load, and a driver who trusts me to choose my footing: I'm your mule. But none of those other arrangements!”
“Naturally,” the horse replied, “not everyone in this world is made in quite the same way. I imagine your relations on your father's side would have trouble understanding quite a few things.”

“Leave my father's family out of it,” Billy snapped. Mules hate reminders that their fathers were donkeys. “My father was a Southern gentleman. He could drag down, bite, and kick to pieces any horse he met. Remember that, you big brown Brumby!”
A Brumby is a wild horse with no pedigree. Imagine Sunol’s outrage if a carriage horse called her a “skate,” and you'll understand the Australian’s feelings. His eye-white flashed in the dark.

“Listen, son of an imported Malaga jackass,” he said through clenched teeth. “On my mother's side I'm related to Carbine, Melbourne Cup winner. In the place where I come from, no parrot-mouthed, pigheaded mule from a pop-gun pea-shooter battery tramples over us. Are you ready?”

“Up on your hind legs!” Billy squealed. Both reared, facing each other. I expected a savage fight, but a deep, bubbling rumble came from the darkness to our right: “Children, why are you fighting? Quiet, please.”
Both dropped to all fours, snorting in disgust. Neither horses nor mules can endure the sound of an elephant’s voice.
“Two Tails!” the horse exclaimed. “I can't bear him. Having a tail at both ends isn't fair!”
“Exactly my thoughts,” Billy agreed, pressing against the horse for comfort. “In some respects we're very similar.”
“Through our mothers, perhaps,” the horse said. “Hardly worth quarreling over. Hey! Two Tails, have they tied you up?”
“Yes,” came a laugh the length of his trunk. “I'm tethered for tonight. I heard your conversation. Don't worry, though. I'm not coming nearer.”

“Afraid of Two Tails--what complete nonsense!” murmured the camel and bullocks. The bullocks added, “Sorry you overheard, but we spoke the truth. Two Tails, why are you so frightened of the guns when they start firing?”
“Well,” he replied, rubbing his hind legs together like a child reciting a poem, “I'm not certain you could understand.”
“We certainly don't. Yet we must pull the guns,” the bullocks answered.
“I realize that, and you're braver than you know. But in my case the whole matter is different. Only the other day, the captain of my own battery called me a Pachydermatous Anachronism.”
“Another style of fighting, presumably?” Billy asked, his spirits beginning to recover.
“You won't know that word, but I do. It means halfway between, which describes me exactly. In my mind I see what happens when a shell explodes. You bullocks cannot.”
“I can imagine it a little,” the horse said. “I try to keep it out of my thoughts.”

“I see more than you, and I keep thinking about it. There's a great deal of body for me to protect. Nobody knows how to cure me if I fall ill. They merely withhold my driver's wages until I recover, and I don't trust him.”
“Ah!” the horse exclaimed. “That explains everything. I know I can rely on Dick.”
“You could put an entire regiment of men like Dick onto my back, and I would not feel any better for it. I understand enough to feel uncomfortable, but not enough to continue despite the discomfort.”
“We cannot understand that,” the bullocks replied.
“Of course you can't. I wasn't addressing you. You don't even know what blood means.”
“Yes we do,” they replied. “It's red stuff that smells and soaks into the earth.”
The cavalry horse kicked out, leaped, and snorted sharply.
“Don't mention it,” he said. “Merely thinking about it makes me smell it again. I feel like bolting--unless Dick is riding me.”
“But none is here,” the camel and bullocks objected. “Why behave so foolishly?”
“Horrible stuff,” Billy agreed. “It doesn't make me run, but I certainly don't want to discuss it.”
“There you have it!” Two Tails said, waving his tail in explanation.
“Certainly. We've been here throughout the night,” the bullocks agreed.
Two Tails stamped, jangling his iron ankle ring. “Oh, I'm not addressing you. You can't see pictures inside your heads.”
“No, we look through our four eyes,” they replied. “And we look straight ahead of us.”

“If that were all I could do, nobody would need you to drag guns. Or if I were like my captain--he sees things in his mind before the shooting, and trembles, but knows too much to flee--then I could haul them myself. With that much wisdom, however, I wouldn't stay here. I'd be a forest king again, sleeping half the day, bathing whenever I chose. It has been a whole month since I last had a really good bath.”
“Very fine,” Billy remarked, “but giving something an elaborate name does nothing to improve it.”
“Hush!” the horse said. “I think I grasp what Two Tails is trying to explain.”
“You will understand a good deal better in another minute,” Two Tails snapped. “Tell me exactly why you dislike this!”
He unleashed furious trumpeting at the very top of his voice.
“Stop it!” mule and horse cried together. Their hooves stamped and their bodies trembled. Elephant trumpeting is unpleasant enough at any time, particularly on a dark night.

“I won't,” said Two Tails. “Please explain your reaction. Hhrrmph! Rrrt! Rrrmph! Rrrhha!” He suddenly fell silent. A small whimper told me Vixen had finally found me. She knew, as I did, that above almost anything else, elephants fear little barking dogs. So she stopped beside him at his stakes to bully him, running and yapping around the great feet that were so much bigger than her whole body. The great elephant shuffled his feet and began squeaking in distress, trying to get away from her while still fastened to his stakes. “Away, little dog! Stop sniffing my ankles or I'll kick. Good dog--nice little doggie! Go home, you noisy little beast! Why won't someone remove her? She'll bite me any moment.”
“It seems to me that our friend is frightened of practically everything,” Billy told the horse. “If I had a meal for each dog I've kicked across the parade-ground, I'd be nearly as fat as Two Tails.”

I whistled. Vixen came running, coated in mud, licked my nose, and described her long search through the camp. I never let her know that I could understand what animals said, because she would certainly have taken all sorts of liberties if she had discovered that. Buttoning her inside my overcoat, I listened to Two Tails shuffle, stamp, and grumble.
“Extraordinary! Quite extraordinary!” he muttered. “It's hereditary in our family. Where has that nasty little animal gone?”
I heard his trunk searching about in the darkness.
“We all seem vulnerable to different things,” he continued, blowing his nose. “You gentlemen appeared frightened when I trumpeted.”
“Not precisely frightened,” the horse corrected him. “More like having hornets where my saddle belongs. Please don't repeat it.”
“I myself am frightened by a little dog; bad nighttime dreams frighten our friend the camel.”
“Fortunate for us, then, that we're not all required to fight alike,” the horse observed.
“What I'd like to understand,” said the young mule, who had remained quiet for a long time, “is why any of us must fight at all.”
“We fight because we're told to,” the horse answered with a scornful snort.
“Orders,” Billy said, snapping his teeth together.
“Hukm hai!” (It's an order!), the camel gurgled. Two Tails and the bullocks echoed, “Hukm hai!”
“But who issues these orders?” the young recruit asked.
“The man leading you--Or riding you--Or holding your nose rope--Or twisting your tail,” replied Billy, the horse, the camel, and the bullocks speaking one after another in that order.
“And who gives those men their orders?”
“That's asking too much, youngster,” Billy replied. “Questions like that earn kicks. All you have to do is obey the man who stands at your head and gives you your orders, and ask him no questions.”

“Correct,” Two Tails agreed. “I don't always manage obedience, being caught halfway between. But Billy's right: obey whoever stands beside you giving commands. Otherwise you halt the entire battery and earn a beating besides.”

The bullocks rose. “Dawn is approaching. We'll return to our lines. Certainly we see only through our eyes and aren't especially clever. But even so, out of everybody who has been talking here tonight, we are the only ones who have never been frightened of anything. Goodnight, brave people.”
Nobody replied. Changing the subject, the horse asked, “Where's that small dog? A dog means there's a man nearby.”
“Here I am,” Vixen barked. “Under this gun's tail with my man. You great clumsy camel, you knocked down our tent. He's very angry with you.”
“Phew!” the bullocks exclaimed. “He must be a white man!”
“Naturally,” Vixen replied. “Surely you don't imagine a black bullock-driver looks after me?”
“Huah! Ouach! Ugh!” the bullocks gasped. “We must leave at once.”
They lunged through the mud and somehow caught their yoke against an ammunition wagon’s pole, where it stuck fast.
“Well done,” Billy remarked calmly. “No struggling now. You're trapped until daylight. What's troubling you, anyway?”
Long, hissing snorts burst from the bullocks, the noise Indian cattle make. They shoved, crowded, twisted, stamped, and slipped, nearly collapsing in the mud as they grunted angrily.
“You'll break your necks,” the horse warned. “What's wrong with white men? I live among them.”
“They--eat--us! Pull!” cried the nearer bullock. With a twang their yoke broke, and both lumbered away together.
Until then I hadn't understood Indian cattle’s fear of Englishmen. We eat beef, which no cattle-driver touches. Naturally the cattle object to that.
“Flog me with my own pad-chains!” Billy exclaimed. “Who expected those two huge lumps to lose their heads?”
“Never mind them. I'll inspect this man,” the horse said. “Most white men keep something interesting in their pockets.”

“Then I'll leave. I'm not especially fond of them either. Besides, a white man without a bed is probably a thief, and my back carries plenty of Government property. Come, youngster; back to our lines. Goodnight, Australia! Presumably we'll meet on tomorrow's parade. Goodnight, old Hay-bale!--keep your feelings under control, won't you? Goodnight, Two Tails! If you pass us tomorrow, don't trumpet. It ruins our formation.”

Billy the mule stumped away with the swaggering, slightly limping walk of an old campaigner. The horse nuzzled my chest, and I fed him biscuits. Vixen, a terribly conceited little dog, meanwhile invented stories about the dozens of horses she and I owned.
“Tomorrow I'll attend the parade in my dog-cart,” she announced. “Where shall I find you?”
“Left of the second squadron. I set the pace for my troop, little lady,” he answered politely. “Now I must find Dick. My tail is muddy; preparing me for parade will cost him two hours' hard work.”

That afternoon all thirty thousand men paraded. Vixen and I had excellent places near the Viceroy and Afghanistan’s Amir, whose tall black astrakhan hat bore a great diamond star. During the first part of the review the sun shone brightly, and we could see the troops passing clearly from the excellent place where we sat. Regiment after regiment passed, legs moving together, guns perfectly aligned, until we grew dizzy watching. Then cavalry cantered beautifully to “Bonnie Dundee.” Vixen pricked an ear from the dog-cart. The Lancers' second squadron swept by. There was our horse, tail like spun silk, head tucked toward his chest, one ear forward, one back. His legs moved like waltz music, setting his squadron's rhythm. After the cavalry, the great heavy guns began to come past our place in the parade. Two Tails and two fellow elephants pulled a forty-pounder siege gun in line, with twenty yoke of oxen behind. Pair number seven wore a new yoke and looked stiff and tired. Last came the screw-guns. Billy carried himself as if commanding the entire army, his oiled and polished harness sparkling. All by myself I gave a cheer for Billy the mule as he passed us. But he never turned his head, never looked to the right or to the left, and went on with his battery.

Rain returned, briefly hiding the troops in mist. They had formed a broad semicircle across the plain and were opening into a line. As we watched, that line stretched farther and farther across the plain. It kept growing until the distance from one wing to the other was three-quarters of a mile: an unbroken wall of men, horses, and guns. Straight toward the Viceroy and Amir it advanced. As it approached, the earth trembled like a steamer’s deck beneath fast-running engines.

Unless you've witnessed it, you cannot imagine how frightening that steady advance looks, even knowing it's merely a review. I watched the Amir. Until that moment he had not shown the slightest trace of surprise, or indeed any other feeling, however closely I watched his face. Now his eyes widened. He gathered the reins from his horse's neck and glanced behind him. For a moment I thought he might draw his sword and cut an escape through the English ladies and gentlemen in the carriages behind. Then, suddenly, the whole advancing line stopped dead where it stood. Not another pace came toward us, and the movement that had seemed so threatening was over. The ground stopped shaking, the entire line saluted, and thirty bands played together. The review ended. Regiments returned to camp through rain, while an infantry band began:

The animals went in two by two,
Hurrah!
The animals went in two by two,
The elephant and the battery mul’,
and they all got into the Ark
To get themselves out of the rain!
I then heard an elderly Central Asian chief, gray-haired and long-haired, who accompanied the Amir, questioning a native officer.
“Tell me,” he asked, “how was this astonishing thing accomplished?”
The officer replied, “They received an order and carried it out.”
“Are the animals as wise as the men?” asked the chief.

“They obey just as men obey. Mule, horse, elephant, bullock--each follows its driver. The driver follows his sergeant, the sergeant his lieutenant, the lieutenant his captain, the captain his major, the major his colonel. The colonel obeys his brigadier, commander of three regiments; the brigadier obeys the general; the general obeys the Viceroy, who serves the Empress. That is how.”
“If only Afghanistan were like that!” the chief exclaimed. “At home we follow only our own wishes.”
“Which is why,” the officer said, twisting his mustache, “the Amir you refuse to obey must come here for orders from our Viceroy.”
Parade Song of the Camp Animals
ELEPHANTS OF THE GUN TEAMS

We lent to Alexander the strength of Hercules,
The wisdom of our foreheads, the cunning of our knees;
We bowed our necks to service: never freed again,--
Make way there--way for the ten-foot teams
Of the Forty-Pounder train!
GUN BULLOCKS

Those heroes in their harnesses avoid a cannon-ball,
And what they know of gunpowder upsets them one and all;
Then we come into action and tug the guns again--
Make way there--way for the twenty yoke
Of the Forty-Pounder train!
CAVALRY HORSES

By the brand on my shoulder, the finest of tunes
Is played by the Lancers, Hussars, and Dragoons,
And it’s sweeter than “Stables” or “Water” to me--
The Cavalry Canter of “Bonnie Dundee”!

Then feed us and train us and handle and groom,
And give us good riders and plenty of room,
And launch us in columns of squadrons and see
The way of the war-horse to “Bonnie Dundee”!
SCREW-GUN MULES

As me and my companions were scrambling up a hill,
The path was lost in rolling stones, but we went forward still;
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
spare!

Good luck to every sergeant, then, who lets us pick our road;
Bad luck to all the driver-men who cannot pack a load:
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
spare!
COMMISSARIAT CAMELS

We haven’t a camelty tune of our own
To help us lumber along,
But every neck is a hair trombone
(_Rtt-ta-ta-ta!_ is a hair trombone!)
And this our marching-song:
_Can’t! Don’t! Shan’t! Won’t!_
Pass it along the line!
Somebody’s pack has slid from his back,
Wish it were only mine!
Somebody’s load has tipped off in the road--
Cheer for a halt and a row!
_Urrr! Yarrh! Grr! Arrh!_
Somebody’s catching it now!
ALL THE BEASTS TOGETHER

Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load.
See our line across the plain,
Like a heel-rope bent again,
Reaching, writhing, rolling far,
Sweeping all away to war!
While the men who walk beside,
Dusty, silent, heavy-eyed,
Cannot tell why we or they
March and suffer day by day.
_Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load!_
